**Claim 18. Bell upper-partial table and its (m,n) labels follow Hibberts' rim-partial data** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/bell_modes.h:53-60, 68-76`)

- Hibbert et al., 'Partial Frequencies and Chladni's Law in Church Bells', Open Journal of Acoustics 4 (2014), Tables 1, 5, 6. *paper*, <https://file.scirp.org/pdf/OJA_2014060315140205.pdf>. Establishes: RIR partials are indexed m = 2 (hum), 3 (tierce), 4 (nominal), 5 (superquint), 6 (octave nominal), 7..11, all with n = 1 except the hum. The 2752-bell average in cents relative to the nominal is m5 677.0, m6 1216.3, m7 1658.0, m8 2028.8, m9 2345.9, m10 2621.1, m11 2874.2. Chladni fit f = C(m+bn)^p with average b = -0.419, p = 1.620.
- Strike tone (Wikipedia), table citing Fletcher & Rossing 2008. *docs*, <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_tone>. Establishes: Deciem (4,1#) 2.5/2.514, undeciem (2,2) 2.667/2.662, twelfth (5,1) 3.0/3.011, upper octave (6,1) 4.0/4.166, (7,1) 5.333/5.433, (8,1) 6.667/6.796, (9,1) 8.0/8.215 (ideal/actual, relative to the prime).

**Claim 19. Bell Strike Position = strike azimuth, weighted by |cos(m*theta)|** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/bell_modes.h:22-40, 78-102`)

- S. Cha, J. Buschert, D. King, 'Pseudo-Degeneracy in Handbell Modes', arXiv:1004.0491 (2010). *paper*, <https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.0491>. Establishes: 'These two modes would be identical in frequency and truly degenerate if the bell were perfectly symmetrical about its axis.' In the pseudo-degenerate case 'the amplitude is nearly constant as the bell rotates'. Only split pairs come and go with the drive point. (arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed.)
- Perrin, Charnley & DePont, 'Normal modes of the modern English church bell', J. Sound Vib. 90(1) (1983). *paper*, <https://www.hibberts.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/perrin_charnley_depont_1982.pdf>. Establishes: Bell modes with m > 0 occur in degenerate pairs (singlets only for m = 0). This is from the search summary; the PDF is a scanned image and I could not read it.
- Hibberts, 'Identifying bell partials' (after Perrin et al.). *docs*, <https://www.hibberts.co.uk/identifying-bell-partials/>. Establishes: Nodal circle heights, as a fraction from lip to shoulder: prime 0.30, tierce 0.54, quint 0.19, nominal 0.54, so strike height re-weights the partials.
- Hibberts, 'Doublets or warble in bells'. *docs*, <https://www.hibberts.co.uk/doublets-or-warble-in-bells/>. Establishes: Doublets arise only when a bell is 'not symmetrical about its vertical axis'; clapper placement matters for reducing doublets in a non-round bell.

**Claim 20. Secondary shell fundamental = head f0 x (1 - 0.75*secondarySize), default 0.625x, cited as a 'Chromaphone rule of thumb'** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:1418-1444 (rule at 1421-1426)`)

- T.D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of drums', Physics Today 45(3) 40-47 (1992). *paper*, <https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf>. Establishes: Snare: lowest (0,1) mode at 183 Hz (complete drum). Shell modes: bare (4,0) 415, (4,1) 611, (5,0) 658, (5,1) 835 Hz; complete drum, shell-dominated: (4,0) 874, (5,0) 1064 Hz.
- AAS Chromaphone 3 user manual, Coupling (as opened by the 2026-06 audit). *docs*, <https://www.applied-acoustics.com/chromaphone-3/manual/>. Establishes: States no 0.6 head/shell ratio; describes coupled resonators often tuned to the SAME fundamental.

**Claim 21. String damping loop filter is the Jaffe-Smith / EKS one-zero form rho*[(1-S)+S z^-1], with rho = 0.001^(1/(f0*T60)), S = brightness/2, and a 1 - z^-M pick-position comb** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/waveguide_string.h:184, 212-214, 431-448, 596-601`)

- J.O. Smith, 'One-Zero String Damping Filter', Faust strings (CCRMA REALSIMPLE). *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/realsimple/faust_strings/One_Zero_String_Damping_Filter.html>. Establishes: H_d(z) = rho[(1-S) + S z^-1]. rho = (0.001)^(PT/t60), in Faust pow(0.001, 1/(freq*t60)). Brightness B maps to b1 = 0.5B, b0 = 1 - b1. Decay is fastest at S = 1/2, and higher frequencies decay faster for 0 < S < 1.
- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Extended Karplus-Strong Algorithm'. *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Extended_Karplus_Strong_Algorithm.html>. Establishes: EKS pick-position comb H_beta(z) = 1 - z^-floor(beta*N + 1/2). The damping filter must satisfy |H_d| <= 1. The string-tuning allpass is H_eta(z) = -(eta - z^-1)/(1 - eta z^-1).

**Claim 22. Linear interpolation inside the loop gives exact fractional delay and keeps the loop gain flat (the code comment's claim)** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/waveguide_string.h:6, 186-191`)

- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Delay-Line Interpolation'. *textbook*, <https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/pasp/Delay_Line_Interpolation.html>. Establishes: Linear interpolation is attenuated near half the sampling rate and is 'nowhere flat within the passband'. Amplitude errors 'can be highly audible (particularly when the loop gain is close to 1)' in feedback loops such as string models. First-order allpass interpolation 'costs the same as linear interpolation' and 'has no gain distortion'.
- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Fractional Delay Filtering by Linear Interpolation'. *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Fractional_Delay_Filtering_Linear.html>. Establishes: Linear interpolation is a one-zero FIR filter and is accurate only at low frequencies. Amplitude-response errors are highly audible in feedback loops, and allpass interpolation is suggested to remove them.
- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Extended Karplus-Strong Algorithm'. *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Extended_Karplus_Strong_Algorithm.html>. Establishes: EKS tunes with a first-order string-tuning allpass H_eta(z) = -(eta - z^-1)/(1 - eta z^-1), with eta in [-1/11, 2/3] for delays of 0.2..1.2 samples, offset to [eps, 1+eps).

**Claim 23. High-frequency decay (brightness) mapping: a fixed S per Material, applied once per period** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/string_mapper.h:43-58 (and waveguide_string.h:184, 212-214)`)

- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Loop Filter Identification' / EDR-based loop-filter design. *textbook*, <https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/pasp/Loop_Filter_Identification.html>. Establishes: The desired loop-filter gain at each harmonic comes from the measured decay rate of the nearest partial. The EDR obeys E_{m+1}(w_k) = |H_l(w_k)|^2 E_m(w_k) once per period, so a partial's decay slope is proportional to log|H_l| at that frequency, which is normalised frequency, not Hz.
- J.O. Smith, 'One-Zero String Damping Filter' (CCRMA REALSIMPLE). *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/realsimple/faust_strings/One_Zero_String_Damping_Filter.html>. Establishes: The filter is applied once per period P. rho is tied to PT and t60. S sets the relative decay of high versus low frequencies, so a fixed S gives an HF decay in seconds that scales with f0 and with fs.
- Chaigne & Askenfelt, 'Numerical simulations of piano strings I', JASA 95(2), 1994. *paper*, no URL. Establishes: String damping terms give a per-mode decay rate sigma = b1 + b3*omega^2, defined in physical frequency, independent of any sampling grid. (Opened and cited by the 2026-06 audit, findings.json research array.)

**Claim 24. The pitch envelope retunes the String waveguide (audit H-3 fix)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/body_bank.h:121-130 (with drum_voice.h:1587-1593, 313-321; waveguide_string.h:134-140, 175-183)`)

- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Extended Karplus-Strong Algorithm'. *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Extended_Karplus_Strong_Algorithm.html>. Establishes: Pitch is set by the delay-line length N plus the string-tuning allpass fractional delay. The damping filter |H_d| <= 1 sets decay, not pitch.
- J.O. Smith, 'One-Zero String Damping Filter' (CCRMA REALSIMPLE). *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/realsimple/faust_strings/One_Zero_String_Damping_Filter.html>. Establishes: rho = 0.001^(PT/t60) is tied to the actual loop period P. Using a frequency other than the actual one gives the wrong decay, which is what the measured 6x T60 shortening shows.

**Claim 25. Tuning compensation for the loop filters' phase delay (fundamental lands on the mapped f0)** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/waveguide_string.h:321-341 (and 515-544, 199-201)`)

- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Extended Karplus-Strong Algorithm'. *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Extended_Karplus_Strong_Algorithm.html>. Establishes: The total loop delay (delay line, damping filter, stiffness allpass and tuning allpass) sets the pitch. The tuning allpass supplies the fractional remainder after the other filters' phase delays.
- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Fractional Delay Filtering by Linear Interpolation'. *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Fractional_Delay_Filtering_Linear.html>. Establishes: Linear interpolation's delay is exact only at DC. The frequency-dependent delay error is what the empirical 0.55 / 0.96 factors try to absorb.

**Claim 26. The String body models a struck string: the exciter's strike excites the waveguide at the Strike Position** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/string_body.h:43-67 (waveguide_string.h:154-234, 407-463)`)

- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'The Ideal Struck String'. *textbook*, <https://www.dsprelated.com/freebooks/pasp/Ideal_Struck_String.html>. Establishes: A struck string starts with zero initial displacement and a nonzero initial velocity distribution. The hammer drives an interior point, which is equivalent to driving two string endpoints in series, so a wavefront emanates in both directions from the strike point.
- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Extended Karplus-Strong Algorithm'. *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Extended_Karplus_Strong_Algorithm.html>. Establishes: The pick-position comb 1 - z^-(beta N) models where the string is excited. It is part of the excitation path, so it must act on whatever excites the string.

**Claim 27. The waveguide string is a linear system (the loop's only nonlinearity is a safety soft clip)** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/waveguide_string.h:196-197, 588-593, 450-463`)

- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Extended Karplus-Strong Algorithm'. *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Extended_Karplus_Strong_Algorithm.html>. Establishes: The EKS loop consists only of linear filters (damping H_d with |H_d| <= 1, stiffness allpass, tuning allpass). No waveshaper is part of the string model.
- Avanzini, Marogna & Bank, 'Efficient synthesis of tension modulation in strings and membranes based on energy estimation', JASA 131(1), 2012. *paper*, no URL. Establishes: The physically relevant string nonlinearity is tension modulation (pitch rises with energy), not amplitude clipping. (Cited and opened by the 2026-06 audit, findings.json research array.)

**Claim 28. String stiffness dispersion (inharmonicity f_n = n f0 sqrt(1+B n^2)) via an Abel-Valimaki-Smith allpass cascade** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/waveguide_string.h:271-275, 308-315, 741-826`)

- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Dispersion Filter Design'. *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/%7Ejos/pasp/Dispersion_Filter_Design.html>. Establishes: Stiff-string dispersion is modelled by allpass filters in the waveguide loop. It cites a dynamically tunable method based on Thiran's closed-form allpass formulas (Rauhala-Valimaki) and an improved closed-form method (Abel-Valimaki-Smith) based on robust high-order allpass design.
- Rauhala & Valimaki, 'Dispersion Modeling in Waveguide Piano Synthesis Using Tunable Allpass Filters', DAFx-2006. *paper*, <https://dafx.de/paper-archive/details/n4Qv1ScD_VbmqShsq0ZVQQ>. Establishes: A tunable closed-form dispersion design is applied to a cascade of first-order allpass filters, extended to any number of sections, inside a waveguide piano model. This is the family the coded design belongs to.
- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (stiff strings). *textbook*, no URL. Establishes: f_n = n f1 sqrt(1 + B n^2), with B proportional to E*I/(T L^2). (Cited by the 2026-06 audit's stiff-string research entry.)

**Claim 29. NoiseBody partial ratios follow the measured-cymbal Chladni law f = C (m+2n)^P with P = 1.7** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/plate_modes.h:26-36, 70-101 (table); used at noise_body_mapper.h:95,105-113`)

- Fletcher, N.H. & Rossing, T.D., The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer 1998, Ch. 20.2 'Modes of Vibration of Cymbals', Table 20.1, Figs. 20.2-20.4; Sec. 3.6. *textbook*, <https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf>. Establishes: Cymbal modes fit f = c(m+2n)^p. Table 20.1 (Rossing 1982) gives n=0 fits of p1 = 1.65-1.86 (c1 7.7-15.9 Hz) and p2 = 1.43-1.56 with a slope break at m_c = 3.6-6. A 35-cm (14-in) thick cymbal fits a single line with p = 1.47, and small cymbals give p = 1.61 and 1.58. 'In flat plates, p = 2, but in nonflat plates (cymbals, bells, etc.), p is generally less than 2.'
- Wilbur, C. & Rossing, T.D., 'Vibrational modes of cymbals and Chladni's law', ASA 132nd meeting abstract 5pMU8, 1996. *paper*, <https://www.auditory.org/asamtgs/asa96haw/5pMU/5pMU8.html>. Establishes: About 300 modes were observed in a 16-in. cymbal. They fit a modified Chladni law f = C_n (m+2n)^P_n (one exponent per n family) or the three-parameter form C (m+bn)^P (Perrin et al. 1985).
- Chladni's law, Wikipedia (citing Fletcher & Rossing 1998 p.680). *docs*, <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chladni%27s_law>. Establishes: For cymbals, handbells and church bells, p can vary from 1.4 to 2.4.
- Chaigne, A., Touze, C., Thomas, O., 'Nonlinear vibrations and chaos in gongs and cymbals', Acoust. Sci. & Tech. 26(5) 403-409, 2005. *paper*, <https://perso.ensta.fr/~touze/PDF/ChaosGong.pdf>. Establishes: FE analysis of cymbals and spherical caps shows that eigenfrequencies are highly sensitive to small changes of curvature and that mode shapes are strongly influenced by slope discontinuities.

**Claim 30. NoiseBody's 64-mode cloud is dense enough to fuse into a cymbal wash** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/noise_body_mapper.h:58-63, 73, 95-106; modal_resonator_bank.h:783-819`)

- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., 1998, Sec. 20.2-20.3, Table 20.1, Fig. 20.2. *textbook*, <https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf>. Establishes: 38-cm cymbal: the first 15 resonances (Fig. 20.2) include modes at 164 and 244 Hz. Above the first six, modes mix into combination modes. n=0 fit constants are c1 = 7.7-20.6 Hz. 'The coupling between vibrational modes in a cymbal is strong, so that a large number of partials quickly appear in the spectrum, however it is excited.'
- Wilbur, C. & Rossing, T.D., 'Vibrational modes of cymbals and Chladni's law', ASA 1996 abstract 5pMU8. *paper*, <https://www.auditory.org/asamtgs/asa96haw/5pMU/5pMU8.html>. Establishes: Some 300 modes were observed in a 16-in.-diameter cymbal.
- Werner, K.J., Abel, J.S., Smith, J.O., 'The TR-808 Cymbal: a Physically-Informed, Circuit-Bendable, Digital Model', Proc. ICMC|SMC 2014, pp. 1453-1460. *paper*, <https://speech.di.uoa.gr/ICMC-SMC-2014/images/VOL_2/1453.pdf>. Establishes: The cymbal/hat source is six rectangular oscillators at 205.3, 369.6, 304.4, 522.7, 359.4-1149.9 (trimmed to 800) and 254.3-627.2 (trimmed to 540) Hz. Their summed odd harmonics form 'tightly-packed, inharmonically-related partials by design', i.e. density, not a sparse ladder, is the load-bearing feature.

**Claim 31. Mode Stretch at its documented 'physical' default (1.0) leaves the Chladni ratios unstretched** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/noise_body_mapper.h:118-120 (same pattern plate_mapper.h:60-62, shell_mapper.h:61, bell_mapper.h:56); modal_resonator_bank.h:783,806-807; pad_config_apply.h:123-126; pad_config.h:212`)

- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., 1998, Sec. 3.6 (circular plates) and 20.2. *textbook*, <https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf>. Establishes: Plate modal frequencies are f_mn = c(m+2n)^p (p = 2 for flat plates, p < 2 for cymbals). The stiffness dispersion of a plate is expressed by this law, not by a string's sqrt(1+B n^2) on a sorted mode index.
- 2026-06 signal-path audit research entry on Stretch (Russell PSU; F&R; Young 1952), plugins/membrum/AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md section 3-B. *docs*, no URL. Establishes: Prescribed widening B_max 0.001 -> 0.01 for STRING-like inharmonicity; it did not consider that the plate/noise mappers feed a non-zero stretch at the default.

**Claim 32. The internal noise layer (white noise through a bandpass at 1.5-6.5 kHz, Q 0.6-1.0, 18-180 ms decay) is the hat / cymbal sizzle band** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/noise_body_mapper.h:152-182; noise_body.h:43-49,73-78; noise_layer.h:47-49,100-115; drum_voice.h:137-147`)

- Werner, K.J., Abel, J.S., Smith, J.O., 'The TR-808 Cymbal: a Physically-Informed, Circuit-Bendable, Digital Model', Proc. ICMC|SMC 2014, Athens, pp. 1453-1460. *paper*, <https://speech.di.uoa.gr/ICMC-SMC-2014/images/VOL_2/1453.pdf>. Establishes: Cowbell, Cymbal, Open and Closed Hihat circuits filter and envelope the same six Schmitt-trigger oscillators. Band pass #1 is centred around 3440 Hz and #2 around 7100 Hz, accentuating upper overtones and de-emphasising fundamentals. A high-pass stage resonates at its corner around 10500 Hz.
- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., 1998, Sec. 20.3 'Transient Behavior', Fig. 20.6. *textbook*, <https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf>. Establishes: The sound level in 2-10 kHz builds up by 10 dB or more during the first 50 ms. The 3-5 kHz range peaks 50-100 ms after striking and 'gives the cymbal its shimmer', often the most prominent feature 1-4 s after the strike.

**Claim 33. A linear modal bank plus enveloped noise reproduces a struck cymbal's time evolution** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/noise_body_mapper.h:122-129,149-150,164-176; drum_voice.h:347-371; default_kit.h:235-250`)

- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., 1998, Sec. 20.3 'Transient Behavior', Figs. 20.5-20.6 (data Rossing & Shepherd 1983). *textbook*, <https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf>. Establishes: (1) Below about 700 Hz the level decreases rapidly during the first 200 ms, 'apparently caused by the conversion of energy into modes of higher frequency'. (2) 700-1000 Hz peaks build up between 10 and 20 ms. (3) 3-5 kHz peaks about 50-100 ms after striking. (4) 3-5 kHz is the most prominent feature 1-4 s after striking. (5) Low frequencies dominate the lingering sound, at a much lower level. Octave-band decay depends on the stroke type (crash, ride, soft).
- Chaigne, A., Touze, C., Thomas, O., 'Nonlinear vibrations and chaos in gongs and cymbals', Acoust. Sci. & Tech. 26(5) 403-409, 2005. *paper*, <https://perso.ensta.fr/~touze/PDF/ChaosGong.pdf>. Establishes: In normal use the vibratory displacement is of the order of the thickness, so nonlinearity is essential. Energy transfer between modes follows from quadratic nonlinearity due to curvature. The chaotic regime 'sounds similar to real instruments normally excited by the strong impact of a mallet'. On thin cymbals, energy transfer and mode coupling appear before pitch glide. Reduced models need only 5 to 10 strongly coupled oscillators.
- Rossing, T.D. & Fletcher, N.H., 'Nonlinear vibrations in plates and gongs', J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 73(1) 345-351, 1983. *paper*, <https://www.phys.unsw.edu.au/music/people/publications/Rossingetal1983.pdf>. Establishes: Flat plates show hardening and most curved plates softening nonlinearity. For a flat plate the frequency rises about 16 % when the amplitude equals the thickness, and 35 % at twice the thickness.
- Touze, C., Ducceschi, M., Bilbao, S., 'Nonlinear plate vibrations: a modal approach with application to cymbals and gongs', Acoustics 2012 Nantes (SFA/IOA). *paper*, <https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/nonlinear-plate-vibrations-a-modal-approach-with-application-to-c/>. Establishes: A von Karman plate projected on its linear modes gives nonlinear coupling coefficients expressed through the linear eigenfunctions. These explain the complex free-oscillation dynamics, a tractable modal route to cymbal and gong synthesis.

**Claim 34. Per-mode decay rate is b1 + b3*f^2 (s^-1), and each mode's pole radius is exp(-rate/fs)** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/modal_resonator_bank.h:10, 106-139, 763-768, 821-824, 938-939, 959-960`)

- Chaigne A., Askenfelt A., Numerical simulations of piano strings. I. A physical model for a struck string using finite difference methods, JASA 95(2), 1994. *paper*, <https://www.math.kent.edu/~zheng/62262/piano_wave.pdf>. Establishes: Eq. (3): alpha = 1/tau = b1 + b3*omega^2, from the -2b1 dy/dt + 2b3 d3y/dt dx2 terms of Eq. (1). b1 and b3 are fitted to measured data. The simplified formula is 'only a fair approximation of the reality', and damping laws that are even-order polynomials in frequency are stable and causal.
- Sterling A., Lin M.C., Interactive Modal Sound Synthesis Using Generalized Proportional Damping, ACM I3D 2016. *paper*, <https://gamma.cs.unc.edu/gpdsynth/data/gpdsynth.pdf>. Establishes: Rayleigh damping C = a1 M + a2 K diagonalises to c_i = a1 + a2*omega_i^2 (Eq. 12), with amplitude decay rate d = c/2. It is the de-facto modal-synthesis damping model, but only a first-order approximation chosen for ease of computation, accurate only while the true damping curve stays approximately linear in that variable.

**Claim 35. Documented b1/b3 override ranges and the 'neutral' 0.5 default disagree with the coded denormalisation** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/pad_config.h:274-283 (also controller/controller.cpp:221-228, dsp/bodies/membrane_mapper.h:56-80, dsp/default_kit.h:241-243, dsp/drum_voice.h:447-449)`)

- Chaigne A., Askenfelt A., JASA 95(2), 1994, Part I. *paper*, <https://www.math.kent.edu/~zheng/62262/piano_wave.pdf>. Establishes: Eq. (3) states the law in omega (rad/s). A b3 given per rad^2 (as pad_config.h:279 does) is therefore a different quantity from the coded Hz-convention b3, which is larger by a factor of 4*pi^2.

**Claim 36. 'Metallic' = frequency-independent damping (b3 -> 0) contradicts the linear-in-frequency internal-friction law for metals; the linear term is missing** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/membrane_mapper.h:64-80 (with plate_mapper.h:56, shell_mapper.h:58, bell_mapper.h:53, noise_body_mapper.h:116; modal_resonator_bank.h:133-139; MANUAL.md:204)`)

- Klatzky R.L., Pai D.K., Krotkov E.P., Perception of Material from Contact Sounds, Presence 9(4):399-410, 2000. *paper*, <https://www.cs.ubc.ca/labs/lci/papers/docs2000/pai-KlaPai00.pdf>. Establishes: Each mode decays as exp(-b(f) t). Wildes & Richards, following Zener on metals and crystalline solids, propose b(f) linear in f: b(f) = pi*tan(phi)*f, so te = 1/(pi f tan phi) (Eq. 1). Chaigne & Doutaut (1997) viscoelastic dissipation adds a quadratic term. A constant term (fluid damping) 'is usually small'. Measured data (Gaver; Chaigne & Doutaut) fit the linear model very well except at the highest frequencies.
- Sterling A., Lin M.C., I3D 2016. *paper*, <https://gamma.cs.unc.edu/gpdsynth/data/gpdsynth.pdf>. Establishes: The Rayleigh (a1 + a2*omega^2) model is accurate only while the true damping curve stays near that shape. A power-law damping model fits recorded objects better, and the paper reports listener preferences per object (metal plate, plastic and others).

**Claim 37. Membrane per-mode damping is monotone in f^2, but drum-head damping is radiation-dominated and depends on mode order: (0,1) decays FASTEST** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/membrane_mapper.h:93-109 (air-loading frequency shift), 146-152 and 177 (damping), membrane_modes.h kMembraneBesselOrder`)

- Packer T.A., Acoustics of the orchestral kettledrum, MSc thesis, Durham University, 1993 (Table 6.1 reproduces Christian, Davis, Tubis, Anderson, Mills, Rossing, JASA 76(5), 1984). *thesis*, <https://etheses.durham.ac.uk/id/eprint/5633/1/5633_3049.PDF>. Establishes: With the kettle as a baffle, the (0,1) mode acts as a monopole and 'will lose its energy quickly'. The (1,1) to (4,1) modes decay much more slowly. Table 6.1 (tension 5360 N/m, 64 cm drum): T60 (0,1) 0.06 s, (1,1) 0.8, (2,1) 1.8, (3,1) 4.6, (4,1) 10.5, (5,1) 16.2, (0,2) 0.2, (0,3) 0.1. In the unbaffled bass drum the (0,1) mode is present 'in no small degree'.
- Chaigne A., Askenfelt A., JASA 95(2), 1994. *paper*, <https://www.math.kent.edu/~zheng/62262/piano_wave.pdf>. Establishes: b1 + b3*omega^2 is derived for, and fitted to, a string, and is 'only a fair approximation' even there.

**Claim 38. Coded T60 ranges: drum-head values are plausible, but the 'woody' end of Material and the default-kit 'wood-block' Perc pad decay like glass or steel** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/plate_mapper.h:56, 65-73 (also membrane_mapper.h:148-152, default_kit.h:274-294 and 409-439, MANUAL.md:204)`)

- Klatzky R.L., Pai D.K., Krotkov E.P., Perception of Material from Contact Sounds, Presence 9(4), 2000. *paper*, <https://www.cs.ubc.ca/labs/lci/papers/docs2000/pai-KlaPai00.pdf>. Establishes: tau_d = 1/(pi tan phi) and te = tau_d/f (Eqs. 1-2). Stimuli used tau_d of about 3, 9, 30, 95 and 300. The critical log10 tau_d for a 50 % material label was 0.46 / 0.50 / 2.10 / 2.65 for rubber / wood / glass / steel, matching the ordering of physical te in Wildes & Richards. Decay mattered more than frequency in similarity judgments.

**Claim 39. Note-off 'release through the body's own damping law' is a per-sample radius multiply: sample-rate dependent, and undone by the next per-chunk retune** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:57-64, 442-452, 589, 605-609, 722-770, 1607-1626 (with modal_resonator_bank.h:501-516, 865-911)`)

- Chaigne A., Askenfelt A., JASA 95(2), 1994. *paper*, <https://www.math.kent.edu/~zheng/62262/piano_wave.pdf>. Establishes: Decay is a continuous-time rate (alpha = b1 + b3*omega^2, s^-1). A per-sample factor exp(-alpha/fs) is the sample-rate-invariant discretisation, while a fixed per-sample multiplier such as 0.997 corresponds to a rate proportional to fs.

**Claim 40. Secondary shell bank damping: b3 rises with secondaryMaterial (inverse of the primary bodies) and b1 ignores the body's legacy decay** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:1450-1483 (pad_config.h:302)`)

- Klatzky R.L., Pai D.K., Krotkov E.P., Presence 9(4), 2000. *paper*, <https://www.cs.ubc.ca/labs/lci/papers/docs2000/pai-KlaPai00.pdf>. Establishes: Metal has the smallest internal friction tan(phi), i.e. the slowest frequency-dependent decay, and wood or rubber the largest. Material and high-frequency damping move in opposite directions.

**Claim 41. Every modal strike is normalised to one fixed peak (-6 dBFS at velocity 1), whatever the body's size, material, damping or strike position** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:73-84, 286-306, 1322-1412, 1717-1729`)

- N.H. Fletcher & T.D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer 1998 (ch. 7 sound radiation; ch. 18 drums / timpani). *textbook*, no URL. Establishes: Radiated power = radiation resistance x mean-square surface velocity. Low-frequency radiation resistance of a baffled piston / monopole source rises as (ka)^2 x area, so a bigger membrane radiates its low modes more efficiently. Strike position weights each mode by its mode shape at the strike point. Timpani are struck about 1/4 of the way in from the edge to reduce the (0,1) mode.
- K. van den Doel & D.K. Pai, Synthesis of Shape Dependent Sounds with Physical Modeling, ICAD 1996 (expanded as 'The Sounds of Physical Shapes', Presence 7(4), 1998). *paper*, <https://www.icad.org/websiteV2.0/Conferences/ICAD96/proc96/dendoel.htm>. Establishes: In a modal impact model, frequencies come from geometry and material, decay rates from internal friction, and initial mode amplitudes from the mode shapes at the impact location. No output normalisation is described, so location and shape changes carry through to the sound.
- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Modal Expansion' (CCRMA online book). *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Modal_Expansion.html>. Establishes: Modal synthesis is a parallel sum of 2nd-order sections with per-mode gains G_i, chosen to match measured peak heights or fitted by least squares. No normalisation by mode count or by a measured total peak.

**Claim 42. The noteOn comments cite Faust / STK / Bilbao for a 1/sqrt(N) output norm, but the code now does a per-configuration measured-peak normalisation that none of those references perform** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:230-239, 246-268 (stale comments) vs 286-305 (actual code)`)

- STK (Synthesis ToolKit), src/Modal.cpp, P. Cook & G. Scavone. *docs*, <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thestk/stk/master/src/Modal.cpp>. Establishes: masterGain_ = 1.0 is fixed. setModeGain passes the gain straight to filters_[modeIndex]->setGain(gain). strike() sets envelope_.setTarget(amplitude) and the resonances. There is no division by nModes_ and no peak measurement.
- GRAME Faust libraries, physmodels.lib (modeFilter, modeInterpRes, djembeModel, marimbaBarModel). *docs*, <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/grame-cncm/faustlibraries/master/physmodels.lib>. Establishes: Mode banks end in ':> /(nModes)'. modeFilter gain gi = gain*44100/SR*(1+t)^2/(4*B0), which compensates for sample rate. marimbaBarModel takes per-mode gains from modesGains(int(exPos), i), so strike position changes the gains. The output 'gain' goes into the excitation (strike), not into a measured-peak normaliser.
- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Modal Expansion'. *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Modal_Expansion.html>. Establishes: Per-mode gains G_i are matched to the measured peak height of each mode. There is no global normalisation by mode count or by summed peak.

**Claim 43. An equal strike PEAK is not an equal LOUDNESS: peak normalisation turns low-pitched bodies into the quietest pads** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h:455-480 (with drum_voice.h:84, 1386)`)

- Y. Suzuki & H. Takeshima, 'Equal-loudness-level contours for pure tones', J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 116(2):918-933, 2004, doi:10.1121/1.1763601 (basis of ISO 226:2003). *paper*, <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15376658/>. Establishes: Gives the equal-loudness contours adopted in ISO 226:2003. The ear's sensitivity falls steeply below about 500 Hz; the new contours differ most from Robinson-Dadson below 500 Hz (up to about 14 dB). The PubMed page needs cookies; the abstract and citation were read through the search index.
- ISO 226:2003 Acoustics - Normal equal-loudness-level contours (formula and af / Lu / Tf table). *docs*, no URL. Establishes: Evaluated here for LN = 60 phon: 80 Hz -> 82.1 dB, 100 Hz -> 78.7, 125 -> 75.6, 160 -> 72.5, 200 -> 69.9 dB SPL, a 12.2 dB difference between 80 and 200 Hz at equal loudness.
- N.H. Fletcher & T.D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., 1998. *textbook*, no URL. Establishes: Larger drums radiate their low modes more efficiently (radiation resistance proportional to (ka)^2 x area below ka ~ 1). Physically the bigger drum is the louder one at equal strike force.

**Claim 44. Strike-force (velocity) dependence survives the normalisation; the v^1.6 peak law is steeper than Hertzian contact** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:159-163, 436-437, 1336-1340 (with dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/impact_exciter.h:129, 134-139)`)

- N.H. Fletcher & T.D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., 1998 (Hertzian hammer / mallet contact). *textbook*, no URL. Establishes: Mallet / hammer contact follows a Hertz-type power law F = K x^alpha. With alpha > 1 the peak force grows faster than linearly with impact speed (v^(2 alpha/(alpha+1))), and contact time decreases with speed, so harder strikes are both louder and brighter.
- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Modal Expansion'. *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Modal_Expansion.html>. Establishes: A linear modal bank scales linearly with excitation amplitude, so strike-force dependence has to come from the excitation. That is what Membrum does: the probe is fixed at v=1 and velocity drives the exciter and the envelope.

**Claim 45. The String body is exempt from the strike normalisation and peaks 6 dB above the budget, at full scale** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:79-80, 277-285 (with plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/string_body.h:62-88)`)

- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing (digital waveguide strings; Modal Expansion). *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Modal_Expansion.html>. Establishes: Waveguide and modal models are both linear. Their output level is set by the excitation and one output scale, so the same peak-budget rule can be applied to a waveguide by a fixed gain.

**Claim 46. The probe does not render 'the real excitation': the mallet size hint is applied after the probe, several exciter parameters are missing from the cache key, and random draws differ between probe and note** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:302-304 vs 340; 318-321; 1301-1363; 1400-1406`)

- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Modal Expansion'. *textbook*, <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Modal_Expansion.html>. Establishes: The output of a linear modal bank is the sum of each mode's response to the excitation. A peak measured with a different excitation spectrum, such as a longer contact pulse, does not bound or equal the peak of the actual note.

MB-id column: a bare id is the finding raised from this exact claim (title and file match the finding). An id with `*` is a finding for the same defect at the same code, raised under a differently worded claim. `cf.` names a related finding on the same code whose verdict or scope differs from this claim; this claim did not itself become that finding. `-` means the claim produced no physics finding.

#### Sources for claims 47-92

**Claim 47: Pitch glide is driven by quasistatic tension proportional to vibrational energy, shifting every mode by the same ratio, upward at high energy and relaxing as energy decays** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:86-100, 408-421, 722-754, 1607-1626; dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/modal_resonator_bank.h 482-499`)

- Marogna, Avanzini, Bank, 'Energy based synthesis of tension modulation in membranes', Proc. DAFx-10, Graz, 2010. Type: paper. <https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf>. Establishes: Eq. 9: Tqs proportional to sum of beta_nm^2 A_nm^2 e^{-2t/tau}. Eq. 19: E(t) = (pi T0 / 2R^2) sum of beta^2 A^2 e^{-2t/tau} / \|\|K\|\|^2. Eq. 20: Tqs = Eh / (2R^2 (1-nu^2) T0) \* E. The quasistatic tension 'leads to a proportional shift (continuous decrease) in the modal frequencies, resulting in a pitch glide'. Tom-toms 'exhibit a characteristic glide at medium-high dynamic ranges'.
- J. O. Smith III, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Tension Modulation' (CCRMA online book). Type: textbook. <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Tension_Modulation.html>. Establishes: Higher-amplitude vibration stretches the string, raising its average tension and its fundamental frequency. The fundamental frequency declines over time as the amplitude decays.
- Avanzini, Marogna, Bank, 'Efficient synthesis of tension modulation in strings and membranes based on energy estimation', JASA 131(1):897-906, 2012 (abstract; full text returned 403). Type: paper. <https://air.unimi.it/handle/2434/654153>. Establishes: Gives one formulation for strings and membranes: the short-time average of the tension variation is approximately proportional to the system energy.

**Claim 48: A 20 ms one-pole follower on modal energy reproduces the 'upward jump at the strike that relaxes back' (Avanzini et al.)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:130-133, 422, 703-717, 902-920, 1069-1083`)

- Marogna, Avanzini, Bank, 'Energy based synthesis of tension modulation in membranes', DAFx-10. Type: paper. <https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf>. Establishes: Fig. 1b caption and text: 'The slow initial rise of the quasistatic tension Tqs is the time-domain side effect of lowpass filtering.' Sec. 4.1: the total energy is 'a slowly decaying signal'. The energy-based Tqs 'shows the correct behavior'. Sec. 4.2: Tqs is computed every 32 samples (0.73 ms) with linear interpolation.
- Kirby & Sandler, 'Advanced Fourier decomposition for realistic drum synthesis', Proc. DAFx-20, pp. 155-162. Type: paper. <https://dafx2020.mdw.ac.at/proceedings/papers/DAFx2020_paper_66.pdf>. Establishes: Analysis of 416 tom samples (13 velocities, 32 drums). The initial samples sit at the tension-modulated frequency and the activity shifts to lower frequencies until the unmodulated frequency is reached. The chirp's upper limit is the 'initial tension-modulated frequency'.
- Kirby & Sandler, 'The evolution of drum modes with strike intensity: Analysis and synthesis using the discrete cosine transform', JASA 150(1):202-214, 2021 (abstract via Crossref). Type: paper. <https://doi.org/10.1121/10.0005509>. Establishes: A tom-tom struck at 67 intensities shows a clear velocity-dependent evolution of the pitch glide in its modes.

**Claim 49: The tension glide is refreshed at block rate, independent of the host buffer size** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:589, 699-754, 902-920, 945-972, 1069-1083; voice_pool/voice_pool.cpp 356, 471`)

- Marogna, Avanzini, Bank, 'Energy based synthesis of tension modulation in membranes', DAFx-10. Type: paper. <https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf>. Establishes: 'the membrane energy can be computed at a lower rate, and the continuous energy curve can be obtained by linearly interpolating between the computed points'. Fig. 3c uses a decimation factor of 32 ('Tqs is computed every 32/44.1 = 0.73 ms') and is perceptually similar to the full model.

**Claim 50: kTensionEnergyScale = 3.3e-5 calibrates a sample-rate-independent glide of about 1-2 semitones on a hard tom hit** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:86-94, 420-421; dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/modal_resonator_bank.h 482-499, 835-839, 938-940`)

- Marogna, Avanzini, Bank, 'Energy based synthesis of tension modulation in membranes', DAFx-10. Type: paper. <https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf>. Establishes: Eq. 19-20 define E(t) and Tqs from physical modal amplitudes A_nm and the membrane constants (T0, R, E, h, nu). Nothing in them depends on the discretisation rate.

**Claim 51: Glide depth follows strike strength (energy ~ velocity^2) and the physical membrane parameters** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:408-421, 86-94`)

- Marogna, Avanzini, Bank, 'Energy based synthesis of tension modulation in membranes', DAFx-10. Type: paper. <https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf>. Establishes: Eq. 20: Tqs = Eh / (2R^2 (1-nu^2) T0) \* E(t). The scale depends on Young's modulus, thickness, radius and rest tension. Simulations use impact velocities of 5 m/s and 20 m/s (20 m/s close to the highest dynamic levels, citing Dahl 2004).
- Kirby & Sandler, 'Advanced Fourier decomposition for realistic drum synthesis', DAFx-20. Type: paper. <https://dafx2020.mdw.ac.at/proceedings/papers/DAFx2020_paper_66.pdf>. Establishes: Fig. 6 caption: 'Higher strike velocities have more peaks and troughs, and a larger chirp width', i.e. a larger glide on the measured toms.

**Claim 52: The hard ceiling kTensionPitchModMax = 1.19 (~+3 st) reflects membrane saturation (Avanzini-Marogna-Bank)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:96-100, 725-728, 948-951`)

- Marogna, Avanzini, Bank, 'Energy based synthesis of tension modulation in membranes', DAFx-10. Type: paper. <https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf>. Establishes: Eq. 7a: omega_nm = sqrt((beta_nm/R)^4 D/sigma + c^2 (beta_nm/R)^2) with c^2 = T0/sigma; Eq. 20: Tqs linear in E. No saturation of the tension-energy law is stated.
- Kirby & Sandler, 'Advanced Fourier decomposition for realistic drum synthesis', DAFx-20. Type: paper. <https://dafx2020.mdw.ac.at/proceedings/papers/DAFx2020_paper_66.pdf>. Establishes: Fig. 7: in a 7x12" Sugar Percussion stave tom, 'The large fundamental chirp spans 100-200 Hz', i.e. the measured glide magnitude of a hard hit.

**Claim 53: Glide depth target of ~1.5 semitones at a hard hit is consistent with measured tom-tom glides** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:86-94; tests/unit/dsp/test_per_mode_damping.cpp 522-527`)

- Kirby & Sandler, 'Advanced Fourier decomposition for realistic drum synthesis', DAFx-20. Type: paper. <https://dafx2020.mdw.ac.at/proceedings/papers/DAFx2020_paper_66.pdf>. Establishes: Fig. 7: a fundamental chirp spanning 100-200 Hz for a 7x12" tom; Fig. 5-6: chirp width (glide magnitude) grows with strike velocity across 13 velocity layers.
- Rossing, 'Percussion Instruments', in Springer Handbook of Systematic Musicology (2018), ch. 9: search-engine excerpt only, not opened. Type: textbook. <https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-662-55004-5_9>. Establishes: (Excerpt) A hard blow can change the drumhead tension enough to raise the frequencies of all modes momentarily. In a 33 cm tom-tom the fundamental changed about 8 % (slightly more than a semitone) in the first 0.2 s.
- Marogna, Avanzini, Bank, DAFx-10. Type: paper. <https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf>. Establishes: Uses 20 m/s impact velocity as 'close to the highest dynamic levels in drum playing [Dahl 2004]'. The glide is shown only as a spectrogram (Fig. 3), with no numeric cents value.

**Claim 54: The energy driver is the unweighted sum of squared oscillator states (sum sin^2 + cos^2)** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/modal_resonator_bank.h:482-499, 835-839, 938-940`)

- Marogna, Avanzini, Bank, DAFx-10. Type: paper. <https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf>. Establishes: Eq. 15-19: kinetic energy sum of zdot_nm^2/\|\|K\|\|^2 and potential energy (T0/2R^2) sum of beta^2 z_nm^2/\|\|K\|\|^2; the total E is the sum of beta^2 A^2 weighted terms.

**Claim 55: Tension modulation is restricted to the Membrane body** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:718-724, 945-947`)

- Avanzini, Marogna, Bank, JASA 131(1):897-906, 2012 (abstract). Type: paper. <https://air.unimi.it/handle/2434/654153>. Establishes: The method gives one formulation for the one-dimensional (string) and two-dimensional (membrane) cases, with the tension variation proportional to the system energy in both.
- J. O. Smith III, PASP, 'Tension Modulation'. Type: textbook. <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Tension_Modulation.html>. Establishes: Plucked strings at high amplitude raise their average tension and the fundamental frequency declines as the amplitude decays.
- Marogna, Avanzini, Bank, DAFx-10. Type: paper. <https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf>. Establishes: The membrane tension term is derived from 'the Berger approximation of the von Karman equations for thin plates'. The membrane effect is perceptually 'even more significant' than in strings.

**Claim 56: Membrane strike weighting is the radial Bessel mode shape \|J_m(j_mn r/a)\|, r/a = 0.9 x knob, with no angular factor** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/membrane_mapper.h:111-118`)

- Fletcher, N.H. & Rossing, T.D., The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., 1998, Ch. 3 (membranes) and Ch. 18 (drums). Type: textbook. URL: none given. Establishes: Circular-membrane modes are J_m(k_mn r)cos(m theta); point excitation weights each mode by its shape at the strike point; the m&gt;0 modes are degenerate pairs.
- Russell, D.A., Vibrational modes of a circular membrane (Penn State Acoustics & Vibration Animations). Type: docs. <https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/MembraneCircle/circle.html>. Establishes: (0,1) is excited for impacts anywhere; a centre strike gives the pitchless thump of (0,1),(0,2),(0,3); (1,1) is excited when struck between centre and edge; ratios (1,1) 1.593, (2,1) 2.135, (0,2) 2.295.
- Rayleigh, On bells, Phil. Mag. 1890 (reprinted by Hibberts). Type: paper. <https://www.hibberts.co.uk/on-bells-lord-rayleigh-1890/>. Establishes: In a perfectly symmetrical body the system of nodal meridians has no fixed position and adapts to the point of the blow. This degeneracy argument applies equally to the circular membrane.

**Claim 57: Plate (and NoiseBody) strike weighting sweeps the strike AZIMUTH through cos(m\*theta) on an axisymmetric free plate, with an m-independent cos(n\*pi\*rho) radial factor** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/plate_modes.h:103-129 (used at plate_mapper.h:45-53, floor 0.05; noise_body_mapper.h:108-113, floor 0.03)`)

- Leissa, A.W., Vibration of Plates, NASA SP-160, 1969. Type: textbook. <https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19700009156>. Establishes: Circular-plate mode shapes are [J_m(kr) + C I_m(kr)] cos(m theta), with C and the eigenvalues fixed by the edge condition (free edge tabulated).
- Rayleigh, On bells, Phil. Mag. 1890 (reprinted by Hibberts). Type: paper. <https://www.hibberts.co.uk/on-bells-lord-rayleigh-1890/>. Establishes: In a perfectly symmetrical shell or plate the nodal meridian system has no fixed position and adapts itself to the point of the blow. Moving the blow round a circle of latitude leaves the vibration unchanged and only moves the nodes.
- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 1998, Ch. 3 (plates) and Ch. 20 (cymbals and gongs). Type: textbook. URL: none given. Establishes: Circular-plate (m,n) modes; strike position on a cymbal (edge vs bow) changes the excited partials radially.

**Claim 58: Bell strike weighting maps the knob to the strike AZIMUTH, \|cos(m\*theta)\|, so whole groups of principal partials (tierce/quint, or hum/prime) are suppressed** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/bell_modes.h:22-40, 72-102 (used at bell_mapper.h:43-48, floor 0.05)`)

Establishes: In a perfectly symmetrical bell 'the system of nodal meridians has no fixed position' and adapts to the point of the blow; moving the blow round a circle of latitude moves only the nodes.
- Hibberts, W., Identifying bell partials (strike-point measurements; author's PhD work). Type: thesis. <https://www.hibberts.co.uk/identifying-bell-partials/>. Establishes: Imperfect circularity splits modes into doublets and the azimuth only shifts amplitude between the doublet halves. Rim partials (tierce, nominal, superquint, octave nominal) are maximal at or near the rim. The quint is 'not much stimulated by blows near the rim'. Other partials are strong only when struck higher in the waist.

Type: paper. <https://www.hibberts.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/perrin_charnley_depont_1982.pdf>. Establishes: Bell modes are classified by 2m nodal meridians and n nodal circles; with axial symmetry the m&gt;0 modes form degenerate doublets differing only in meridian placement.

- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 1998, section 2.14 (transverse vibrations of a free-free bar). Type: textbook. URL: none given. Establishes: Free-free bar modes satisfy cos(bL)cosh(bL)=1 (bL = 4.730, 7.853, 10.996, ...); the mode shape is the cosh/cos/sinh/sin combination with antinodes at the free ends and first-mode nodes at 0.224 L.

Establishes: Corroborates the hyperbolic-plus-trigonometric eigenfunction form and the cos(bL)cosh(bL)=1 free-free frequency equation (listed in a search result; not opened).

- Jaffe, D. & Smith, J.O., Extensions of the Karplus-Strong plucked-string algorithm, Computer Music Journal 7(2), 1983. Type: paper. URL: none given. Establishes: The pick-position comb 1 - z^-(beta N) nulls the harmonics with a node at the pick point; beta and 1-beta give the same null set.
- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 1998, sections 2.14 and 2.8 (bars, plucked strings). Type: textbook. URL: none given. Establishes: Each mode's excitation is proportional to its shape at the strike point, so the total radiated level changes with strike position; timpani are struck about a quarter of the way in from the rim to favour the musically useful modes.

**Claim 62: Impact (Impulse / Mallet) pulse: velocity shortens contact time by (1-v)^0.2 and sets force amplitude as v^0.6 ('Hertzian scaling')** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/impact_exciter.h:129-139 (amplitude, T), 77-80 + 296-301 (energy cap); consumers plugins/membrum/src/dsp/exciters/impulse_exciter.h:37-39, mallet_exciter.h:81-90; voice plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:163, 302-304, 436, 1336-1338`)

- F. Avanzini, D. Rocchesso, 'Physical modeling of impacts: theory and experiments on contact time and spectral centroid', SMC 2004. Type: paper. <https://avanzini.di.unimi.it/downloads/publications/avanzini_smc04_finalsub.pdf>. Establishes: Eq. (1) f = k x^alpha, alpha = 1.5 for ideal spheres, 1.5-3.5 for piano felt; Eq. (12): t0 depends only on lambda, alpha, m/k and the impact velocity vin, with t0 proportional to (m/k)^(1/(alpha+1)); a short t0 gives an impulse-like, rich, bright attack and the attack centroid correlates with contact time; a larger impact force can produce multiple bounces.
- S. Bilbao, A. Torin, V. Chatziioannou, 'Numerical modeling of collisions in musical instruments', Acta Acustica united with Acustica 101(1), 2015 (arXiv:1405.2589). Type: paper. <https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1405.2589>. Establishes: Collision potential Phi = K[u]+^(alpha+1)/(alpha+1), force K[u]+^alpha; mallet equation of motion M d2w_h/dt2 = f; mallet-membrane example K = 1.6e8, alpha = 2.54, M = 0.028 kg; force histories show 'a general decrease in contact time with increasing strike velocity'.
- 'Hertz beyond belief' (arXiv:1306.4952). Type: paper. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1306.4952>. Establishes: Abstract: collision time and maximum contact area have a very weak dependence on impact velocity, and Hertz's elastic theory predicts them accurately even with ~40 % viscous energy loss (the weak v^-1/5 law).
- K. L. Johnson, 'Contact Mechanics', Cambridge University Press 1985, ch. 11 (impact of spheres). Type: textbook. URL: none given. Establishes: Classical Hertz impact: duration tau proportional to (m^2/(R E\*^2 v))^(1/5), peak force proportional to m^(3/5) v^(6/5); impulse = m v (1+e).

**Claim 63: Mallet 'Hertzian' contact: duration scales as mass^0.4, hardness sets pulse peakiness gamma = 1..4 (spec FR-011: 8 ms -&gt; 1 ms, alpha 1.5-4)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/exciters/mallet_exciter.h:10-15 (stale header), 81-90; dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/impact_exciter.h:120-134, 193-217`)

Establishes: t0 proportional to (m(h)/k)^(1/(alpha+1)); contact time varies slowly with the damping parameter while m/k and alpha dominate; when the force increases the resonator bounces multiple times on the hammer, raising the centroid.
- S. Bilbao, A. Torin, V. Chatziioannou, Acta Acustica 2015 (arXiv:1405.2589). Type: paper. <https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1405.2589>. Establishes: alpha and K are empirically determined per striker (piano hammer alpha 2.5, mallet alpha 2.54); stiffness K and alpha, not a pulse-shape exponent, define the contact.

**Claim 64: Friction exciter produces stick-slip from the STK power-law bow table** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/exciters/friction_exciter.h:79-89, 121-125; dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/bow_exciter.h:284-323`)

- J. O. Smith III, 'The Bow-String Scattering Junction', Physical Audio Signal Processing (CCRMA online book). Type: textbook. <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Bow_String_Scattering_Junction.html>. Establishes: Delta = v_b - v_s with v_s the sum of the travelling waves meeting at the bow; reflection coefficient rho(Delta+) = r/(1+r), r = 0.25 R_b(Delta)/R_s; outgoing waves v_s,r- = v_s,l+ + rho\*Delta+, so the friction force depends on the string velocity at the bow point.

Establishes: Bowed/blown self-oscillation arises from a nonlinear excitation element (friction curve) coupled in a feedback loop to a linear resonator described by its reflection function; the oscillation is a property of the loop, not of the nonlinearity alone.

Establishes: Trigger converted into 30 ms wide pulses; Q73 switching produces repeated narrow pulses forming 'a unique sawtooth shape' envelope (cycle runs to the middle of the third pass); white noise through band-pass filter IC21 feeds two VCAs with different envelopes, one with a relatively long decay that creates the reverberation.

'a short t0 corresponds to an impulse-like transient with a rich spectrum ... a long t0 ... little energy in the high frequency region'.

The noise level is driven by the excitation energy.

Establishes: Snare drum: 'When the upper, or batter, head is struck, the snare head vibrates against the snares. Establishes: The snare head vibrates against the snares, and removing them gives 'a totally different sound'. The wire component is constitutive of the snare's sound, not a -12 dB accent.
- A. Wagner, 'Analysis of drumbeats', MSc thesis, KTH 2006. Type: thesis. <https://www.speech.kth.se/publications/masterprojects/2006/AndreasWagner.pdf>. **Claim 72: Head-to-shell coupling is feedforward only (body drives shell, shell is summed into the output, nothing returns to the head)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:380-406, 802-846, 979-1044, 1486-1497`)

Type: textbook. <https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf>. Establishes: Coupling between the two heads gives a doublet in the lowest modes. Bass drum (01) pair at 44 and 104 Hz, (11) pair at 76 and 82 Hz. Two-mass oscillator f1 = f0, f2 = sqrt(f0^2 + 2 fc^2), fc = 67 Hz. Side drum: the 'Drum' column gives (01) at 182 and 330 Hz, (11) at 278 and 341 Hz, against 227 Hz for the batter head alone.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of drums', Physics Today 45(3):40-47, March 1992. Type: paper. <https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf>. Establishes: In a two-headed drum there is appreciable coupling between the heads, acoustically through the enclosed air or mechanically through the shell, which leads to the formation of mode pairs. In a snare drum: (0,1) at 183 Hz with the heads in phase; (1,1) pair at 275 Hz (antiphase, air sloshes) and 344 Hz.
- Torin, Hamilton & Bilbao, 'An energy conserving finite difference scheme for the simulation of collisions in snare drums', DAFx-14, 2014. Type: paper. <https://www.pure.ed.ac.uk/ws/files/17485699/dafx14_submission_56_3.pdf>. Establishes: Batter and carry membranes are coupled through the enclosed air. Energy is conserved by construction, otherwise it is monotonically dissipated, and stability follows from the energy terms being positive. Passive bidirectional coupling is stable.

Type: paper. <https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf>. Establishes: The lowest modes of the free drum shell are cylindrical-shell modes with m axial nodes and n circular nodes. Snare shell modes: (4,0) 415 Hz, (4,1) 611 Hz, (5,0) 658 Hz, (5,1) 835 Hz, and 874 / 1064 Hz. The complete drum's (0,1) mode is at 183 Hz.
- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Table 18.6, 1998. Type: textbook. <https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf>. Establishes: 36 cm side drum: batter (01) 227 Hz, snare head (01) 299 Hz, complete drum (01) 182/330 Hz. The low-frequency partner of the batter head is the snare head coupled through the air.

**Claim 74: Snare wire buzz = noise layer scaled by the head's self-normalised modal-energy envelope** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:423-426, 542-549, 857-864, 910-920, 1047-1051, 1073-1083, 1499-1515, 1697-1706; plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h:112-131`)

Type: textbook. <https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf>. Establishes: 'For the snares to sound at all requires a certain amplitude of the snare head. This critical amplitude increases with the snare tension.' Snares leave the head and return to strike it; the impact excites higher modes. The damping effect of the snares shows as a broadening of the fundamental head resonance. Spectra at three blow strengths show the critical amplitude being crossed.
- Torin, Hamilton & Bilbao, 'An energy conserving finite difference scheme for the simulation of collisions in snare drums', DAFx-14, 2014. Type: paper. <https://www.pure.ed.ac.uk/ws/files/17485699/dafx14_submission_56_3.pdf>. Establishes: The bottom membrane and snares are set in motion by the cavity air pressure. The snares reach maximum displacement at t = 6 ms and hit the membrane almost coherently at about 9 ms; after that their behaviour becomes rapidly chaotic. The paper cites Bilbao, 'Time domain simulation and sound synthesis for the snare drum', JASA 131:914-925, 2012.
- Torin & Newton, 'Collisions in drum membranes: a preliminary study on a simplified system', ISMA 2014. Type: paper. <https://www.ness.music.ed.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2014/05/Snare_final.pdf>. Establishes: Membrane and cavity vibrations cause secondary collisions between the lower membrane and the snares. The contact is modelled as a power-law force. The number of collisions and the decay depend strongly on snare mass, stiffness and tension.

**Claim 75: Cross-pad 'sympathetic resonance' rings resonators tuned to the STRUCK voice's own partials, not the unstruck pads** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/systems/sympathetic_resonance.h:38-40, 113-168, 179-259, 312-358; plugins/membrum/src/voice_pool/voice_pool.cpp:243-248; plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:1250-1258; plugins/membrum/src/processor/processor.cpp:688-708`)

Establishes: The (01) mode of a side drum 'loses energy so rapidly (by sound radiation) that after a half second it has fallen below some of the antisymmetric modes'. Snares need a critical snare-head amplitude to sound at all.
- Yamaha Hub, 'Discover the sonic possibilities of your drums, part 2'. Type: docs. <https://hub.yamaha.com/drums/d-how-to/discover-the-sonic-possibilities-of-your-drums-part-2/>. Establishes: Tom or kick partials near the snare-head modes make the wires vibrate. Weak corroboration, not the basis for the verdict.

**Claim 76: CouplingMatrix category routing (Snare Buzz: Kick-&gt;Snare, Tom Resonance: Tom-&gt;Tom) decides which pads excite which** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/coupling_matrix.h:4-11, 42-77; plugins/membrum/src/processor/processor.cpp:131-143, 411-424`)

Establishes: The snare response requires the snare head to be driven above a critical amplitude. Type: textbook. <https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf>. Establishes: The speed of sound in air is about 343 m/s at room temperature, so 0.5-2 ms corresponds to 0.17-0.69 m of propagation.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of drums', Physics Today 45(3), 1992. Type: paper. <https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf>. Establishes: Coupling between drum parts happens acoustically through the air or mechanically through the shell. Both paths exist, so a purely acoustic delay is one of two mechanisms.

**Claim 78: Mode Stretch reproduces stiffness inharmonicity f_n = n f0 sqrt(1 + B n^2) on every body** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/modal_resonator_bank.h:776-807 (B = stretch^2 * 0.01 at :783; f_w = f_k * sqrt(1 + B*(k+1)^2) at :806-807); callers plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/membrane_mapper.h:123-138, plate_mapper.h:58-62, shell_mapper.h:60-62, bell_mapper.h:55-57, noise_body_mapper.h:118-120`)

- Torin & Bilbao, 'Numerical experiments with non-linear double membrane drums', SMAC 2013. Type: paper. <https://www.ness.music.ed.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/BassDrumSMAC13_corrections.pdf>. Establishes: Eq. (1) and (3): a linear stiff membrane with membrane speed c = sqrt(T/(rho H)) on the Laplacian and stiffness kappa = sqrt(E H^2 / (12 rho (1 - nu^2))) on the biharmonic. Dispersion therefore depends on the wavenumber k (omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + kappa^2 k^4), not on a mode's rank.
- D. Russell (Penn State), 'Inharmonicity due to stiffness for guitar and piano strings'. Type: docs. <https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/Stiffness-Inharmonicity/Stiffness-B.html>. Establishes: f_n = n f0 sqrt(1 + B n^2) for a stiff, pinned string, with n the partial number of a harmonic series and B = pi^2 Y S kappa^2 / (T L^2), a 1-D string result.
- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed. (1998). Type: textbook. URL: none given. Establishes: Stiff-string inharmonicity f_n = n f1 sqrt(1 + B n^2). Bars (Euler-Bernoulli, free-free) already have f proportional to (2n+1)^2, and thin plates have frequencies proportional to the square of the wavenumber.

**Claim 79: Mode Stretch 1.0 is 'natural / no stretch' (and &gt; 1 tighter, &lt; 1 sparser)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/plate_mapper.h:58-62 (same at shell_mapper.h:60-62, bell_mapper.h:55-57, noise_body_mapper.h:118-120; membrane_mapper.h:123-138; claims at dsp/voice_common_params.h:23, dsp/pad_config_apply.h:123-126, dsp/pad_config.h:212, MANUAL.md:346)`)

- Plugin's own cited tables: plate_modes.h:6-35 (Rossing & Peterson, Chladni, Leissa), bell_modes.h:6-20 (Perrin, Charnley & DePont 1983; Rossing 2000; Hibberts 2014). Type: docs. URL: none given. Establishes: The headers derive the ratio tables from these sources. The default stretch then moves the realized partials away from them by the cent values listed above.
- AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md, REMEDIATION line 64. Type: docs. URL: none given. Establishes: 'Accepted consequence (user-approved): widening B_max changes the DEFAULT timbre of all Membrum bodies, because the mappers feed a non-zero stretch at the unity default (membrane material\*0.3; plate/shell/bell/noisebody stretchNorm=0.333)'. The deviation is deliberate and documented there, but not in the code comments or the manual.

**Claim 80: NonlinearCoupling imitates the von Karman energy cascade: amplitude-dependent brightening and delayed HF bloom** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/unnatural/nonlinear_coupling.h:6-15, 78-92, 99-127 (applied to body + noise + click + modeInject at plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:550-558, 893-895, 1056-1058)`)

- Chaigne, Touze & Thomas, 'Nonlinear vibrations and chaos in gongs and cymbals', Acoust. Sci. & Tech. 26(5) 2005. Type: paper. <https://perso.ensta.fr/~touze/PDF/ChaosGong.pdf>. Establishes: Typical features: 'amplitude-dependent level of harmonics..., pitch glide, bifurcations, energy exchange between modes through nonlinear coupling and chaos'. 'The energy transfer between modes is a consequence of quadratic nonlinearity due to curvature of the shell and is fully governed by frequency rules' (combination resonances p\*Omega = a_i omega_i + a_j omega_j).
- Poirot, Bilbao & Kronland-Martinet, 'A coupled resonant filter bank for the sound synthesis of nonlinear sources', DAFx 2023. Type: paper. <https://www.dafx.de/paper-archive/2023/DAFx23_paper_42.pdf>. Establishes: Nonlinear plates need 'energy transfer between different modes', which 'may cause the delayed and sustained appearance of tonal components that cannot be generated by linear filtering'. Eq. (15)/(19): sum_i T_i &lt;= 0, which 'impedes the creation of energy during transfer'. Sec. 5.1: transfers to near-frequency filters give 'a gradual cascade of energy towards the high-frequency range', followed by 'a usual exponential decay after the delayed appearance of the high frequency component'.
- Ducceschi & Touze, 'Modal approach for nonlinear vibrations of damped impacted plates: Application to sound synthesis of gongs and cymbals', J. Sound Vib. 344 (2015). Type: paper. <https://perso.ensta-paris.fr/~touze/modalsynthesis.html>. Establishes: Energy-conserving modal scheme of nonlinearly (cubically) coupled modal ODEs for von Karman plates, with per-mode damping (abstract, via search).

**Claim 81: Envelope-controlled waveshaping is 'the accepted cheap approximation' because the cited coupled models are too costly** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/unnatural/nonlinear_coupling.h:9-15`)

- Poirot, Bilbao & Kronland-Martinet, DAFx 2023 (journal version EURASIP JASMP 2024, doi 10.1186/s13636-024-00358-2). Type: paper. <https://www.dafx.de/paper-archive/2023/DAFx23_paper_42.pdf>. Establishes: Contrasts the 'heavy computational cost' of Foppl-von Karman / Ducceschi-Touze with its own 'efficient and controllable filters' that 'can yield real-time event-driven synthesis'. Stability follows from the non-positive transfer sum (Sec. 3.2).

**Claim 82: Gong / plate pitch glide is provided (left to the tension feature)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:718-728 and 939-950 (tensionActive gated on BodyModelType::Membrane); AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:92`)

- Chaigne, Touze & Thomas, Acoust. Sci. & Tech. 26(5) 2005, Sec. 4.1 'Pitch Glide'. Type: paper. <https://perso.ensta.fr/~touze/PDF/ChaosGong.pdf>. Establishes: Large Chinese opera gongs: 'a downward glide in pitch by as much as three semitones'; 'smaller gongs with a pronounced curvature, glide upward'. Hardening corresponds to a downward glide in free vibration, softening to an upward one. 'Pitch glides are frequently heard on thick gongs, but not on thin cymbals.'
- Torin & Bilbao, SMAC 2013. Type: paper. <https://www.ness.music.ed.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/BassDrumSMAC13_corrections.pdf>. Establishes: Pitch glide and HF build-up at high excitation are observed in bass drums and toms. A Berger-type (tension) model gives the glide but 'is not able to render the build-up of high-frequency energy'.

**Claim 83: Decay Skew inverts the Chaigne-Lambourg decay-vs-frequency law (fundamental dies, shimmer sustains)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/membrane_mapper.h:140-173 (same pattern plate_mapper.h:68-91, shell_mapper.h:69-89, bell_mapper.h:64-86, noise_body_mapper.h:125-145); b3 clamp at dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/modal_resonator_bank.h:767 and dampingLawFromLegacy :133-139`)

- Chaigne & Lambourg, 'Time-domain simulation of damped impacted plates. I. Theory and experiments', JASA 109 (2001). Type: paper. <https://hal-ensta.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00830699>. Establishes: The model's thermoelastic, viscoelastic and radiation damping terms reproduce the measured frequency dependence of decay factors in plates of four materials (abstract, via search). This is the natural law Decay Skew is specified to invert.
- specs/137-membrum-phase2-exciters-bodies/research.md §9 and contracts/unnatural_zone_contract.md:39-52,165. Type: docs. URL: none given. Establishes: Decay Skew = -1 means 'fundamental decays fast, high modes sustain', and the acceptance test measures T60 of mode 0 vs the highest mode. The scalar-bias approach was a stopgap with a per-block per-mode fallback 'if the US6-2 inversion test cannot be satisfied'.

**Claim 84: Mode Inject uses the natural (sawtooth / bowed) 1/k harmonic falloff and dies with the drum** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/unnatural/mode_inject.h:47-67 (1/k amplitudes), 84-93 and 137-153 (single T60 one-pole envelope), 124-126 (skipNormalization=true); wiring plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:326-332`)

- Acoustics Today, Summer 2016, 'Violin Acoustics', p. 26. Type: paper. <https://acousticstoday.org/issues/2016AT/2016Summer/files/basic-html/page26.html>. Establishes: The Helmholtz wave is a Fourier sum of harmonic modes with 'amplitudes varying as 1/n, where n is an integer and f1 is the frequency of the fundamental component'.
- Chaigne & Lambourg, JASA 109 (2001). Type: paper. <https://hal-ensta.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00830699>. Establishes: Measured decay factors depend on frequency. The physical expectation is faster decay of higher partials, unlike one shared T60.

**Claim 85: The configured pitch sweep (start -&gt; end over Time) actually reaches the modal body on the paths a host uses** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:313-321, 589, 613-620, 703-746, 960-965; dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/modal_resonator_bank.h 213, 431-434, 526-533, 647, 906-914`)

- J.O. Smith III, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Digital Sinusoid Generators' (CCRMA online book). Type: textbook. <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Digital_Sinusoid_Generators.html>. Establishes: Magic-circle (modified coupled form) update x1(n) = x1(n-1) + eps\*x2(n-1), x2(n) = -eps\*x1(n) + x2(n-1), with eps = 2 sin(pi f_n T), where f_n is the instantaneous frequency at sample n. So the frequency coefficient is defined per sample, which is the form a swept resonator should follow.
- Werner, Abel & Smith, 'A Physically-Informed, Circuit-Bendable, Digital Model of the Roland TR-808 Bass Drum Circuit', DAFx-14, 2014. Type: paper. <https://dafx14.fau.de/papers/dafx14_kurt_james_werner_a_physically_informed,_ci.pdf>. Establishes: The 808's defining pitch events happen within about 6 ms (an attack jump of more than an octave, 'less than a single period at the higher frequency'). A renderer whose pitch control lags by hundreds of ms cannot produce them.

**Claim 86: Block-rate (once per host block) pitch update is fine enough for 5-50 ms sweeps** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:589, 613-620, 699-746, 960-965, 1015-1022`)

- J.O. Smith III, Physical Audio Signal Processing, 'Digital Sinusoid Generators' (CCRMA). Type: textbook. <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Digital_Sinusoid_Generators.html>. Establishes: eps = 2 sin(pi f_n T) with f_n the instantaneous frequency at sample n: the resonator's frequency is a per-sample quantity.
- Werner, Abel & Smith, DAFx-14 TR-808 bass drum. Type: paper. <https://dafx14.fau.de/papers/dafx14_kurt_james_werner_a_physically_informed,_ci.pdf>. Establishes: Section 8.1: the bridged-T centre frequency rises by more than an octave for about 6 ms ('less than a single period at the higher frequency'). That timing detail 'greatly affects the sound of the bass drum's attack', so control resolution has to be finer than a few ms.

**Claim 87: The 'Exp' pitch-sweep curve is an exponential, analogue-style glide** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/pitch_segment_envelope.h:60-73, 103-134; dsp/include/krate/dsp/core/curve_table.h 46, 65-79; plugins/membrum/src/dsp/tone_shaper.h 286-294, 503-512; plugins/membrum/src/dsp/pad_config_apply.h 108-111; plugins/membrum/src/dsp/pad_config.h 205; plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h 478; tools/membrum_preset_generator.cpp 88-93`)

- Gordon Reid, 'Synth Secrets: Practical Bass Drum Synthesis', Sound On Sound (mirror). Type: blog. <https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/bassdrumsynth.html>. Establishes: TR-909: the oscillator's pitch is defined by EG3, 'which has an instant Attack and slow Decay'. TR-808: a bridged-T oscillator that decays on its own; the pitch 'always swoops down'. No Hz or ms figures are given, so this is corroboration only.
- Werner, Abel & Smith, DAFx-14 TR-808 bass drum. Type: paper. <https://dafx14.fau.de/papers/dafx14_kurt_james_werner_a_physically_informed,_ci.pdf>. Establishes: Section 8: the pitch events come from an RC envelope generator (Q41/Q42, settling about 5 ms after the trigger) and from leakage through R161 that changes the effective resistance. Fig. 11 shows a smooth, decaying instantaneous-frequency curve (the 'pitch sigh'), not a power-law landing at a fixed time.

**Claim 88: The factory '808' and default kick pitch sweeps match TR-808 / TR-909 kick pitch behaviour** (`tools/membrum_preset_generator.cpp:1126-1143 (808 Electronic Kit pad 0), 2926-2934 (909 Drum Machine pad 0), 3747-3754 (Trap Modern 'Sub 808'); plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h 54-61`)

- Werner, Abel & Smith, 'A Physically-Informed, Circuit-Bendable, Digital Model of the Roland TR-808 Bass Drum Circuit', DAFx-14, pp. 159-166. Type: paper. <https://dafx14.fau.de/papers/dafx14_kurt_james_werner_a_physically_informed,_ci.pdf>. Establishes: Bridged-T centre frequency about 49.5 Hz (Roland chart 56 Hz). Section 8.1: a 6 ms attack rise of more than an octave, under one period, not perceived as pitch. Section 8.2: the 'pitch sigh' is a subtle leakage-driven modulation. Fig. 11: instantaneous frequency about 56 -&gt; 49.5 Hz over 0.3 s.
- Gordon Reid, 'Synth Secrets: Practical Bass Drum Synthesis', Sound On Sound (mirror). Type: blog. <https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/bassdrumsynth.html>. Establishes: The TR-909 kick pitch comes from EG3 (instant attack, slow decay) driving an oscillator waveshaped to near-sine. The TR-808 bridged-T rings on its own and 'goes slightly flat at long decays'.

**Claim 89: SC-009 '808 kick' test pins the pitch envelope to 808 behaviour and covers the real render path** (`plugins/membrum/tests/unit/tone_shaper/test_pitch_envelope_808.cpp:1-13, 74-88, 92-142, 173-203`)

- Werner, Abel & Smith, DAFx-14 TR-808 bass drum. Type: paper. <https://dafx14.fau.de/papers/dafx14_kurt_james_werner_a_physically_informed,_ci.pdf>. Establishes: 808 rest frequency about 49.5 Hz, attack jump of more than an octave for about 6 ms, pitch sigh about 56 -&gt; 50 Hz over 300 ms. There is no 160 -&gt; 50 Hz, 20 ms sweep.

**Claim 90: A zero-look-ahead, instantaneous-attack limiter is an acceptable brickwall stage for percussive material** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/true_peak_limiter.h:4-18, 246-257 (used at plugins/membrum/src/processor/processor.cpp:710-717, 1086-1088)`)

- D. Giannoulis, M. Massberg, J. D. Reiss, 'Digital Dynamic Range Compressor Design - A Tutorial and Analysis', JAES 60(6):399-408, 2012. Type: paper. <https://web.archive.org/web/2016/http://www.eecs.qmul.ac.uk/~josh/documents/2012/GiannoulisMassbergReiss-dynamicrangecompression-JAES2012.pdf>. Establishes: Sec. 1: instantaneous compressor response is not sought because it introduces distortion. Sec. 4.1 / Fig. 9: smoothing the detector visibly reduces THD, and the decoupled smooth detector minimises distortion at the attack/release transition. Sec. 3: a feedforward design can act as a perfect limiter and allows a look-ahead function.
- P. Hämäläinen, 'Smoothing of the Control Signal without Clipped Output in Digital Peak Limiters', Proc. DAFx-02, Hamburg, pp. 195-198, 2002. Type: paper. <https://dafx.de/paper-archive/2002/DAFX02_Hamalainen_smoothing_peak_limiters.pdf>. Establishes: The output x\*g convolves the spectra, and faster reaction gives stronger artifacts. Preventing clipping without look-ahead requires zero attack, which gives sharp gain transitions heard as clicks. A delay with a max filter, clipping control and averaging gives a smooth gain with no clipped output, and N = 64 already gives good results.
- M. Holters, limiter.m, companion code to U. Zölzer (ed.), DAFX: Digital Audio Effects, 2nd ed., Wiley 2011, sec. 4.2.1 'Limiter'. Type: textbook. <https://dafx.de/DAFX_Book_Page_2nd_edition/M_files_chap04.zip>. Establishes: The textbook limiter uses peak detection with attack coefficient 0.3 and release coefficient 0.01, a gain smoother with the same coefficients, and a 5-sample delay buffer in the audio path: y(n) = g \* buffer(end).
- Faust compressors.lib, limiter_lad_N (D. Sanfilippo), after J. Zmölnig / P. Falkner. Type: docs. <https://sources.debian.org/src/faust/2.30.5~ds0-2/libraries/compressors.lib>. Establishes: The input path is delayed by the same amount as the attack time (look-ahead). Gain fluctuations above about 15 Hz are perceived as timbral effects.
- J. Zmölnig, digital limiter notes, IEM Graz, 1999 (after P. Falkner's thesis). Type: docs. <https://users.iem.at/zmoelnig/publications/limiter/>. Establishes: Delaying the signal lets the limiter regulate the gain before the triggering moment. Very fast, hard regulation removes dynamics and adds inharmonic components.

**Claim 91: The detector is a 4x true-peak (BS.1770-style) measurement, so inter-sample peaks are bounded to within the detector's accuracy** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/true_peak_limiter.h:4-6, 15-17, 62-71, 173-215; dsp/include/krate/dsp/primitives/oversampler.h:509-535, 623-643`)

- ITU-R BS.1770-5 (11/2023), Annex 2 'Guidelines for accurate measurement of true-peak level' and its Attachment 1. Type: docs. <https://www.itu.int/dms_pubrec/itu-r/rec/bs/R-REC-BS.1770-5-202311-I!!PDF-E.pdf>. Establishes: 4x oversampling to 192 kHz with an order-48, 4-phase symmetric FIR interpolator (coefficients tabled). Maximum under-read is 20·log(cos(pi·fnorm/n)): 0.554 dB (fnorm 0.45) and 0.688 dB (fnorm 0.5) at 4x. Higher ratios are preferred. Individual transients with high-frequency content under-read the most.
- EBU R 128 (2020), Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals. Type: docs. <https://tech.ebu.ch/docs/r/r128.pdf>. Establishes: Programme true peak shall not exceed -1 dBTP, measured with a BS.1770 / EBU Tech 3341 meter, with a measurement tolerance of +-0.3 dB for 20 kHz band-limited signals.
- P. Hämäläinen, DAFx-02 'Smoothing of the Control Signal without Clipped Output in Digital Peak Limiters'. Type: paper. <https://dafx.de/paper-archive/2002/DAFX02_Hamalainen_smoothing_peak_limiters.pdf>. Establishes: A delay in the limiter output, with envelope detection over the samples in the delay line, is what lets the gain act before the peak it responds to.

**Claim 92: The -1 dBTP bus ceiling is the EBU R128 / streaming output ceiling and bounds the mix** (`plugins/membrum/src/processor/processor.cpp:710-737, 1086-1088 (constant at dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/true_peak_limiter.h:49)`)

- EBU R 128 (2020), Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals. Type: docs. <https://tech.ebu.ch/docs/r/r128.pdf>. Establishes: The True Peak Level of a programme shall not exceed -1 dBTP during production, measured with an ITU-R BS.1770 / EBU Tech 3341 meter, tolerance +-0.3 dB.
- ITU-R BS.1770-5 Annex 2. Type: docs. <https://www.itu.int/dms_pubrec/itu-r/rec/bs/R-REC-BS.1770-5-202311-I!!PDF-E.pdf>. Establishes: dBTP is defined on the signal as delivered: decibels relative to full scale, true-peak measurement.
