Claims 95, 97, 98, 100, 106, 110, 112, 114 and 118 repeat the subject of physics findings raised from earlier claims (MB-222, MB-223, MB-198, MB-199, MB-200, MB-203, MB-204, MB-206). Their titles there differ, so these claims are listed without an MB-id of their own. Claims 106 and 110 did become findings of their own (MB-245, MB-246). Claims 102, 105, 113, 116, 128 and 134 are rated low or medium, yet none of them matches a physics finding.

#### Sources for claims 93-136

URLs and the "establishes" text are as recorded by the research agent. "Auditor's measurement" marks a computation the research agent ran itself; it has no URL.

**93. The 80 ms one-pole release is a 'program-dependent recovery'** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/true_peak_limiter.h:50, 139-144, 248-251`)
- D. Giannoulis, M. Massberg, J. D. Reiss, JAES 60(6), 2012 (paper). https://web.archive.org/web/2016/http://www.eecs.qmul.ac.uk/~josh/documents/2012/GiannoulisMassbergReiss-dynamicrangecompression-JAES2012.pdf. Establishes: Fig. 9 (THD against frequency, attack 1 ms, release 15 ms) shows smoothing clearly reduces harmonic distortion; the decoupled detector minimises distortion at the attack/release transition; a smooth log-domain release gives artifact-free compression.
- Faust compressors.lib, limiter_lad_N (D. Sanfilippo) (docs). https://sources.debian.org/src/faust/2.30.5~ds0-2/libraries/compressors.lib. Establishes: gain fluctuations above about 15 Hz are heard as timbral effects; a hold time keeps low-frequency distortion minimal.
- J. Zmölnig, IEM 1999 limiter notes (docs). https://users.iem.at/zmoelnig/publications/limiter/. Establishes: the gain is held for a hold time, then recovers exponentially.

**94. The bus limiter is a safety device that owns only the N-voice coincident sum; single voices stay below it** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:80, 564-565`, with `processor.cpp:710-717`)
- D. Giannoulis, M. Massberg, J. D. Reiss, JAES 60(6), 2012 (paper). https://web.archive.org/web/2016/http://www.eecs.qmul.ac.uk/~josh/documents/2012/GiannoulisMassbergReiss-dynamicrangecompression-JAES2012.pdf. Establishes: a limiter is the infinite-ratio case of the feedforward gain computer (sec. 3, Eq. 19); above threshold it removes all level variation, so it should engage only on the peaks it is meant to catch.
- EBU R 128 (2020) (docs). https://tech.ebu.ch/docs/r/r128.pdf. Establishes: -1 dBTP is a technical upper limit for compliance checking, separate from loudness normalisation; peaks should sit below it, not be driven into it.

**95. The tension glide peaks at the strike and relaxes as energy decays** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:130-133, 703-728, 902-920, 1069-1083`)
- F. Avanzini, R. Marogna, B. Bank, 'Efficient synthesis of tension modulation in strings and membranes based on energy estimation', JASA 131(1):897-906, 2012 (paper). https://avanzini.di.unimi.it/downloads/publications/avanzini_jasa12.pdf. Establishes: Eq. 26, Tqs is proportional to sum lambda_g·A_g²·e^(-2t/tau_g) and only decays; Eq. 36, Tqs = C_NL·E/(S0·T0); the Fig. 1 caption attributes the slow initial rise to the running-average filter used to estimate it; Sec. V.A downsamples the energy by 32 (0.73 ms) with linear interpolation; Eq. 37 gives an energy-storage model driven by the hammer's energy loss.
- R. Marogna, F. Avanzini, B. Bank, 'Energy based synthesis of tension modulation in membranes', DAFx-10, Graz, 2010 (paper). https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf. Establishes: Eq. 20, Tqs = Eh/(2·R²·(1-nu²)·T0)·E(t); Sec. 2.3, the slow initial rise of Tqs is a side effect of lowpass filtering; the quasistatic tension produces a continuous decrease of the modal frequencies.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of drums', Physics Today 45(3):40, 1992 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: just after the strike each mode has a higher frequency, which decreases as the amplitude dies down.

**96. Glide magnitude: '~2 semitones at max, matches JASA 2021 (Kirby & Sandler) tom-tom measurements', with velocity^2 depth** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/pad_config.h:141-144, 308-311`; also `drum_voice.h:86-100, 408-421`, `default_kit.h:84, 140, 178-183`, `tests/unit/dsp/test_per_mode_damping.cpp:481-528`)
- T. Kirby, M. Sandler, 'Advanced Fourier decomposition for realistic drum synthesis', DAFx-20, 2020 (paper). https://dafx2020.mdw.ac.at/proceedings/papers/DAFx2020_paper_66.pdf. Establishes: 416 tom samples (32 drums, 13 velocities); chirp width runs from the initial tension-modulated frequency down to the unmodulated one and grows with velocity (Fig. 6); a 7x12" tom's fundamental chirp spans 100-200 Hz (Fig. 7).
- T. Kirby, M. Sandler, 'The evolution of drum modes with strike intensity: Analysis and synthesis using the discrete cosine transform', JASA 150(1):202-214, 2021 (paper; repository record only, full text not opened). https://qmro.qmul.ac.uk/xmlui/handle/123456789/98182. Establishes: DCT analysis of one tom struck at 67 intensities, with modes interpolated across velocity; no 2-semitone figure is visible in what was opened.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of drums', Physics Today 45(3):40, 1992 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: dT ∝ amplitude² and f ∝ sqrt(T+dT); a full blow on a bass drum (6 mm amplitude) shifts it up about 10 %, 'nearly a whole tone'.
- Springer chapter, DOI 10.1007/978-3-662-55004-5_9 (textbook; search snippet only, chapter and authors unverified). https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-662-55004-5_9. Establishes: a 33 cm tom's fundamental rises about 8 % (slightly more than a semitone) during the first 0.2 s.

**97. Glide depth scales as velocity^2 (via strike energy)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:408-421`; comment `pad_config.h:143`)
- F. Avanzini, R. Marogna, B. Bank, JASA 131(1):897-906, 2012 (paper). https://avanzini.di.unimi.it/downloads/publications/avanzini_jasa12.pdf. Establishes: Eq. 36, Tqs ∝ E; Eqs. 39-40, the energy input is the hammer's energy change, ½·m_h·v² plus contact energy.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of drums', Physics Today 45(3):40, 1992 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: the average tension increase dT is proportional to the square of the displacement amplitude, and frequency to sqrt(T+dT).
- T. Kirby, M. Sandler, DAFx-20, 2020 (paper). https://dafx2020.mdw.ac.at/proceedings/papers/DAFx2020_paper_66.pdf. Establishes: higher strike velocities give a larger chirp width (Fig. 6, 13 velocities).

**98. Glide depth is independent of drum size and head tension (one global energy scale)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:94, 420-421`; `dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/modal_resonator_bank.h:493-499`)
- R. Marogna, F. Avanzini, B. Bank, DAFx-10, 2010 (paper). https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf. Establishes: Eq. 20, Tqs = E·h/(2·R²·(1-nu²)·T0)·E(t); Eq. 19 gives the membrane energy as a weighted modal sum.
- F. Avanzini, R. Marogna, B. Bank, JASA 131(1):897-906, 2012 (paper). https://avanzini.di.unimi.it/downloads/publications/avanzini_jasa12.pdf. Establishes: Eq. 34, E = ½·sum [rho·zdot_g² + T0·lambda_g·z_g²]/‖K_g‖²; Eq. 36, Tqs = C_NL·E/(S0·T0).
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of drums', Physics Today 45(3):40, 1992 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: f ∝ sqrt(T+dT), the exact form the code linearises.

**99. Glide direction is up at the strike, then relaxes downward, for toms (and is Membrane-only)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:722-728, 945-951`)
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of drums', Physics Today 45(3):40, 1992 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: just after the strike each mode has a higher frequency, which decreases as the amplitude dies down.
- T. Kirby, M. Sandler, DAFx-20, 2020 (paper). https://dafx2020.mdw.ac.at/proceedings/papers/DAFx2020_paper_66.pdf. Establishes: in tom samples, activity starts at the tension-modulated frequency and moves down until it reaches the unmodulated frequency.
- R. Marogna, F. Avanzini, B. Bank, DAFx-10, 2010 (paper). https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf. Establishes: tom-toms show a characteristic glide at medium-high dynamics; quasistatic tension continuously lowers the modal frequencies.

**102. Air loading 'raises the axisymmetric (0,n) modes' while (0,1) and (1,1) stay at the ideal 0.628 ratio** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/membrane_modes.h:64-67, 82-86, 98-105`)
- Fletcher & Rossing 1998, §18.1 p. 499 and Tables 18.1 / 18.2 (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: the stiffness of the enclosed air raises the axisymmetric modes, especially (0,1); with the kettle (0,1)/(1,1) = 0.87 calculated and 0.81 measured (0.54 without); air loading shifts all modes down, the low ones most.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of Drums', Physics Today 45(3), 1992, p. 44 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: a smaller kettle raises (0,1), (0,2), (0,3) through the stiffness of the enclosed air but lowers (1,1), (2,1), (3,1), (4,1).

**103. Modes with n >= 2 and (m >= 6, 1) left unshifted because 'Rossing's published data doesn't quantify them'** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/membrane_modes.h:88-91, 98-105`)
- Fletcher & Rossing 1998, Tables 18.1 and 18.2, and §18.1 p. 498 (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: calculated with kettle, f/f11: 12 2.34, 22 2.74, 32 3.28, 61 3.38, 13 3.38, 42 3.80; measured: 12 2.00, 22 2.86, 03 2.71; Rayleigh's overtones at 1.50, 1.88 and 2.00 come from (21), (31) and (12).

**104. (1,1) as the perceptual fundamental (principal tone) of a timpani** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/membrane_modes.h:82-86`)
- Fletcher & Rossing 1998, §18.1 p. 498 and §18.10 p. 515 (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: Rayleigh identified the timpani principal note as the (11) mode; in the 36 cm side drum the symmetric (01) mode at 195 Hz dominates the spectrum at first.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of Drums', Physics Today 45(3), 1992 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: the principal note comes from (1,1); the (m,1) family radiates partials near 2:3:4:5:6.

**105. Timpani (kettle) air-loading curve applied to the default kit's toms, snare and kick** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h:76, 134, 164`; PadConfig default 0.6 at `pad_config.h:291`)
- Fletcher & Rossing 1998, Table 18.5 (82 cm bass drum, Rossing 1987) (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: carry head at lower tension, 01 39, 11 80, 21 121, 31 162, 41 204, 51 248 Hz; (01)..(41) fall near a harmonic series.
- Fletcher & Rossing 1998, Table 18.6 (36 cm side drum, Zhao 1990) (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: batter head (snare head damped, backed by the enclosed air), 01 227, 11 284, 21 403, 02 445, 31 513, 12 555, 41 619 Hz.
- Fletcher & Rossing 1998, Table 18.7 and §18.11 Tom-Toms (Rossing 1977; Bork 1983) (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: 30 cm single-head tom without a dot, 147, 318, 461, 526, 591, 684, 703 Hz for 01, 11, 21, 02, 31, 12, 41; a 32 cm two-headed tom has a (01) pair at 101 / 191 Hz and (11) at 179 Hz.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of Drums', Physics Today 45(3), 1992 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: in two-headed drums, coupling through the enclosed air splits (0,1) and (1,1) into mode pairs; the bass drum's (0,1) split is especially large.

**106. Manual and header comments describe air loading as a low-mode depression curve that 'makes it deeper'** (`plugins/membrum/MANUAL.md:239-247`; also `src/dsp/pad_config.h:121-125, 286-290`, `src/dsp/voice_common_params.h:45-47`)
- Fletcher & Rossing 1998, Table 18.1 and §18.1 (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: air loading shifts all modes down, the low ones most; the harmonic relationship comes from the low modes moving down further than the high ones.

**107. Default snare Size 0.4 gives f0 of about 199 Hz, 'on the measured 14-inch (0,1) mode (Rossing & Bork 1992)'** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h:99-103`; same Size feeds `membrane_mapper.h:100`)
- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed. (Springer 1998), Sec. 18.10 Side Drums, Table 18.6 and Fig. 18.7 (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: 36 cm side drum (Zhao 1990), mode 01 at 227 Hz on the batter head, 299 Hz on the snare head and 182 / 330 Hz for the drum; the (01) mode at 195 Hz dominates the spectrum at first; heads at playing tension, set by a percussionist; an orchestral snare is 35 cm (14 in).

Establishes: the lowest (0,1) mode of a 35 cm snare is at 183 Hz, with the two heads in phase; the lower (1,1) is at 275 Hz and the upper at 344 Hz; cites Rossing, Bork, Zhao & Fystrom (JASA, in press).
- Skrodzka, Hojan & Proksza, 'Vibroacoustic investigation of a batter head of a snare drum', Archives of Acoustics 31(3):289-297, 2006 (paper). https://acoustics.ippt.pan.pl/index.php/aa/article/download/674/592/1079. Establishes: a 36 cm snare batter head has (0,1) at 224 Hz and (1,1) at 322 Hz; Table 1 quotes Rossing et al., JASA 92(1):84-94 (1992), with (0,1) 224, (1,1) 280, (2,1) 403, (0,2) 445 Hz, which confirms that the citation is about a snare.

**108. 'Was 0.5 -> ~158 Hz, a whole tone flat'** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h:102`; also `INVESTIGATION-snare-body-2026-07-01.md:35-36`)
- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Table 18.6 and Sec. 18.10 (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: 36 cm side drum, drum (0,1) at 182 Hz, batter (0,1) at 227 Hz, (01) spectral peak at 195 Hz.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of Drums', Physics Today 45(3), 1992 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: the snare drum's lowest (0,1) mode is at 183 Hz.

**109. The Size to f0 law (500 * 0.1^Size) as a drum-size and tom-pitch map: the default High Tom (Size 0.4) shares the snare's 199.05 Hz** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h:143-147, 413-423, 459-480`; `bodies/membrane_mapper.h:100`)
- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Sec. 18.11 Tom-Toms, Table 18.7, Fig. 18.8 (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: toms range from 20 to 45 cm; a 30 cm single-head tom has (01) at 147 Hz (140-144 Hz with dots); a 32 cm two-headed tom has (01) at 101 / 191 Hz and (11) at 179 Hz (Bork 1983); a 33 cm tom's fundamental is about 8 % higher in the first 0.2 s (Rose 1978), and about 10 % in Bork & Meyer.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of Drums', Physics Today 45(3), 1992, Fig. 2 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: ideal-membrane ratios 1.000, 1.594, 2.136, 2.296, ...; actual frequency = ratio × (2.405 / 2πa) × sqrt(T/σ).

**110. 'modeScatter 0.28 reproduces the (0,1)/(1,1) mode splitting of a real snare head'; the coded low-mode ratios against the measured snare** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h:132-135`; `dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/modal_resonator_bank.h:784, 810, 655-656`; `membrane_modes.h:98-105`)
- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Table 18.6 and Sec. 18.10 (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: 36 cm side drum, the drum's 01 modes are a pair at 182 / 330 Hz and its 11 modes a pair at 278 / 341 Hz; batter-head 01 / 11 / 21 / 02 at 227 / 284 / 403 / 445 Hz; the second (01) mode, with the heads moving in opposition, is weak because the heads differ in mass.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of Drums', Physics Today 45(3), 1992 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: the two heads couple through the enclosed air and the shell, forming mode pairs (lower (1,1) at 275 Hz, upper at 344 Hz); a two-mass, three-spring model describes the first two modes.
- Skrodzka, Hojan & Proksza, Archives of Acoustics 31(3):289-297, 2006, Table 1 (paper). https://acoustics.ippt.pan.pl/index.php/aa/article/download/674/592/1079. Establishes: Rossing et al. 1992 batter-head ratios 1 : 1.25 : 1.80 : 1.99 for (0,1), (1,1), (2,1), (0,2); the authors' own 36 cm head gives 1 : 1.44 : 2.24 : 2.32.

**111. Classical free-plate Chladni law is f ~ (m+2n)^2 for a flat circular plate, and the lowest elastic mode is (2,0)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/plate_modes.h:14-35, 67-69`)
- Wikipedia, 'Chladni's law' (citing Rossing & Fletcher, Principles of Vibration and Sound, 2004, pp. 73-74, and Fletcher & Rossing 1998, p. 680) (docs). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chladni%27s_law. Establishes: p is roughly 2 for flat circular plates; for cymbals, handbells and church bells it ranges from 1.4 to 2.4 and can differ between mode families.
- C. Wilbur & T. D. Rossing, 'Vibrational modes of cymbals and Chladni's law', ASA 132nd meeting, 5pMU8, 1996 (paper). https://www.auditory.org/asamtgs/asa96haw/5pMU/5pMU8.html. Establishes: f(m,n) = C(m+2n)² for a flat circular plate; a variable-exponent law and a three-parameter C(m+bn)^P law were fitted to about 300 modes of a 16-inch cymbal; the abstract gives no exponent value.
- Dong & Liu, 'An Absolute Acoustic Readout of Plate Wave Speed for Bullion Authentication...', arXiv 2610.29194 (2026), Appendix A, Table IX, reproducing Leissa, Vibration of Plates, NASA SP-160 (1969), Tables 2.5/2.6 (paper). https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29194. Establishes: free circular plate λ² at nu = 1/3: (2,0) 5.253, (0,1) 9.084, (3,0) 12.23, (1,1) 20.52, (2,1) 35.25, (0,2) 38.55; the free-edge frequency equation; the fundamental of a free disc is (2,0).
- Auditor's measurement: free-plate Kirchhoff solver (scratchpad free_plate.js). Establishes: it reproduces Leissa within 0.1 % and adds (4,0) 21.492 and (5,0) 33.012; the local exponent of the n = 0 family is 1.90-2.08.

**112. Chladni exponent P = 1.7 as 'the measured-cymbal exponent reported by Rossing & Peterson', applied to every mode family** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/plate_modes.h:6-9, 26-28, 37-38`; `tools/gen-plate-chladni.js:7-9, 19, 24`)
- Wikipedia, 'Chladni's law' (citing Fletcher & Rossing 1998, p. 680) (docs). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chladni%27s_law. Establishes: for cymbals, handbells and church bells p varies from 1.4 to 2.4 and can depend on the mode family within one object.
- C. Wilbur & T. D. Rossing, 'Vibrational modes of cymbals and Chladni's law', ASA 5pMU8, 1996 (paper). https://www.auditory.org/asamtgs/asa96haw/5pMU/5pMU8.html. Establishes: a modified Chladni law with a per-family exponent P_n, and the form C(m+bn)^P, fitted to about 300 cymbal modes; no exponent value given.
- Brezas, Kaselouris, Orphanos, Bakarezos, Dimitriou, Papadogiannis, 'Experimental and computational vibroacoustic study of cymbals', Forum Acusticum 2023, DOI 10.61782/fa.2023.0309 (paper). https://dael.euracoustics.org/confs/fa2023/data/articles/000309.pdf. Establishes: ESPI cymbal modes (2,0) 210, (3,0) 555, (4,0) 1040, (5,0) 1520, (3,1) 1630, (4,1) 1740, (2,1) 1760, (5,1) 2030 Hz.

**113. Circular-family split (1 + kappa*n) with kappa = 0.11 models the stiffening of free-plate nodal-circle families** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/plate_modes.h:29-33, 70-101`; `tools/gen-plate-chladni.js:20, 24`)
- Leissa, Vibration of Plates, NASA SP-160 (1969), Tables 2.5/2.6 (free circular plate), as reproduced and re-solved in Dong & Liu, arXiv 2610.29194, Table IX (textbook). https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29194. Establishes: λ² at nu = 1/3: (2,0) 5.253, (0,1) 9.084, (3,0) 12.23, (1,1) 20.52, (2,1) 35.25, (0,2) 38.55, so (0,1)/(2,0) = 1.729 and (1,1)/(3,0) = 1.678.
- Auditor's measurement: free-plate solver (scratchpad free_plate.js, Leissa frequency equation, within 0.1 % of Table IX). Establishes: equal-(m+2n) family ratios of 1.728, 1.679, 1.640, 1.603 for n = 1 and 1.792, 1.813 for n = 2; the flat-plate mode order (2,0), (0,1), (3,0), (1,1), (4,0), (5,0), (2,1), (0,2), (6,0), (3,1).
- C. Wilbur & T. D. Rossing, ASA 5pMU8, 1996 (paper). https://www.auditory.org/asamtgs/asa96haw/5pMU/5pMU8.html. Establishes: the cymbal fit uses per-family parameters (C_n, P_n or the empirical b), not a single family term.
- Brezas et al., Forum Acusticum 2023 cymbal ESPI study (paper). https://dael.euracoustics.org/confs/fa2023/data/articles/000309.pdf. Establishes: the cymbal's (2,1)/(4,0) split is 1760/1040 = 1.69, close to the flat-plate 1.64; all (m,1) modes lie above 7.7 × (2,0).

**114. Free-plate strike weighting phi = R_mn(r)*cos(m*theta), with R approximated by cos(n*pi*rho) and the Strike Position knob sweeping both radius and azimuth** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/plate_modes.h:103-129`; `plate_mapper.h:46-53`; `noise_body_mapper.h:110`)
- Leissa, Vibration of Plates (1969), free circular plate mode shape W = A·J_n(kr) + C·I_n(kr), as given in Dong & Liu, arXiv 2610.29194, Appendix A (textbook). https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.29194. Establishes: the mode shape is J plus modified-Bessel I under free-edge moment and shear conditions; (0,1) has a nodal circle at r ≈ 0.68a and a centre antinode.
- Auditor's measurement: shape probe (scratchpad shape_probe.js) comparing computePlateAmplitude with the true R_mn. Establishes: at strikePos 0.5 the fundamental (2,0) is nulled to the 0.05 floor (-26 dB); at strikePos 1.0, (3,0), (1,1) and (5,0) are floored although the true rim responses of (3,0) and (5,0) are 0.80 and 0.72; at strikePos 0 the code gives every n = 0 mode 1.00 against true values of 0.19 / 0.05 / 0.03 for (2,0) / (4,0) / (5,0).
- Perrin, Swallowe, Zietlow, Moore, 'The normal modes of cymbals', Proc. IoA, 2008 (paper; seen only through a search-result summary, the PDF did not load). https://www.ioa.org.uk/system/files/proceedings/r_perrin_gm_swallowe_sa_zietlow_tr_moore_the_normal_modes_of_cymbals.pdf. Establishes (weak, corroboration only): a cymbal is a slightly perturbed axisymmetric plate, and imperfections split the degenerate pairs and fix the orientation of the nodal diameters.

**115. The five principal bell partials (hum, prime, tierce, quint, nominal) are 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.6 / 0.75 / 1.0 of the nominal** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/bell_modes.h:16-19, 56-58`)
- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed. (2008), p. 682 (Ross & Perrin 1987 data), as tabulated in Wikipedia 'Strike tone' (textbook). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_tone. Establishes: relative to the prime, (2,0) hum 0.500; (2,1#) prime 1.000; (3,1) tierce 1.200 ideal / 1.189 ET / 1.183 actual; (3,1#) quint 1.500 / 1.498 / 1.506; (4,1) nominal 2.000.
- B. Hibberts, 'Identifying bell partials' (The Sound of Bells) (docs). https://www.hibberts.co.uk/identifying-bell-partials/. Establishes: the five main partials and their intervals below the nominal: hum two octaves, prime one octave, tierce a major sixth (about 0.6), quint a fourth (0.75).
- Hibbert, Sharp, Taherzadeh & Perrin, 'Partial Frequencies and Chladni's Law in Church Bells', Open Journal of Acoustics 4(2):70-77, 2014 (paper). https://file.scirp.org/Html/3-1610109_46533.htm. Establishes: true-harmonic bells (about 36.5 % of 2,752 measured) have the hum at -2400 cents and the tierce at -900 cents from the nominal.

**116. The upper partial ratios (entries 5..15) come from 'Hibberts' big-bell Chladni fit'** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/bell_modes.h:20, 53-60`)
- Fletcher & Rossing (2008), p. 682, via Wikipedia 'Strike tone' (textbook). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_tone. Establishes: actual-bell ratios relative to the prime: (4,1#) 2.514, (2,2) 2.662, (5,1) 3.011, (6,1) 4.166, (7,1) 5.433, (8,1) 6.796, (9,1) 8.215.
- Hibbert, Sharp, Taherzadeh & Perrin, 'Partial Frequencies and Chladni's Law in Church Bells', Open Journal of Acoustics, 2014 (paper). https://file.scirp.org/Html/3-1610109_46533.htm. Establishes: rim partials obey f = C(m+b)^p, with b, p and C different for each bell; the modified law predicts individual bells well but gives no single model across bells; rim partials are labelled by m (hum 2, tierce 3, nominal 4, superquint 5, octave nominal 6, ...).
- Hibberts, 'Identifying bell partials' (docs). https://www.hibberts.co.uk/identifying-bell-partials/. Establishes: the superquint lies about a fifth above the nominal (10 nodal lines) and the octave nominal about an octave above (12), followed by I-7 (14) and I-8 (16).

**117. (m,n) group assignments of the bell partials (nodal meridians per partial)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/bell_modes.h:35-40, 68-76`)
- Hibberts, 'Identifying bell partials' (nodal-line census of the Perrin, Charnley & DePont bell) (docs). https://www.hibberts.co.uk/identifying-bell-partials/. Establishes: nodal meridian lines: hum 4, prime 4 (group II, nodal circle at 0.30), tierce 6 (circle 0.54), quint 6 (circle 0.19), nominal 8 (0.54), superquint 10 (0.54, 1.00), octave nominal 12 (0.28, 0.98), I-7 14, I-8 16.
- Fletcher & Rossing (2008), p. 682, via Wikipedia 'Strike tone' (textbook). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_tone. Establishes: mode labels (2,0) hum, (2,1#) prime, (3,1) tierce, (3,1#) quint, (4,1) nominal, (4,1#) deciem, (2,2) undeciem, (5,1) twelfth, (6,1) upper octave, (7,1), (8,1), (9,1).

**118. Strike Position -> strike azimuth with meridional |cos(m*theta)| weighting is the right mode shape for a bell struck at the soundbow** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/bell_modes.h:22-40, 78-102`; also `bell_mapper.h:43-48`)
- Perrin, Charnley & DePont, 'Normal modes of the modern English church bell', J. Sound Vib. 90(1), 1983 (also IOA proceedings) (paper; quoted from the search excerpt, the scanned PDF could not be text-extracted). https://www.hibberts.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/perrin_charnley_depont_1982.pdf. Establishes: in a perfectly axisymmetric bell, every m > 0 mode belongs to a degenerate doublet whose members have the same nodal pattern apart from orientation; imperfections fix the nodal meridians and split the doublet frequencies.
- Hibberts, 'Identifying bell partials' (docs). https://www.hibberts.co.uk/identifying-bell-partials/. Establishes: struck on the soundbow on a nodal line of one doublet half, that half is quietest and its partner loudest; rim partials (tierce upward) are strongest at the rim; partials other than hum and prime are quiet at the soundbow and strong in the waist.
- Hibberts, 'Doublets or warble in bells' (docs). https://www.hibberts.co.uk/doublets-or-warble-in-bells/. Establishes: doublets come from departures from axial symmetry; striking between the two special points sounds both notes (warble), so azimuth changes beating, not whether the partial is present.
- Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, Ch. 21 (bells) / Ch. 3 (membranes: J_m(kr)·cos(mθ) and sin(mθ) degenerate pairs), via the Wikipedia circular-membrane article (textbook). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibration_of_a_circular_membrane. Establishes: each m ≥ 1 mode exists as a cos/sin degenerate pair; the axisymmetric problem has no preferred azimuth.
- Bilbao, 'Modal synthesis' (CCRMA) (textbook). https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~bilbao/booktop/node14.html. Establishes: a point excitation drives each mode by the projection of the input onto that mode shape at the excitation point.

**119. Base mallet contact of ~9.5 ms at mass 0.3 is a realistic drumhead contact time** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/exciters/mallet_exciter.h:51-58, 81-90`; backend `dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/impact_exciter.h:131-146, 239-242`)
- A. Wagner, 'Analysis of drumbeats - interaction between drummer, drumstick and instrument', MSc thesis, KTH (supervisors S. Dahl, A. Askenfelt), 2006 (thesis). https://www.speech.kth.se/publications/masterprojects/2006/AndreasWagner.pdf. Establishes: stick-membrane contact lasts 3-6 ms (abstract); at the centre it falls from about 7-7.5 ms (piano) to about 4.5-6 ms (forte), and at the rim from about 4.5 to 3 ms (Fig. 4.7); contact time decreases as stick velocity rises; the forte contact time falls as head tension rises, about 4.6 to 3.5 ms (Fig. 4.10).
- S. Dahl, 'Striking movements: a survey of motion analysis of percussionists', Acoust. Sci. & Tech. 32(5), 2011 (paper). https://vbn.aau.dk/ws/files/65339564/Dahl_J_AST_review_submi.pdf. Establishes: typical stick-drumhead contact durations are 5-8 ms for a mezzoforte stroke at the centre of a tom or snare.
- F. Avanzini & D. Rocchesso, 'Physical modeling of impacts: theory and experiments on contact time and spectral centroid', SMC 2004 (paper). https://avanzini.di.unimi.it/downloads/publications/avanzini_smc04_finalsub.pdf. Establishes: against a resonator, t0 is always longer than the rigid prediction because of the struck object's compliance; a short t0 gives a bright attack and a long t0 a low spectral centroid.

**120. Contact time follows Hertzian scaling T ~ m^(2/5) k^(-2/5) v^(-1/5)** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/impact_exciter.h:119-143`)
- A. He & J. S. Wettlaufer, 'Hertz beyond belief', Soft Matter 10, 2014 (arXiv:1306.4952) (paper). https://arxiv.org/pdf/1306.4952. Establishes: Eq. (1a), Hertz collision time Te = 2.8683·(M²/(R·V·E²))^(1/5); collision time and maximum contact area depend only weakly on impact velocity.
- F. Avanzini & D. Rocchesso, SMC 2004 (paper). https://avanzini.di.unimi.it/downloads/publications/avanzini_smc04_finalsub.pdf. Establishes: Eq. (12), t0 depends only on dissipation, alpha, m/k and the input velocity, with t0 ∝ (m/k)^(1/(alpha+1)); the spectral centroid is strongly correlated with contact time.
- A. Wagner, KTH MSc thesis, 2006 (thesis). https://www.speech.kth.se/publications/masterprojects/2006/AndreasWagner.pdf. Establishes: over an 8-stroke piano-to-forte crescendo the centre contact time falls gradually, from about 7 to about 4.5-6 ms (Fig. 4.7).

**121. An ~8 ms Hann-like pulse has a spectral null region near ~244 Hz** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/exciters/mallet_exciter.h:52-54`)
- J. O. Smith III, 'Spectral Audio Signal Processing', CCRMA online book, Hann or Hanning or Raised Cosine (textbook). https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Hann_Hanning_Raised_Cosine.html. Establishes: the Hann main lobe is twice as wide as the rectangular window's, so its first zero is at 2/T; side lobes fall off at about 18 dB per octave.
- A. Wagner, KTH MSc thesis, 2006 (thesis). https://www.speech.kth.se/publications/masterprojects/2006/AndreasWagner.pdf. Establishes: measured force pulses show reflected-wave bumps at about 3.75-6 ms and multiple contacts at high dynamics, so they are not clean symmetric windows (Sec. 4.1).

**122. A harder (faster) hit gives a shorter contact** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/impact_exciter.h:136-139, 119-126`)
- A. Wagner, KTH MSc thesis, 2006 (thesis). https://www.speech.kth.se/publications/masterprojects/2006/AndreasWagner.pdf. Establishes: with increasing dynamic level, i.e. increasing stick velocity, the contact time decreases (Fig. 4.7).
- A. He & J. S. Wettlaufer, 'Hertz beyond belief', 2014 (paper). https://arxiv.org/pdf/1306.4952. Establishes: Te ∝ V^(-1/5), so collision time decreases weakly with impact velocity.

**123. The struck body's size sets the mallet contact time (D4 piecewise cubic mass scaling)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/exciters/mallet_exciter.h:51-67, 88-90`; caller `plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:336-340`)
- A. Wagner, KTH MSc thesis, 2006 (thesis). https://www.speech.kth.se/publications/masterprojects/2006/AndreasWagner.pdf. Establishes: contact time falls as the strike moves from centre to rim (Fig. 4.7); higher tension gives shorter force pulses, an earlier reflected wave and shorter contact (Fig. 4.10).
- F. Avanzini & D. Rocchesso, SMC 2004 (paper). https://avanzini.di.unimi.it/downloads/publications/avanzini_smc04_finalsub.pdf. Establishes: t0 ∝ (m/k)^(1/(alpha+1)); against a resonator, t0 exceeds the rigid prediction because of the struck object's compliance.

**124. Mallet velocity mapping gives an 8 ms (soft) to 1 ms (hard) contact (header comment, spec FR-011 / spec 135)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/exciters/mallet_exciter.h:10-18` comment vs `81-90` code; `specs/135-membrum-drum-synth.md:127, 644-648`)
- A. Wagner, KTH MSc thesis, 2006 (thesis). https://www.speech.kth.se/publications/masterprojects/2006/AndreasWagner.pdf. Establishes: stick-membrane contact lasts 3-6 ms (abstract); the forte minimum is about 3 ms at the rim (Fig. 4.7).
- S. Dahl, Acoust. Sci. & Tech. 32(5), 2011 (paper). https://vbn.aau.dk/ws/files/65339564/Dahl_J_AST_review_submi.pdf. Establishes: typical stick-drumhead contact durations are 5-8 ms for a mezzoforte stroke.

**125. The noise component of the impact pulse is 'pinked' by a one-pole filter** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/impact_exciter.h:244-250`)
- J. O. Smith III, 'Introduction to Digital Filters', CCRMA online book, One-Pole section (textbook). https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/fp/One_Pole.html. Establishes: the filter has a pole at z = -a_1; it is lowpass when the pole is near z = 1 (a_1 approaching -1) and highpass when a_1 is positive.

**126. The R = b1 + b3*f^2 per-mode damping law is used as the drum-head (Membrane) loss law** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/modal_resonator_bank.h:106-139, 362-368`; also `plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/membrane_mapper.h:53-80, 148-152, 177`)
- N. H. Fletcher & T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer 1998, Table 18.4, Sec. 18.7, Table 18.8 (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: on timpani (after Christian et al. 1984) the (11), (21), (31), (41) modes decay much more slowly than (01), (02), (03), e.g. with kettle at T = 3710 N/m (01) 0.4 s, (11) 2.3 s, (21) 3.7 s, (31) 4.6 s; radiation accounts for a major part of the damping, and the monopole (01) damps out fast; on a 32 cm tom-tom (Bork 1983), (01) T60 is 0.8-1.05 s against 1.1-2.7 s in the 500 Hz third-octave band.
- C. J. Webb, Parallel computation techniques for virtual acoustics and physical modelling synthesis, PhD thesis, Univ. of Edinburgh, 2014, ch. 7 (Bilbao/Webb timpani model), Eq. 7.2 (thesis). https://www.ness.music.ed.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2014/07/CJWebb_thesis-1.pdf. Establishes: the membrane PDE carries a viscothermal term c_M²·eta·Laplacian(dw/dt), which gives a mode decay ∝ k², i.e. ∝ f².
- A. Sterling, N. Rewkowski, R. L. Klatzky, M. C. Lin, 'Audio-Material Reconstruction for Virtualized Reality Using a Probabilistic Damping Model', IEEE TVCG 2019 (paper). https://gamma.cs.unc.edu/ProbDampModel/data/pdm.pdf. Establishes: Eq. 1, Rayleigh damping c_i = alpha1 + alpha2·lambda_i (lambda = omega²) is the most common damping model for sound synthesis, i.e. the b1 + b3·f² form.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of Drums', Physics Today 45(3):40-47, 1992 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: air loading sets the harmonic relation of kettledrum modes, and the other effects can strongly affect how fast the sound decays.

**127. Shell/head damping comments cite 'Chaigne (1993) / Chaigne & Askenfelt 1993' as the source of the shell's b1 + b3*f^2 law** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:1450-1452`; also `plugins/membrum/src/dsp/pad_config.h:111-116`)
- A. Chaigne & A. Askenfelt, 'Numerical simulations of piano strings. I. A physical model for a struck string using finite difference methods', JASA 95(2):1112-1118, 1994 (paper). https://www.math.kent.edu/~zheng/62262/piano_wave.pdf. Establishes: received 8 March 1993, published February 1994; Eq. (3) gives 1/tau = b1 + b3·omega² for a stiff damped STRING; the constants are fitted empirically and lump air, material and soundboard losses together; the law is 'only a fair approximation'; even-order polynomials in frequency were chosen for stability and causality.
- N. H. Fletcher & T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Sec. 2.13 (Eq. 2.42, Fig. 2.15) (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: internal damping gives tau2 = E1/(π·f·E2), a loss rate ∝ f when E2/E1 is frequency-independent; air viscosity gives tau ∝ 1/sqrt(f); only when end or support losses dominate does tau vary as about 1/f².
- R. L. Klatzky, D. K. Pai, E. P. Krotkov, 'Perception of Material from Contact Sounds', Presence 9(4):399-410, 2000 (paper). https://www.cs.ubc.ca/labs/lci/papers/docs2000/pai-KlaPai00.pdf. Establishes: following Wildes & Richards, b(f) = π·tan(phi)·f, linear in frequency; Chaigne & Doutaut (1997) show that viscoelastic dissipation adds a quadratic term; a constant term is usually small.

**128. Material identity (metal / wood / plastic) is mapped mainly onto b3 (the f^2 term)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/pad_config.h:111-116, 274-283`; with `membrane_mapper.h:121, 148-152`, `modal_resonator_bank.h:133-139`, `shell_mapper.h:56-58`)
- A. Sterling, N. Rewkowski, R. L. Klatzky, M. C. Lin, 'Audio-Material Reconstruction for Virtualized Reality Using a Probabilistic Damping Model', IEEE TVCG 2019 (paper). https://gamma.cs.unc.edu/ProbDampModel/data/pdm.pdf. Establishes: Table 1 Rayleigh fits (alpha1, alpha2): porcelain plate 3.9 / 1e-8, travertine 1.3 / 2.5e-8, wood block 39.0 / 1.3e-7, steel wrench 2.3 / 6.9e-8, plastic bowl 39.8 / 1.3e-7, glass tile 2.0 / 7.8e-8; listeners confuse wood and plastic.
- R. L. Klatzky, D. K. Pai, E. P. Krotkov, 'Perception of Material from Contact Sounds', Presence 9(4), 2000 (paper). https://www.cs.ubc.ca/labs/lci/papers/docs2000/pai-KlaPai00.pdf. Establishes: the decay parameter tau_d = 1/(π·tan(phi)) (a decay rate linear in f) strongly determined perceived material; the constant term is usually small and the viscoelastic quadratic term secondary.

**129. Low-mode decay range (b1) covers measured timpani and tom-tom T60** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/membrane_mapper.h:53-80, 148-152`; with `modal_resonator_bank.h:133-139`, `default_kit.h:46-51, 143-148`)
- N. H. Fletcher & T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Tables 18.4 and 18.8 (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: timpani mode T60 from under 0.3 s to 4.6 s, depending on mode and tension; tom-tom (01) T60 0.8-1.05 s across five head types.

**130. The b3 ceiling (1e-3 s, 'widened empirically') and the default tom b3 (1.5e-4) damp drum-head partials far faster than measured** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/membrane_mapper.h:56-63, 75-78`; with `default_kit.h:128-131, 166-174`, `pad_config.h:276-279`)
- N. H. Fletcher & T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Table 18.8 (after Bork 1983) and Table 18.4 (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: on a 32 cm tom-tom, (01) T60 is 0.8-1.05 s and the 500 Hz third-octave T60 is 2.5 / 2.7 s (Ambassador), 2.5 / 1.4 s (Diplomat) and 1.1 s (Emperor); timpani (31) and (41) modes ring for 1.7-4.6 s.
- A. Sterling, N. Rewkowski, R. L. Klatzky, M. C. Lin, IEEE TVCG 2019 (paper). https://gamma.cs.unc.edu/ProbDampModel/data/pdm.pdf. Establishes: wood block and plastic bowl have Rayleigh alpha2 = 1.3e-7 (per omega², on c = 2d), about 2.6e-6 s as a Hz-convention amplitude decay rate, the largest f² coefficient among the measured materials.

**131. Secondary shell bank damping: references a fake body b1 on sentinel pads, and its b3 direction inverts the 'Material' semantic** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:1464-1483`; with `pad_config.h:296-306`)
- A. Sterling, N. Rewkowski, R. L. Klatzky, M. C. Lin, IEEE TVCG 2019 (paper). https://gamma.cs.unc.edu/ProbDampModel/data/pdm.pdf. Establishes: steel wrench alpha1 2.3, alpha2 6.9e-8 against wood block alpha1 39.0, alpha2 1.3e-7, so metal is lower in both terms.
- N. H. Fletcher & T. D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Sec. 2.13 (textbook). https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/The_Physics_of_Musical_Instruments.pdf. Establishes: internal damping is negligible in solid metal and dominant in lossy materials (gut, nylon), where it makes the upper partials decay faster; a less lossy material gives a brighter, longer tail.

**132. Snare wires are driven by head motion (citation: Bilbao 2012)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h:120-124`; also `pad_config.h:262-266`, `drum_voice.h:1697-1705`, `CHANGELOG.md:75-80`)
- S. Bilbao, A. Torin, V. Chatziioannou, 'Numerical Modeling of Collisions in Musical Instruments', Acta Acustica united with Acustica (2012/2015 r2) (paper). https://www.ness.music.ed.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/bilbao_acustica_r2.pdf. Establishes: Sec. 8.4, the snares are in contact with the lower membrane and are launched by contact with it; their motion starts coherent and is quickly randomised by repeated collisions; ref. [5] is S. Bilbao, JASA 131 (2012) 914-925, in which the collisions were treated by ad hoc methods.
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of Drums', Physics Today 45(3), March 1992 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: the snares stretch across the lower head, and when the batter head is struck the snare head vibrates against them; the heads couple acoustically through the enclosed air or mechanically through the shell.

**133. Wire buzz as a linear, peak-normalised follower of the batter-body modal energy (no contact threshold, no cavity delay)** (`plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:1499-1515` computeWireGainMod; `857-861, 910-918` fast path; `1051, 1073-1081` slow path; `542-549` process() leaves wireGainMod_ = 1)
- A. Torin, B. Hamilton, S. Bilbao, 'An Energy Conserving Finite Difference Scheme for the Simulation of Collisions in Snare Drums', DAFx-14, 2014 (paper). https://www.pure.ed.ac.uk/ws/files/17485699/dafx14_submission_56_3.pdf. Establishes: Sec. 5.2, a pressure rise in the cavity pushes the lower membrane and the snares down; the snares reach maximum displacement at about 6 ms, strike the membrane almost coherently at about 9 ms, and then move chaotically.
- S. Bilbao, A. Torin, V. Chatziioannou, 'Numerical Modeling of Collisions in Musical Instruments', Acta Acustica 2012 (paper). https://www.ness.music.ed.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/bilbao_acustica_r2.pdf. Establishes: the wire/membrane interaction uses a power-law collision potential, so the contact force exists only under penetration, which makes it strongly nonlinear and amplitude-dependent.

**134. '4 partials capture ~95% of audible sympathetic energy (Lehtonen et al. 2007)', plus the amount range 'calibrated per Lehtonen et al. (2007)'** (`dsp/include/krate/dsp/systems/sympathetic_resonance.h:38-40, 146-149`; used by `plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:1250-1258`)
- H.-M. Lehtonen, H. Penttinen, J. Rauhala, V. Välimäki, 'Analysis and modeling of piano sustain-pedal effects', J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 122(3):1787, 2007 (paper; abstract). https://pubs.aip.org/asa/jasa/article-abstract/122/3/1787/853180. Establishes: the sustain pedal lengthens the decay of partials in the middle of the keyboard; the synthesis model uses 12 string models for the lowest tones; the abstract gives no partial count and no energy percentage.
- S. Zambon, H.-M. Lehtonen, B. Bank, 'Simulation of piano sustain-pedal effect by parallel second-order filters', DAFx-08 (paper). https://dafx.de/paper-archive/2008/papers/dafx08_37.pdf. Establishes: describes the 2007 model as a reverberation algorithm of 12 simplified string models for the lowest piano tones; uses a few (4-32) resonators for the first partials of each key.

**135. Cross-pad coupling makes idle drums ring in sympathy ('kick makes snare wires buzz', Snare Buzz / Tom Resonance route energy through a category matrix into other pads' excitation)** (`plugins/membrum/MANUAL.md:426-437`; code `plugins/membrum/src/processor/processor.cpp:131-143, 411-424, 693-706`, `plugins/membrum/src/voice_pool/voice_pool.cpp:243-248`, `dsp/include/krate/dsp/systems/sympathetic_resonance.h:179-249, 312-348`)
- T. D. Rossing, 'Acoustics of Drums', Physics Today 45(3), 1992 (paper). https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v45.i3.40_1.online.pdf. Establishes: the two heads of a drum couple strongly, acoustically through the enclosed air or mechanically through the shell; the snare head vibrates against the snares; a drum responds through its own (paired) modes.
- S. Bilbao, A. Torin, V. Chatziioannou, 'Numerical Modeling of Collisions in Musical Instruments', Acta Acustica 2012 (paper). https://www.ness.music.ed.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/bilbao_acustica_r2.pdf. Establishes: in the snare model the drum sits in a box of air, and the snares are launched by contact with the pressure-driven lower membrane; buzz is wire collision driven by snare-head motion, not a tuned resonance of the source drum.

**136. Coupling Delay above 1.5 ms 'simulates larger physical rooms where sympathetic resonance has to travel further'** (`plugins/membrum/MANUAL.md:529`; control row 433; code `processor.cpp:425-430, 693-702, 1082`)
- J. O. Smith III, Physical Audio Signal Processing (CCRMA online book), 'Converting Propagation Distance to Delay Length' (textbook). https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp05/Converting_Propagation_Distance_Delay.html. Establishes: c = 345 m/s at 22 °C and 1 atm; delay length M = d/(c·T) samples.
- CCRMA Music 152 course notes, 'Auditorium Acoustics' (citing Beranek 1962) (docs). https://ccrma.stanford.edu/CCRMA/Courses/152/auditorium_acoustics.html. Establishes: early reflections usually arrive within about 50 ms; a hall reads as intimate when the gap between the direct sound and the first reflection is under 20 ms; room character comes from reflection delays of tens of ms, not from sub-2 ms paths.

## 6. Findings

### Critical (6)

#### MB-001 — Kit/pad preset browser loads (and setState) rewrite the voice pool, allocator, pad configs and coupling engine on the message thread while process() runs. A probe reproduces the crash.

**Severity:** critical · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Category:** threading · **Dimension:** rt-safety · **Also flagged by:** lifecycle-state, test-gaps

**Corroborated by measurement:** Probe focus2:double-apply:interleave: "~70 field types differ (hybrid kit; noiseLayerGain stays K2) / 0.477 / none" (fields != K2 after K1 edits / snare max diff vs pure K2 / after K2 edits). processor.cpp:1239 applies the kit on the message thread; processor.cpp:232 `voicePool_.setPadConfigField(padIdx, padOff, fValue);` later on the audio thread.

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/src/processor/processor.cpp:1222-1266](plugins/membrum/src/processor/processor.cpp#L1222) (notify LoadPresetState / LoadPadPreset), [processor.cpp:905-1003](plugins/membrum/src/processor/processor.cpp#L905) (setState / applyKitSnapshot), [processor.cpp:1005-1018](plugins/membrum/src/processor/processor.cpp#L1005)

**Problem.** Processor::notify() runs on the host's UI/message thread. It parses the blob and calls applyKitSnapshot() / applyPadPresetSnapshot() directly. Those functions write:
- every DrumVoice through resetAllVoicesForKitSwitch() (voice_pool.cpp:268-281: 32 voice resets, metas, allocator_.reset(), setVoiceCount);
- voicePool_.setMaxPolyphony() (which can std::swap voices, voice_pool.cpp:570-588);
- all 32 PadConfigs through padConfigMut();
- the choke table;
- couplingEngine_.reset() / setAmount();
- couplingDelay_.reset();
- the plain float energyEnvelope_;
- selectedPadIndex_ and padCategories_;
- couplingMatrix_;
- the MacroMapper cache (invalidateCache / syncCacheFromCfg).

At the same time the audio thread runs VoicePool::noteOn / processBlock, couplingEngine_.process(), applyEnergyLimiter() and macroMapper_.apply(). No transfer object, flag, atomic or lock exists. Processor::setState (905-916) has the same exposure in hosts that load state during playback. getState (871-903) also reads padConfigs_ from the UI thread while processParameterChanges writes them.

**Why wrong.** Project rule: state written from another thread must reach the audio thread through an atomic or a transfer object, never by writing engine members directly. VST3 sends IConnectionPoint messages on the UI thread, never on the audio thread. VoiceAllocator, SympatheticResonance (activeCount_, resonator arrays), DelayLine and DrumVoice are single-threaded objects. Ruinae (RTTransferT stateTransfer_, ruinae/src/processor/processor.h:526-530) and Disrumpo (pendingState_, disrumpo/src/processor/processor.h:459-592) already hand presets to the audio thread. The Ruinae-audit fix plan that introduced these handlers (specs/ruinae-audit/fix-plan.md:941, T1.37) assumed "the same thread hand-off setState uses", but setState has no hand-off.

**Consequence.** Loading a kit or pad preset from the inline browser while the transport plays (or while a pad rings) can crash the host. It can also corrupt the allocator or the coupling pool (stuck or ghost voices, leaked resonators), or render a half-old / half-new kit. Measured, see evidence. This is a regression from R-202 / R-203 in the latest merged commit 536d8af3: before that commit, notify() handled only AuditionPad / AuditionPadOff.

**Evidence.** processor.cpp:1239 `applyKitSnapshot(kit);` and :1265 `applyPadPresetSnapshot(static_cast<int>(pad), preset);` sit inside notify(). Body: processor.cpp:927 `voicePool_.resetAllVoicesForKitSwitch();`, :932 `voicePool_.setMaxPolyphony(...)`, :939-942 `State::applyPadSnapshot(..., voicePool_.padConfigMut(pad))`, :965-967 `couplingEngine_.reset(); couplingDelay_.reset(); energyEnvelope_ = 0.0f;`, :1000-1002 macroMapper_ cache writes. `git show 7ac00404` has no LoadPresetState handler; it arrived in 536d8af3.

PROBE C:/Users/scab/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/af40cef86e602ebb/69f67fe4-9e20-4f6f-a325-fd4459c6f76b/scratchpad/rtprobe/probe3.cpp, built against the real voice_pool.cpp and KrateDSP.lib. The audio thread runs noteOn + VoicePool::processBlock(128) + SympatheticResonance::process. A second thread mirrors applyKitSnapshot every 2 ms: resetAllVoicesForKitSwitch, setMaxPolyphony(4..16), overwrite padConfigsArray (default kit vs an FMImpulse+String kit), engine.reset/setAmount.
- Unserialised: 3 of 3 runs crashed (exit 0xC0000409); the first build crashed with 0xC0000005.
- Control (same code with a mutex around both sides): 21826 blocks, 192 kit loads, 0 non-finite samples, exit 0.

**Suggested fix.** Parse on the message thread into a preallocated KitSnapshot / PadPresetSnapshot. Publish it with Steinberg::Vst::RTTransferT (as Ruinae does) or an atomic slot (as Disrumpo does). Apply it at the top of process(), before processParameterChanges, on the audio thread. Route setState through the same path when the processor is active. Test: a two-thread case where one thread drives notify('LoadPresetState') with alternating blobs and the other drives process() with notes, run under ASan. It must not crash, and allocator / meta counts must stay consistent. Keep the probe above as the reproducer.

**Verifier notes:**
- Could not refute: notify("LoadPresetState") (processor.cpp:1222-1241) and notify("LoadPadPreset") (:1247-1267) apply the preset directly; the controller sends both synchronously from the UI thread (controller_state.cpp:150-158, 247-256); applyKitSnapshot writes engine members at :927, :932, :939-942, :945-946, :965-967, :985-988, :999-1002 with no mutex, RTTransfer or atomic hand-off (the only atomic in notify() is pendingAudition_, :1194-1198). Regression confirmed via `git show 7ac00404`. The probe mirrors the applyKitSnapshot writes on a second thread rather than driving the real Processor::notify.
- Confirmed from source (same lines); a grep of src/processor for mutex, lock_guard, atomic_flag, RTTransfer, pending or spin finds nothing. The setState sub-claim depends on the host (most serialise setState with processing), but the browser load is a UI action during playback, so critical stands.
- Confirmed and re-ran probe3.exe: unserialised, 6 runs gave one segmentation fault (exit 139), one exit 127 with no output, and the rest finished ~520 loads in 8 s with a stale activeVoices(meta)=1; CONTROL=1 exited cleanly with 0 non-finite samples. About one crash per 1-3k loads at the probe's cadence, so a single click rarely crashes, but browsing kits during playback is the normal workflow. Also notes a std::vector allocation at :1232 (message thread) and that the setState exposure predates 536d8af3.

#### MB-008 — Modal retunes (pitch envelope, tension, Material Morph) converge with a time constant of 2 ms x host block size, so the 808 pitch sweep does not happen at normal buffer sizes

**Severity:** critical · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Category:** measured-dsp-numerics · **Dimension:** dsp-numerics

**Location:** [dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/modal_resonator_bank.h:210-219, 303-305, 431-447, 906-914](dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/modal_resonator_bank.h#L210); [plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:244, 318-321, 734-770, 1607-1626](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h#L244)

**Problem.** ModalResonatorBank::smoothCoefficients() applies the one-pole step `x += (1 - smoothCoeff_) * (target - x)` once per processBlock() call, but smoothCoeff_ = exp(-1/(2 ms * sr)) is a PER-SAMPLE coefficient. updateModes() (the state-preserving retune every Membrum modulation path uses: retuneFundamental -> updateModalFundamentalOnBank, refreshBodyForMaterialOnBank, the tension branch, updateModalParameters) only moves the targets, never snaps. So the audible epsilon/radius reach about 1.1 % of the remaining distance per host block at 44.1 kHz: tau = 2 ms x blockSize (128 ms at 64 samples, 1 s at 512, 4 s at 2048). In addition, noteOn seeds the start pitch with updateModes after configureForNoteOn's setModes has snapped the bank to the NATURAL pitch, so every note starts at the body's natural f0 instead of the envelope's start frequency.

**Why wrong.** The pitch envelope is specified as an absolute Hz trajectory (spec 137 SC-009: 160 -> 50 Hz over 20 ms reaches the target within +/-10 % at t = 20 ms). The retune must reach the bank within its own chunk; the bank's banner (modal_resonator_bank.h:307-327) already admits the render depends on call partitioning and offers snapCoefficients() for callers on a control grid, which Membrum never calls. Output must not depend on the host block size.

**Consequence.** In a DAW (blocks of 64 to 2048 samples) every pitch-envelope pad (the default-kit kick, 160 -> 50 Hz / 20 ms, default_kit.h:54-61, and all factory 808/tom sweeps) plays at the body's natural pitch with a slow drift instead of the sweep. Tension glide, Material Morph and live Size/Material edits on a ringing voice lag the same way. The result changes with the host buffer size. Only per-sample rendering (block 1) is correct. Both tests miss it: test_pitch_envelope_808.cpp:119 renders through the per-sample process(), which smooths once per sample. test_pitch_env_all_bodies.cpp:123-127 reads getModeFrequency(), which returns the TARGET epsilon (modal_resonator_bank.h:529), not the coefficient that is sounding.

**Evidence.** Measured with a standalone probe that links the built KrateDSP.lib (scratchpad probe/voice_probe.cpp, pitchEnv()). Membrane size 0.2 (natural 316 Hz), pitch env 160 -> 50 Hz / 20 ms, f0 from zero crossings of the lowpassed output.
- 44.1 kHz, block 1: 50.2 / 50.0 / 50.0 Hz in the 30-100 / 100-250 / 250-500 ms windows.
- Block 64: 216.6 / 123.4 / 67.1 Hz. Block 512: 299.8 / 274.6 / 235.0 Hz. Block 2048: 311.3 / 304.1 / 292.1 Hz.
- 96 kHz gives the same figures per block size, so tau scales with blockSize, not with time.
- Tension 1.0 on Membrane size 0.4 (natural ~199 Hz), 50-100 ms window: 208.6 Hz at block 32, 201.0 at 256, 199.7 at 1024, 199.5 at 2048.

Code: `void smoothCoefficients() { const float oneMinusCoeff = 1.0f - smoothCoeff_; ... epsilon_[k] += oneMinusCoeff * (epsilonTarget_[k] - epsilon_[k]);` called once at the start of processBlock (:433). updateModes -> computeModeCoefficients(..., snapSmoothing=false) (:303-304).

**Suggested fix.** Membrum-local, so Innexus and Seraphis output stay unchanged: when the pitch envelope, tension or morph is active, split processBlockFast/Slow into sub-chunks of 32 or 64 samples. After each updateModes call sharedBank.snapCoefficients(), as Seraphis ContinuousBody does. Snap after the noteOn seed retune (drum_voice.h:318-321) too. Alternative in the bank, gated by an opt-in like the output-stage setters: use 1 - smoothCoeff^numSamples per processBlock. Tests: render the 160 -> 50 Hz kick through DrumVoice::processBlock at blocks 64, 512 and 2048 at 44.1 and 96 kHz. Assert a zero-crossing f0 within +/-10 % of 50 Hz in the 30-100 ms window and agreement across block sizes. Change test_pitch_env_all_bodies to measure the audio, not epsilonTarget_.

**Verifier notes:**
- Could not refute: smoothCoeff_ is per sample (modal_resonator_bank.h:213) but smoothCoefficients (:906-914) runs once per processBlock (:431-447, :450-458) and once per prepareBlockSmoothing (:386-389); updateModes (:294-305) writes only the targets (:837-839) and skips the snap (:877-881); no snapCoefficients call in plugins/membrum/src/dsp. The chunk equals the host block (drum_voice.h:589, :701, :734-770, :799; voice_pool.cpp:356, 410, 471, 528; processor.cpp:636/663), so tau = 2 ms x blockSize; the noteOn seed (:318-321) only moves the target; the tests read targets or render per sample (test_pitch_envelope_808.cpp:119, test_pitch_env_all_bodies.cpp:123/127).
- Confirmed, no upstream sub-chunking guards it; the comment at drum_voice.h:613-619 assumes a 64-sample refresh rate, so the lag is not a design choice; test_per_pad_pitch_env.cpp:122-139 only checks that two pads differ in energy; no spec, comment or prior audit treats it as intended.
- Could not refute: kSmoothingTimeMs = 2.0f (:647); every body forwards the whole chunk to sharedBank.processBlock (membrane_body.h:68, plate_body.h:63, bell_body.h:59, shell_body.h:71, noise_body.h:117); the comment at drum_voice.h:616-619 assumes ~14 refresh points per sweep, which the smoothing defeats; the quoted figures fit the arithmetic (one 1 - exp(-1/88.2) step per call at 44.1 kHz).

#### MB-026 — Pitch envelope, tension glide and Material Morph barely move the sounding modes on the block path: the bank's smoothing step runs once per block, and the result depends on host block size (H-3 fix not effective)

**Severity:** critical · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Category:** measured-body-model · **Dimension:** bodies-modal · **Also flagged by:** layers-shaper

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:318-321, 734-770, 1607-1626](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h#L318)

**Problem.** retuneFundamental, updateModalFundamentalOnBank, the tension branch and refreshBodyForMaterialOnBank call ModalResonatorBank::updateModes(). That call only writes the coefficient TARGETS (computeModeCoefficients(..., snapSmoothing=false), modal_resonator_bank.h:303, 877-881). The bank moves epsilon_/radius_/inputGain_ toward those targets in smoothCoefficients() (modal_resonator_bank.h:906-914). The step coefficient is the PER-SAMPLE one, 1-exp(-1/(2 ms*sr)) = 1.1 % at 44.1 kHz, but processBlock applies it only ONCE per processBlock call (:431-447). DrumVoice calls bodyBank_.processBlock once per chunk, and VoicePool passes the whole host block (voice_pool.cpp:356, 471). Each retune therefore moves the sounding frequency 1.1 % of the way per host block. At noteOn, setModes snaps the bank to the NATURAL f0 (configureForNoteOn, line 244). The start-Hz retune at 318-321 is an unsnapped updateModes, so the note also starts at the natural pitch.

**Why wrong.** The pitch envelope must sweep the sounding body pitch from Start to End within Time (spec 137 SC-009: 160->50 Hz in 20 ms, within +/-10 % at t = 20 ms). The smoothing law is meant to be a 2 ms de-zipper. Applied once per block it becomes a 2 ms x blockSize lag (88 blocks to 1/e), so the trajectory depends on how the host partitions the buffer. The bank's own banner (modal_resonator_bank.h:314-323) admits this and provides snapCoefficients(), which Membrum never calls. The three renderers are not equivalent: process() smooths per sample and does sweep.

**Consequence.** Default kit kick (default_kit.h:58-61, natural f0 79 Hz, envelope 160->50 Hz over 20 ms) at 44.1 kHz:
- With 512-sample blocks it sounds 80.1 / 80.3 / 79.3 / 73.1 Hz at 0 / 20 / 50 / 299 ms. The 808 drop is gone.
- With 64-sample blocks it sounds 83 Hz at 20 ms and 68 Hz at 100 ms.
- The per-sample process() path sounds 115 Hz at 10 ms and 50 Hz at 50 ms.

The same applies to the 6 default-kit toms (default_kit.h:459-481), every factory pad with a pitch envelope, tension glide (Membrane) and Material Morph sweeps. The render changes audibly with the host buffer size. Prior audit H-3/M-1 is marked fixed, but its tests only read the TARGET:
- getModeFrequency() reads epsilonTarget_ (modal_resonator_bank.h:526-533), at test_pitch_env_all_bodies.cpp:121 and 126.
- The tension test reads the target too (test_per_mode_damping.cpp:506).
- SC-009 is tested only through the per-sample process() path (test_pitch_envelope_808.cpp:119).

**Evidence.** Code: modal_resonator_bank.h:303 `computeModeCoefficients(..., false)`; :433 `smoothCoefficients();` once at processBlock start; :213 `smoothCoeff_ = std::exp(-1.0f / (kSmoothingTimeMs * 0.001f * sampleRate_))`; :910 `epsilon_[k] += oneMinusCoeff * (epsilonTarget_[k] - epsilon_[k]);`. drum_voice.h:244 configureForNoteOn (setModes, snapped) precedes the :320 `retuneFundamental(initialPitchHz)` (updateModes). Measured with a node model of this exact smoothing law (scratchpad pitchsmooth.js), default-kit kick, 44.1 kHz, f0 at 0 / 10 / 20 / 50 / 100 / 299 ms:
- per-sample: 80.1 / 115.3 / 60.9 / 50.0 / 50.0 / 50.0
- 64-sample blocks: 80.1 / 83.5 / 83.2 / 76.2 / 67.8 / 53.7
- 512-sample blocks: 80.1 / 80.1 / 80.3 / 79.3 / 78.0 / 73.1

H-3 test sweep 800->100 Hz over 60 ms at 48 kHz with 256-sample blocks: the sounding f0 peaks at 193 Hz (the test asserts on targets only).

**Suggested fix.** Fix in Membrum, so Innexus keeps bit-identity. When pitch env, tension or morph is active, split each processBlockFast / processBlockSlow chunk into a fixed control grid of 16-32 samples (independent of host block size). At each grid point call updateModes() and then sharedBank.snapCoefficients(), the Seraphis ContinuousBody pattern. Snap after the noteOn seed retune at line 320, and run the strike-norm probe at the seeded start pitch.

Tests:
- Render the default-kit kick through VoicePool / DrumVoice::processBlock at block sizes 32, 64, 512 and 2048. Measure the SOUNDING f0 (zero-crossing or short FFT, not getModeFrequency) at 20 ms: it must be within +/-10 % of 50 Hz (SC-009 on the block path).
- The f0 trajectories must agree within 2 % across block sizes.
- Rewrite the H-3 and tension tests to measure audio, not epsilonTarget_.

**Verifier notes:**
- Could not refute: updateModes (modal_resonator_bank.h:294-305) writes only targets; smoothCoefficients (:906-914) runs once at processBlock start (:433, :453 for Shell's decayScale overload) with kSmoothingTimeMs = 2.0 (:647); the kernel reads epsilon_, not the target (:440-442); snapCoefficients (:342-351) is never called from plugins/membrum/src/dsp. Retunes happen once per chunk (drum_voice.h:589, :701, :734-770, :799; slow path :960-977, :1002) and the pool and processor never split the host block (voice_pool.cpp:356, 410, 471, 528; processor.cpp:636, 663); the note starts at the natural pitch because configureForNoteOn's setModes snaps first.
- Confirmed from source (node model not re-run); the comment at drum_voice.h:704-707 ("~14 refresh points ... well below any audible stair-stepping") shows the sweep was meant to be heard; the strike-norm probe's bank.reset() (:1295, :1359) also precedes the unsnapped seed at :320; the tests read only targets (modal_resonator_bank.h:526-533).
- Confirmed with an independent node model of the smoothing law, default-kit kick at 44.1 kHz: per-sample reaches 50.0 Hz by 50 ms, while 512-sample blocks give 79.9 / 79.9 / 79.9 / 78.9 / 77.6 / 72.8 Hz at 0 / 10 / 20 / 50 / 100 / 300 ms and 2048-sample blocks never leave ~78-80 Hz; this matches the reviewer's figures within the difference in sweep shape.

#### MB-027 — Feedback-exciter voices never retire: the slow path never calls flushSilentModes, so getNumActiveModes() stays above 0 forever

**Severity:** critical · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Category:** voice-path · **Dimension:** bodies-modal · **Also flagged by:** gestalt-voice

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:610-624, 989-1067, 644-669](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h#L610)

**Problem.** processBlockSlow is selected for every Feedback pad (useSlowPath = feedbackExciter, line 620). It drives the bank only through body.processSampleNoSmooth(). That function (modal_resonator_bank.h:399-412) and processSampleCore never call flushSilentModes(); only the two processBlock overloads do (:446, :457). numActiveModes_ only drops in flushSilentModes (:461-474), so it keeps the count that setModes gave at noteOn. Retirement (lines 644-669) needs bankSilent = getNumActiveModes() == 0 for BOTH the normal path (bankSilent && envFinished) and the 256-block safety net. bankSilent is never true for a Feedback voice.

**Why wrong.** A voice must retire once its body and envelope are silent. Voices that never retire are the CPU-leak hazard the task lists. VoicePool frees a slot only when voice.isActive() turns false (voice_pool.cpp:514-519), and a note-off cannot retire this voice either.

**Consequence.** Every hit on a Feedback pad holds its voice slot forever, even after the body has decayed to silence. That pad uses the costliest per-sample render path. Feedback pads exist in factory kits (tools/membrum_preset_generator.cpp:1408, 1515, 1579, 3465, 3586, ...).
- After maxPolyphony such hits the pool is permanently full, so every new note steals. Ringing tails of other pads get cut, the meters' active-voice count never returns to 0, and the main-bus silence flag is never set.
- CPU stays at the per-voice slow-path cost for each leaked voice.

**Evidence.** drum_voice.h:620 `const bool useSlowPath = feedbackExciter;`; :1030 `const float bodyOut = body.processSampleNoSmooth(sharedBank, exc);` (the only bank call in the loop); :645 `const bool bankSilent = sharedBank.getNumActiveModes() == 0;`; :647 `if (bankSilent && envFinished)`; :660 `if (bankSilent) { ++silentBlockCount_; ...`. modal_resonator_bank.h:399-412 processSampleNoSmooth has no flush; :446 / :457 are the only flushSilentModes() calls. Grep of plugins/membrum/src: flushSilentModes is never called directly. No test checks Feedback voice retirement (grep for isActive in tests that mention Feedback: test_feedback_exciter.cpp:118 only checks the exciter).

**Suggested fix.** Call sharedBank.flushSilentModes() once at the end of processBlockSlow, after the per-sample loop (and on the secondary bank if it gets retirement). Alternatively give the bank a processBlockPerSampleFeedback helper that flushes.

Test: a DrumVoice with ExciterType::Feedback on Membrane, noteOn(1.0), noteOff after 100 ms. Render 10 s in 256-sample blocks: REQUIRE(!voice.isActive()). Do the same without a noteOff and REQUIRE retirement within the safety net. Also add a VoicePool-level case: after 16 Feedback hits and 10 s of silence, getActiveVoiceCount() == 0.

**Verifier notes:**
- Could not refute (static trace, nothing run): the slow path's only bank calls are prepareBlockSmoothing (:1002), processSampleNoSmooth (:1030) and secondaryBank_.processSampleNoSmooth (:1041); every body forwards straight to the bank (membrane_body.h:57, plate_body.h:54, shell_body.h:50, bell_body.h:50, noise_body.h:94); numActiveModes_ is decremented only at modal_resonator_bank.h:471; active_ is cleared only at drum_voice.h:649 and :664. No test covers it (test_exciter_body_matrix.cpp:258, :293 use Impulse/Mallet).
- Confirmed from source: damp() (modal_resonator_bank.h:507-516), called by noteOff at drum_voice.h:451, only scales radii; the comment at drum_voice.h:633-634 assumes processBlock runs; the pool frees a slot only when isActive() turns false (voice_pool.cpp:354, :386-394) and its auto-noteOff (:380-384) cannot make bankSilent true; the prior audit findings.json records no ruling on this.
- Confirmed, but this verifier judges the impact overstated and argued for a downgrade from critical: the real consequences are a permanent CPU leak (up to maxPolyphony slow-path voices), meters that never return to 0, a main-bus silence flag that is never set, and a steal on every new note once the pool is full; "ringing tails of other pads get cut" is mostly mitigated because Oldest and Quietest stealing pick the silent leaked voices first, and no audible corruption, NaN or click comes from the leak. Factory kits use Feedback (10 ExciterType::Feedback hits in membrum_preset_generator.cpp).

#### MB-087 — MB-S01: Kit- and pad-preset SAVE build the blob from controller parameters: every pad's noiseLayerGain is saved as 0 (loads as 0.1), and damping sentinels are saved as explicit 0.5 overrides

**Severity:** critical · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Category:** lifecycle-state · **Dimension:** lifecycle-state · **Also flagged by:** parallel-paths

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/src/controller/controller_state_codec.cpp:116-181](plugins/membrum/src/controller/controller_state_codec.cpp#L116) (kLateSlots [58-93](plugins/membrum/src/controller/controller_state_codec.cpp#L58)); callers [plugins/membrum/src/controller/controller_state.cpp:105-118, 196-215](plugins/membrum/src/controller/controller_state.cpp#L105)

**Problem.** Controller::kitPresetStateProvider (controller_state.cpp:111) and padPresetStateProvider (:201) build the blob with ControllerState::buildSnapshot / buildPadSnapshotFromParams. That function fills sound[0..27], [28..29], [30..33] and the 24 kLateSlots rows (snapIndex 34..56 and 58). No row exists for snapIndex 57 (comment at :91: "snapIndex 57 = noiseLayerGain"), so sound[57] keeps the value-initialised 0.0 of PadSnapshot::sound (state_codec.h:60 `std::array<double, 59> sound{}`). On load, State::applyPadSnapshot / applyPadPresetSnapshot clamp it: `cfg.noiseLayerGain = std::clamp(static_cast<float>(snap.sound[57]), 0.1f, 16.0f)` (state_codec.cpp:243, :326). Slots 42/43 are read from the per-pad B1/B3 parameters (registered default 0.5, controller.cpp:227-228). The -1 sentinel cannot be represented, and on load the replay skips the sentinel (controller_state_codec.cpp:263-268, 309-316), so the controller keeps a stale value that the next save writes as an explicit override. Host getState (processor.cpp:895-899, State::toPadSnapshot of the live PadConfig) is the only save path that keeps both fields.

**Why wrong.** A saved preset must reload into the same processor state it was saved from (spec 139 SC-002: kit preset round-trips all 32 pads bit-exactly; FR-061 pad preset carries the sound). Two save paths that serialise the same struct from different sources (processor PadConfig vs controller parameters) must agree. Here they cannot, because two persisted fields have no parameter. noiseLayerGain is a load-bearing sound field: CHANGELOG 0.11.0 "Per-pad noise-layer gain ... snares push it above 1 so the wire can reach near-body level".

**Consequence.** Measured on the shipped factory kits (scratchpad kitscan.js parsing the 20 .vstpreset files): 640 pads, 14 with noiseLayerGain != 1 (snares 6.2 in Acoustic Studio, Orchestral, Rock Big Room and Vintage Wood; claps 2.2; cymbals 3.5 / 3.0), none with damping sentinels.
- Load a factory kit, then save it as a user kit: on reload every pad's noise layer drops 20 dB (1.0 -> 0.1), snare wires drop 35.8 dB (6.2 -> 0.1), cymbal wash 30.9 dB and clap tail 26.8 dB. Hats (noiseLayerMix 0.95, noise-dominated) lose most of their sound and snares turn into the "hollow woodblock" that 0.11.0 fixed.
- Damping, with the default kit (host state path, sentinels present): the tom pads (B1 sentinel) are saved with B1 = 0.5, so b1 goes from 2.43 to 25.1 s^-1 and T60 from 2.85 s to 0.275 s (a 10x shorter tom). The kick T60 goes from 1.54 s to 0.275 s, and its b3 from 2.8e-5 to 5e-4. The hat's 8 kHz modal decay rate goes from 77 to 32000 s^-1, so the modal body vanishes.
- Pad presets saved from the browser have the same 0.1 noise gain.

The user's saved kits and pads are silently degraded: data loss in normal use. The tests do not catch it. test_kit_uimode_roundtrip.cpp:44-135 goes controller to controller and never compares slot 57. test_pad_preset.cpp:78-153 checks only size, version, exciter, body and material. test_pad_preset.cpp:662 starts from a hand-built blob with 3.0.

**Evidence.** controller_state_codec.cpp:91 `// Wire coupling (sound[58] -> offset 65). snapIndex 57 = noiseLayerGain.` (no row for 57); :159-163 loop over kLateSlots only; state_codec.h:60 `std::array<double, 59> sound{};`; state_codec.cpp:243 and :326 clamp to 0.1..16; controller.cpp:227-228 B1/B3 defaultValue 0.5; membrane_mapper.h:71-77 `law.b1 = 0.2f + n * 49.8f` / `law.b3 = n * 1.0e-3f`; modal_resonator_bank.h:136-138 legacy b1 = 1/decayTime, b3 = (1-brightness)*4e-5; default_kit.h:120 snare noiseLayerGain 6.2, :171-174 tom B1 left at sentinel. kitscan output: "pads 640 nlg!=1 14 sentinelB1 0 sentinelB3 0 outOfRange slots {}". Computed: nlg 1->0.1 = -20.0 dB, 6.2->0.1 = -35.8 dB; tom legacy b1 2.43 (T60 2.85 s) vs override 25.1 (T60 0.275 s).

**Suggested fix.** Make the processor the only source of saved sound data. Option A: the controller keeps a per-pad mirror of the parameterless fields (noiseLayerGain, plus "damping overridden" flags or raw B1/B3 including -1). Every load path fills the mirror (setComponentState, kitPresetLoadProvider, padPresetLoadProvider, the default kit at initialize), and buildPadSnapshotFromParams reads from it. Option B (simpler, exact): the save providers request the processor's blob (an IMessage round trip, or cache the last processor getState plus parameter deltas). Regression tests: (1) processor P1 with the default kit or any factory kit, then setComponentState(controller, P1.getState), then kitPresetStateProvider, then load into a fresh processor P2 via setState, then compare P2.getState with P1.getState byte for byte (fails today at slot 57 on every pad and at slots 42/43 on sentinel pads). (2) The same for padPresetStateProvider -> LoadPadPreset -> toPadSnapshot of that pad.

**Verifier notes:**
- Confirmed from source: both preset managers are built with processor=nullptr and a state provider (controller.cpp:735-741, 755-761), so savePreset takes the blob from stateProvider_ (preset_manager.cpp:309, 359-361); kLateSlots (controller_state_codec.cpp:58-93) has no snapIndex 57; the load clamps slot 57 to 0.1 (state_codec.cpp:243, :326) against defaults of 1.0 (pad_config.h:261) and default-kit 6.2 / 3.5 / 2.2 (default_kit.h:120, 262, 336); the damping sentinel survives toPadSnapshot (state_codec.cpp:124-125) but not the controller path (controller.cpp:227-228; controller_state_codec.cpp:263-268, 309-316; state_codec.cpp:214-221; membrane_mapper.h:71-72). dB/T60 figures not re-run, but -20 dB and -35.8 dB follow directly; severity stands.
- Confirmed, with no guard, design note or test: the tests that touch sound[57] (test_pad_preset.cpp:539, :556, :662-671; test_kit_browser_load.cpp:207) start from hand-built blobs and exercise LOAD only; the R-202/R-203 comments (controller_state.cpp:146-149, 243-246) cover load only. Silent degradation of every user-saved kit and pad preset in a normal workflow, so critical holds.
- Could not refute: useStateProvider = processor_ == nullptr && stateProvider_ (preset_manager.cpp:309, :417); writeKitBlob writes every slot verbatim (state_codec.cpp:386-387); the gain multiplies the noise-layer output directly (drum_voice.h:549/861/1051); the override gives b1 = 25.1 s^-1, b3 = 0.5e-3 (membrane_mapper.h:71-77), and the default-kit tom deliberately leaves B1 on the sentinel.

#### MB-162 — Kit/pad preset SAVE from the editor drops noiseLayerGain and replaces the body-damping 'auto' sentinel, so a saved kit reloads with quieter noise and shorter decays (lead 1 confirmed)

**Severity:** critical · **Verdict:** CONFIRMED · **Category:** prior-audit-regression · **Dimension:** gestalt-controller

**Corroborated by measurement:** Probe focus1:save-path:kit:default-kit: "slot57 (noiseLayerGain) x32 pads, slot42 (B1) x22, slot43 (B3) x16; bytes not identical". pad38: "6.2->0.1 / -7.84->-42.35 / -9.52->-13.89" (noiseLayerGain / energy above 3 kHz dB / peak dBFS). Factory: "Acoustic snare -12.83->-48.37 dB", "808 snare -23.13->-42.35 dB". Pad preset: "pad38: slot57 6.2->0.1". Code: controller_state_codec.cpp:91 comment "snapIndex 57 = noiseLayerGain" with no table row; state_codec.cpp:243 `cfg.noiseLayerGain = std::clamp(static_cast<float>(snap.sound[57]), 0.1f, 16.0f);`

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/src/controller/controller_state_codec.cpp:58-93, 116-181](plugins/membrum/src/controller/controller_state_codec.cpp#L58); [plugins/membrum/src/controller/controller_state.cpp:105-118, 196-215](plugins/membrum/src/controller/controller_state.cpp#L105)

**Problem.** kitPresetStateProvider and padPresetStateProvider build their blob from controller parameter values (buildSnapshot / buildPadSnapshotFromParams). kLateSlots has no row for sound[57] (noiseLayerGain has no ParamID), so the value-initialised 0.0 is written there. Slots 42/43 are always written from the B1/B3 parameter, and the registered default is 0.5 (controller.cpp:227-228, 621-625). The replay skips the sentinel on load (codec.cpp:263-268, 309-316), so the controller keeps whatever value it held before. Host getState (processor, State::toPadSnapshot, state_codec.cpp:124-125, 147) is the only save path that keeps both values.

**Why wrong.** A kit or pad preset saved with the plugin's own Save button must reload to the same processor state (spec 139 SC-002: "Kit preset round-trips all 32 pads bit-exactly"). On load, State::applyPadSnapshot clamps slot 57 to [0.1,16] (state_codec.cpp:243, 326), so 0.0 becomes 0.1. A B1/B3 value >= 0 is an explicit override: membrane_mapper.h:71-78 gives b1 = 0.2 + n*49.8 and b3 = n*1e-3. At n = 0.5 that is b1 = 25.1 s^-1 and b3 = 5e-4 instead of the decay/brightness-derived law.

**Consequence.** Computed from the code, no probe run. Every default-kit pad's noise layer (PadConfig default 1.0, pad_config.h:261) drops 20 dB. The default snare's wires (noiseLayerGain 6.2, default_kit.h:120) drop 35.8 dB, and the 3.5 / 2.2 pads (default_kit.h:262, 336) drop 30.9 / 26.8 dB. Factory kits re-saved unmodified lose their generator gains the same way. Pads still on the sentinel (default-kit toms leave B1 at -1 on purpose, default_kit.h:171-174) become b1 = 25.1 s^-1: the fundamental's T60 is ln(1000)/25.1 = 0.28 s, and b3 = 5e-4 adds about 500 s^-1 at 1 kHz, so toms and kick lose their ring and top end. Stale B1/B3 values from a previously loaded kit are also written into the next save. A double-click "reset" on the B1/B3 knob sets the 0.5 override (vst3editor.cpp:287 uses ParameterInfo.defaultNormalizedValue), so the UI cannot return a pad to "auto".
