(d) Exciter: mallet mass and hardness set the transferred impulse. A physical modal model keeps these as relative per-mode gains under one fixed output scale. A level control for the user can still be added on top, but a per-configuration renormalisation to a constant peak removes (a), (b) and (d) completely, and removes the peak part of (c). Two things survive: velocity, because the probe runs at v=1 and velocity enters through the exciter amplitude and the ADSR, and per-pad Level.

Sources (evidence quality strong):
- N.H. Fletcher & T.D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., Springer 1998 (ch. 7 sound radiation; ch. 18 drums / timpani) [textbook] — radiated power = radiation resistance x mean-square surface velocity; low-frequency radiation resistance of a baffled piston / monopole rises as (ka)^2 x area; strike position weights each mode by its mode shape at the strike point; timpani are struck about 1/4 of the way in to reduce the (0,1) mode.
- K. van den Doel & D.K. Pai, Synthesis of Shape Dependent Sounds with Physical Modeling, ICAD 1996 (expanded as "The Sounds of Physical Shapes", Presence 7(4), 1998) [paper] https://www.icad.org/websiteV2.0/Conferences/ICAD96/proc96/dendoel.htm — frequencies from geometry and material, decay rates from internal friction, initial mode amplitudes from the mode shapes at the impact location; no output normalisation described.
- J.O. Smith, Physical Audio Signal Processing, "Modal Expansion" (CCRMA online book) [textbook] https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Modal_Expansion.html — modal synthesis is a parallel sum of 2nd-order sections with per-mode gains G_i matched to measured peak heights or fitted by least squares; no normalisation by mode count or by a measured total peak.

**Consequence.** Yes, this stage makes differently configured pads sound alike in level. At v=1 every modal body peaks at -6 dBFS +/-0.7 dB (measured), so turning Size, Strike Position, Material, Decay, Air Loading, body damping or the exciter type does not change the body's peak level. A rim strike is as loud as a centre strike. A 24-inch floor tom and a 10-inch rack tom peak identically, and the kit then needs per-pad Level hand-tuning to put back a size relation the physics would give for free (default_kit.h:467-469; the inversion is covered in a separate claim). Across a factory kit, level contrast between drums can only come from the Level column and the noise / click layers. This is a direct contributor to the "kits sound generic / alike" symptom, and it removes a level cue that real players use for dynamics (strike position).

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: 2026-06 research entry #4 ruled the then-coded 1/sqrt(N) body norm "oversimplified (strong)". It said the norm ignored per-body amplitude, so "two presets with very different modal amplitude distributions are normalized to similar levels", and recommended 1/Sum|a_k| or Faust's 1/N. The code has changed since: the N-1 batch (AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:113-124, 160-202) replaced 1/sqrt(N) and then 1/Sum|a_k| with this per-configuration measured-strike normalisation, and "Snare-body Fix D" moved the probe to the real exciter. The prior concern about loss of amplitude-aware level differentiation still applies and is now stronger: the old norm only partly equalised level, and the new one equalises the v=1 peak exactly (measured within 0.7 dB).

**Suggested fix.** Keep the measured strike peak as a CEILING, not a target. Measure once per BODY TYPE at a reference configuration (size 0.5, strikePos 0.3, default damping, Impulse at v=1) to get refPeak_body. Set outputGain = kBodyHeadroom / refPeak_body, then apply min(1, kBodyHeadroom*kCeil / (peak_thisConfig * outputGain)) only when this configuration would exceed the ceiling (e.g. kCeil = 1.6, about -2 dBFS). Size, strike position and damping then move level as they do physically, and a hot configuration is still bounded. Alternatively add a per-pad "Level Normalise" amount g in [0,1] with outputGain = kBodyHeadroom / (refPeak^(1-g) * peak^g). Tests: (1) Membrane, Impulse, v=1: peak(strikePos 0.9) <= peak(strikePos 0.1) - 3 dB; (2) peak(size 0.8) >= peak(size 0.4) at equal level; (3) no body exceeds the +/-1 hardClip rail at v=1, level 1, across a size x strikePos x material grid (the existing test_body_headroom_budget.cpp guarantee); (4) update the default kit so tomLevel no longer needs the "Fix D" compensation.

**Verifier notes:**
- Confirmed: drum_voice.h:84, :73-84 (deliberate), :286-306 (Feedback gets gain 1 plus soft clip and String kBodyHeadroom/getInputGainSum at :270-285), probe :1322-1363, gain :1380-1387, cache :1394-1412 / StrikeNormKey :1717-1727; every key input is divided back out, so the v=1 body peak always lands at kBodyHeadroom; default_kit.h:456-457 and :467-469 compensate by hand. Caveat: the hidden case "audit probe 07a" was not found in the tree, so the dB figures are unverified, but the equalisation follows from the code. Documented intent makes it a design deviation; medium stands.
- Mechanism confirmed; AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:121 and :400-412 record N-1 as intentional, while its gain table (:400) says the body peak "carries Material/Size/StrikePos/damping", which the normaliser cancels. (b) Strike position holds: van den Doel & Pai (fetched) "the initial amplitudes are determined by the location of the impact"; membrane_mapper.h:111-117 drops the (0,1) weight about 21 dB at strikePos 1 (J0(2.405*0.9) ≈ 0.09) and the normaliser adds it back. (a) Size is wrong: for a fixed impulse into modal mass ∝ area, stored energy falls with size and ka stays roughly constant, so "bigger tom louder for free" is not supported. (c, d) have no physical reference level; timpani strike-point effect is disputed (Benade vs Rossing 1982a).
- Refuted as a defect: documented at drum_voice.h:73-83 and AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:160-202 ("N-1 DESIGN DECISION — settled 2026-06-07"), where a spike measured F_strike 3.5-18x, mostly from Size, and rejected "a precomputed per-body scalar (wrong by up to ~18× at the Size extremes)"; :124 accepts "peak now equalised across damping configs"; :400 sets the -6 dBFS budget; default_kit.h:456-469 handles the side effect. The suggested ceiling fix reintroduces the rejected ~25 dB Size spread. Membrum models no radiation, so the (ka)^2 argument does not apply.

#### MB-220 — Physics (oversimplified): An equal strike PEAK is not an equal LOUDNESS: peak normalisation turns low-pitched bodies into the quietest pads

**Severity:** low (filed medium, downgraded in verification) · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-oversimplified · **Dimension:** research:strike-normalisation · **Source:** research

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h:455-480](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h#L455) (with [drum_voice.h:84](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h#L84), [1386](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h#L1386))

**Problem.** The body is normalised on its PEAK (drum_voice.h:1352 peak = max|lastBody|; 1386 kBodyHeadroom / peak), not on any loudness measure. The default kit puts the six toms at natural f0 = 79.24 / 99.76 / 125.59 / 158.11 / 177.42 / 199.05 Hz (sizes 0.8..0.4, line 462). The code says the normaliser "otherwise makes the floor tom the QUIETEST body of the row" (456-457). It compensates with linear per-pad Level tomLevel = {0.95, 0.88, 0.82, 0.76, 0.71, 0.67} (469): 0.95/0.67 = +3.0 dB from floor to high tom. Level is a linear multiplier (drum_voice.h:566 hardClip(shaped * env * level_)).

**Why wrong.** Perceived loudness of equal-peak sounds depends on frequency and duration. On the ISO 226:2003 equal-loudness contours (derived from Suzuki & Takeshima 2004), the 60-phon contour needs 82.1 dB SPL at 80 Hz, 78.7 at 100, 75.6 at 125, 72.5 at 160 and 69.9 at 200 Hz. I computed these from the ISO 226:2003 formula and its parameter table; they reproduce the standard's 109.5 dB at 20 Hz. So a 79 Hz tom fundamental at the same peak as a 199 Hz one is about 12 dB less loud (pure-tone estimate, upper bound; the overtones narrow the gap). Temporal integration also makes a longer-decaying body at equal peak louder than a short one. Peak normalisation therefore removes the physical size->level relation and puts a perceptual inverse one in its place, because larger bodies have lower f0. The kit's +3.0 dB Level ramp repairs only part of a gap of up to about 12 dB.

Sources (evidence quality strong):
- Y. Suzuki & H. Takeshima, "Equal-loudness-level contours for pure tones", J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 116(2):918-933, 2004, doi:10.1121/1.1763601 (basis of ISO 226:2003) [paper] https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15376658/ — the contours adopted in ISO 226:2003; sensitivity falls steeply below about 500 Hz; the new contours differ most from Robinson-Dadson below 500 Hz (up to about 14 dB). (PubMed page needs cookies; abstract and citation read through the search index.)
- ISO 226:2003 Acoustics - Normal equal-loudness-level contours (formula and af / Lu / Tf table) [docs] — evaluated for LN = 60 phon: 80 Hz -> 82.1 dB, 100 Hz -> 78.7, 125 -> 75.6, 160 -> 72.5, 200 -> 69.9 dB SPL, a 12.2 dB difference between 80 and 200 Hz at equal loudness.
- N.H. Fletcher & T.D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd ed., 1998 [textbook] — larger drums radiate their low modes more efficiently (radiation resistance proportional to (ka)^2 x area below ka ~ 1); physically the bigger drum is the louder one at equal strike force.

**Consequence.** The floor tom reads as the quietest drum in the row even after the +3 dB Level fix, and the kick (lowest body) needs Level or master make-up to compete. Users editing Size get a counter-intuitive result: making a drum bigger makes it sound quieter. The stage also squeezes everyone toward the same peak, so loudness differences become a side effect of pitch and decay rather than a designed parameter.

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: Not ruled in 2026-06. The N-1 batch introduced the peak normaliser after that research pass. "Fix D" (default_kit.h:456-469) is the project's own later acknowledgement of this effect.

**Suggested fix.** If the peak normaliser is kept as a ceiling (see the first claim), this mostly disappears. Otherwise set the target loudness-aware: normalise on the K-weighted / BS.1770 short-term loudness of the 30 ms probe plus a 200 ms tail, or on band energy, rather than on peak, and keep the peak only as a ceiling. Test: render the six default-kit toms at v=1 and require the ITU-R BS.1770 momentary loudness (400 ms) to be non-increasing from floor tom to high tom, and the floor tom >= high tom + 2 LU.

**Verifier notes:**
- Code confirmed, lower severity: peak normalisation at drum_voice.h:302-304, :1394-1411, :1380-1387, :1322-1363 (:1338-1352 `peak = std::max(peak, std::abs(lastBody))`), kBodyHeadroom :84; secondary bank uses the same scheme (:1273-1299, :1370-1377); default_kit.h:456-457, :460-480 (tomEndHz = 500*0.1^size, membrane_mapper.h:100; 20*log10(0.95/0.67) = +3.03 dB); drum_voice.h:566 linear Level. The ~12 dB is an unmeasured pure-tone upper bound; larger membranes ring longer (membrane_mapper.h:149; weaker b3*f^2 at low f0, drum_voice.h:292-294), which raises their integrated loudness; Fix D already mitigates.
- Mechanism real, size overstated: test_tom_body_depth.cpp:302-308 checks only level grading; plugins/membrum/docs/tom-depth-implementation-plan.md:16 measured "the 16-inch floor tom is the quietest body of the row by ~4-5 dB", :196 says Fix D "partially offsets" it, :204-205 leave peak -> RMS open, so about 1-2 dB remains. ISO 226 numbers recomputed and correct (gap 15.1 dB at 40 phon, 9.4 dB at 79 phon), but they describe steady pure tones, not a broadband tom transient with partials at 126-230 Hz and shared click/noise layers; the Fletcher & Rossing size claim has no page cited and does not follow from the (ka)^2 law.
- Refuted: deliberate and documented (drum_voice.h:73-84; AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:121, :160-192, :397-415), loudness set per pad by Level, as Fix D does. The audit's own kit probe (specs/membrum-audit/probes/kit-pads.csv) gives tom centroids 237-880 Hz and shows the floor tom LOUDER in rms500 with longer decay than the high tom: Acoustic Studio Kit MIDI 41 -28.55 dBFS / 1.37 s vs MIDI 50 -32.54 / 0.61 s; Rock Big Room -28.11 / 1.46 vs -31.56 / 0.76; Vintage Wood -28.67 vs -33.43; Jazz Brushes -30.54 vs -32.69; Orchestral flat (-35.69 vs -36.65). A BS.1770 target would redesign a settled decision.

#### MB-224 — Physics (unsupported): The hard ceiling kTensionPitchModMax = 1.19 (~+3 st) reflects membrane saturation (Avanzini-Marogna-Bank)

**Severity:** low · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-unsupported · **Dimension:** research:tension-modulation · **Also flagged by:** research:extra:tension-mod-2-semitones

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:96-100, 725-728, 948-951](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h#L96)

**Problem.** tensionPitchMod = min(1 + k*E, 1.19). The comment says "Real membranes saturate; the linear energy law only holds for moderate amplitudes (Avanzini-Marogna-Bank)" (96-99). The map is linear in E up to a hard knee. Measured: size 1.0 at knob 1 holds at exactly +3.01 st from 20 ms to 100 ms (a flat pitch plateau). At 96 kHz the generic tom holds at +3.01 st from 10 ms to 200 ms.

**Why wrong.** MAB state no saturation. Tqs is linear in E (Eq. 20), and the modal frequencies follow omega ~ sqrt((T0 + Tqs)/sigma) (Eq. 7a with c = sqrt(T/sigma)), so the pitch ratio is sqrt(1 + Tqs/T0). That curve flattens with energy on its own, with no knee. Measured tom glides can be much larger than 3 st: a 7x12" tom's fundamental chirp spans 100-200 Hz at high intensity (Kirby & Sandler DAFx-20, Fig. 7), i.e. up to about an octave. A rail is legitimate for safety, but it should sit far above musical use, and the shape below it should be sqrt(1 + kE).

Sources (evidence quality moderate):
- Marogna, Avanzini, Bank, "Energy based synthesis of tension modulation in membranes", DAFx-10 [paper] <https://people.ece.cornell.edu/land/courses/ece5760/LABS/s2016/MarognaAvanziniBank_tension_modulation.pdf>: Eq. 7a: omega_nm = sqrt((beta_nm/R)^4 D/sigma + c^2 (beta_nm/R)^2) with c^2 = T0/sigma; Eq. 20: Tqs linear in E. No saturation of the tension-energy law is stated.
- Kirby & Sandler, "Advanced Fourier decomposition for realistic drum synthesis", DAFx-20 [paper] <https://dafx2020.mdw.ac.at/proceedings/papers/DAFx2020_paper_66.pdf>: Fig. 7: in a 7x12" Sugar Percussion stave tom, "The large fundamental chirp spans 100-200 Hz", i.e. the measured glide magnitude of a hard hit.

**Consequence.** Wherever the clamp engages (large pads, hot exciters, high sample rates), the glide turns into a fixed +3 st detune plateau followed by a late fall. That sounds like an out-of-tune note, not a tom glide. The clamp also hides the velocity and sample-rate errors above.

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: 2026-06 research[6] called the old 0.15 ceiling "an arbitrary perceptual cap, not a calibrated physical constant". The current 1.19 cap (N-1) adds a saturation citation that the source does not support. The prior verdict still applies, and the comment now misattributes the cap.

**Suggested fix.** Replace 1 + kE with sqrt(1 + 2kE) (the same small-signal slope, physically curved). Keep a safety rail of about 2.0 (+12 st) that only catches runaway Feedback energy. Test: at knob 1, v 1, sizes 0.2-1.0, the mode-0 trajectory has no interval > 5 ms where the pitch is constant within 0.01 st while the energy is falling.

**Verifier notes.**
- Code lens: confirmed. drum_voice.h:96-100 declares kTensionPitchModMax = 1.19f (12*log2(1.19) = 3.01 st); both renderers compute `std::min(1.0f + tensionAmtEffective_ * energyEnv_, kTensionPitchModMax)` (725-728, 948-951), a linear map with a hard knee that multiplies frequency directly (736-737, 752, 962-963, 970); tensionAmtEffective_ = knob * 3.3e-5 (420-421). Nothing caps modal energy by size or sample rate before the clamp; the comment at 86-93 (hard tom peak ~2.4e3, ~1.3 st) does not stop other sizes or rates reaching the rail. Repeats the 2026-06 research[6] verdict; physics-fidelity and documentation issue, low stands.
- Research lens: confirmed from the papers (pdftotext). MAB DAFx-10 Eq. 20 makes Tqs linear in E and the Conclusion calls the method "based on the linear relationship"; "saturat*" and "moderate amplitude" appear nowhere as a validity limit, and the linear law is validated up to 20 m/s (Fig. 3). The file's own comments at 408-411 and modal_resonator_bank.h:488-491 say the law is linear, contradicting the "saturate" claim at 98-99. The Kirby & Sandler Fig. 7 quote is verbatim, but it is an RDFT chirp width, so "about an octave" is an upper-bound reading. The +3.01 st plateau was not reproduced (consistent with the code: the cap engages once modal energy reaches ~5760).
- Context/impact lens: refutes as a defect. The cap is a documented safety rail (drum_voice.h:96-100) above a documented 1-2 st design range (drum_voice.h:86-94; MANUAL.md:263; pinned 1 < glide < 2.5 st by test_per_mode_damping.cpp:522-527; "clamped ≤+3 st" recorded in the tabla-bayan archetype). Large tom drops are modelled by the pitch envelope (acoustic-rack-floor-tom archetype:14; tom-depth-implementation-plan.md:83). The prior audit ruled the linear law fine within the budget (AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:319). At the cap the linear and sqrt shapes differ by ~0.2 st. Any plateau at size 1.0 / 96 kHz is the energy-scale finding, not the cap; what survives is a comment-only misattribution at drum_voice.h:98-99.

#### MB-226 — Physics (contradicted): The click burst length (2-5 ms, shortened by velocity) represents the stick/beater contact time on a drum head

**Severity:** low · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-contradicted · **Dimension:** research:click-noise-layers

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/src/dsp/click_layer.h:6-16, 34, 93-104, 160-164](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/click_layer.h#L6)

**Problem.** The header (click_layer.h:9-12) describes the click as a "2-5 ms shaped filtered-white-noise burst ... modeling the finite contact time". denormContactMs maps norm [0,1] to 2..5 ms (160-164). trigger() then multiplies by vScale = 1 - 0.3*velocity and floors at 0.5 ms: burstMs = max(0.5, contactMs*(1-0.3v)) (95-96). Rise = burst/5 as a raised cosine, then exp(-6.9078*k/decaySamples), which falls to -60 dB at the end of the burst (99-102, 121-130), so most of the energy sits in the first ~0.5-1 ms. The real range is 1.4-5 ms, not 2-5. Default kit (default_kit.h) contact norms are 0.05-0.20, which gives 2.15-2.6 ms before velocity. Measured burst length at 48 kHz (layer_probe): kick 1.71 ms, snare 1.81, tom 1.65, hat 1.50, perc 1.81 at v=1.0; 1.96-2.38 ms at v=0.3. The click is the same stick-like tick on the felt-beater kick (cfg comment "mallet felt", default_kit.h:73) as on the snare.

**Why wrong.** Measured stick-drumhead contact times are 3-6 ms on a snare (Wagner 2006, force plus contact-foil measurement) and 5-8 ms for a mezzoforte stroke at the centre of a tom or snare (Dahl 2011 review). Contact time DECREASES with striking velocity, so the coded sign is right (Wagner 2006 summary list; Avanzini & Rocchesso 2004). It increases with mallet mass and with the compliance of the struck object (Avanzini & Rocchesso: t0 ~ (m/k)^(1/(alpha+1)), and is always longer against a compliant resonator). So a felt bass-drum beater should be longer still. The default-kit click (1.5-1.8 ms at full velocity, effective energy duration well under 1 ms) is 2-5x shorter than any published stick contact. Its velocity scaling (at most -30 %) is in the right direction. Note: the body's actual contact pulse is ImpactExciter (0.5-15 ms, mass-dependent), and the click is an extra layer on top. That makes the click a perceptual "tick", not a contact model, which contradicts the header's own description.

Sources (evidence quality moderate):
- S. Dahl, "Striking movements: A survey of motion analysis of percussionists", Acoustical Science and Technology 32(5):168-173, 2011 [paper] <https://vbn.aau.dk/ws/files/65339564/Dahl_J_AST_review_submi.pdf>: "Typical contact durations between drumstick and drumhead are 5-8 ms for a mezzoforte stroke at the center of a tom tom or snare drum". Sound level and timbre follow the history of the force pulse.
- A. Wagner, "Analysis of drumbeats - interaction between drummer, drumstick and instrument", MSc thesis, KTH 2006 [thesis] <https://www.speech.kth.se/publications/masterprojects/2006/AndreasWagner.pdf>: Abstract: 3-6 ms of stick-membrane contact. Sec. 4.2.1: "With increasing dynamic level, i.e. increasing velocity of the drumstick, the contact time decreases". The main pulse ends at ~3.5 ms and reflections extend contact. Contact time also decreases with head tension and toward the rim.
- F. Avanzini & D. Rocchesso, "Physical modeling of impacts: theory and experiments on contact time and spectral centroid", SMC 2004 [paper] <https://avanzini.di.unimi.it/downloads/publications/avanzini_smc04_finalsub.pdf>: t0 ~ (m_h/k)^(1/(alpha+1)); always longer against a resonating (compliant) object than the rigid-surface prediction; "a short t0 corresponds to an impulse-like transient with a rich spectrum ... a long t0 ... little energy in the high frequency region".

**Consequence.** Every pad, including the felt-beater kick and the toms, starts with the same sub-millisecond-weighted tick. It reads as a hard stick tip regardless of the beater the preset describes. Because the click is the brightest layer on most pads, this shared onset makes kits more alike. The documented 2-5 ms range is also not what plays: with velocity scaling the range is 1.4-5 ms.

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: no literature verdict on the click layer in AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07 (its "research" array covers the ImpactExciter contact law, entry 8: nuanced, velocity sign correct). Code findings H-2 and M-7 touched only the click's gain (x2 -> 0.445, b4c63577). Duration and shape are unchanged since that audit, so the point is new, not a repeat.

**Suggested fix.** Either (a) re-document the click as a perceptual attack tick (not a contact model) and keep the range, or (b) re-range denormContactMs to about 3-10 ms with the velocity factor (1-0.3v) kept, add a mass/beater term so felt pads sit at the long end, and fix the header's "2-5 ms" claim. Pin it with a click_layer test: burst length at v=1 and v=0.3 for contact norm 0 and 1 lies in the documented range, and burst(v=1) < burst(v=0.3).

**Verifier notes.**
- Code lens: confirmed. click_layer.h:160-164 gives 2 + 3*norm ms; 95-96 applies vScale and the 0.5 ms floor, so the documented 2-5 ms is not met at high velocity; 99-102 and 121-130 front-load the energy. drum_voice.h:377-378 and 787-794 trigger the click on every note-on at half gain into the excitation and full gain (x 0.445) to the output. default_kit.h:72-73: kick norm 0.15 → 2.45 ms → 1.715 ms at v=1 (matches the probe); default norms 0.05-0.20 (lines 72, 126, 161, 203, 266, 289, 341). Real but minor documentation/physics mismatch; low fits.
- Research lens: confirmed. Dahl 2011 ("5-8 ms for a mezzoforte stroke") and Wagner 2006 (abstract "3-6 ms"; Sec. 4.2.1 contact time decreases with velocity; shorter toward the rim and with higher tension) are quoted verbatim and measure the very system the header claims to model. The separate contact model is ImpactExciter (kTMin 0.5 ms, kTMax 15 ms, impact_exciter.h:132-133). The only partial defence (the click is an additive Cook-style transient) is a caveat the finding states itself.
- Context/impact lens: refutes as physics. The header cites Cook's "Sines + Noise + Transients" (click_layer.h:6-8); contact duration lives in ImpactExciter, already ruled sensible (docs/correctness-audit.md:219; 2026-06 literature verdict 8). Short values are deliberate per-pad choices (default_kit.h:72, 125, 203; tom-depth-implementation-plan.md:90) and user-controllable (MANUAL.md:298). The kick's click differs in brightness (0.4, ~1 kHz, default_kit.h:73) and mix, so "the same tick" is overstated; the click sits ~6 dB under the body strike (click_layer.h:151-157). What survives is documentation drift in the header (line 12).

#### MB-235 — Physics (oversimplified): Gong / plate pitch glide is provided (left to the tension feature)

**Severity:** low · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-oversimplified · **Dimension:** research:nonlinear-coupling

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:718-728, 939-950](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h#L718) (tensionActive gated on BodyModelType::Membrane); [plugins/membrum/AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:92](plugins/membrum/AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md#L92)

**Problem.** Energy-dependent pitch glide (pitch multiplied by 1 + kTensionEnergyScale*knob*energyEnv, capped at 1.19) runs only when the body is Membrane. Plate, NoiseBody, Bell and Shell have no amplitude-dependent frequency shift: only the user pitch envelope, which follows a fixed curve, not the level. The 2026-06 redesign note says pitch glide was "intentionally left to the separate §3-A tension feature".

**Why wrong.** Thick gongs glide in pitch when struck: large flat-centred Chinese opera gongs glide DOWN "by as much as three semitones" (hardening, cubic nonlinearity), and smaller gongs with pronounced curvature glide UP (softening, where quadratic curvature terms dominate). Thin cymbals reach energy transfer before any glide (Fletcher 1985; Legge & Fletcher 1989; Touze & Thomas).

Sources (evidence quality strong):
- Chaigne, Touze & Thomas, Acoust. Sci. & Tech. 26(5) 2005, Sec. 4.1 "Pitch Glide" [paper] <https://perso.ensta.fr/~touze/PDF/ChaosGong.pdf>: large Chinese opera gongs: "a downward glide in pitch by as much as three semitones"; "smaller gongs with a pronounced curvature, glide upward". Hardening corresponds to a downward glide in free vibration, softening to an upward one. "Pitch glides are frequently heard on thick gongs, but not on thin cymbals."
- Torin & Bilbao, SMAC 2013 [paper] <https://www.ness.music.ed.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/BassDrumSMAC13_corrections.pdf>: pitch glide and HF build-up at high excitation are observed in bass drums and toms. A Berger-type (tension) model gives the glide but "is not able to render the build-up of high-frequency energy".

**Consequence.** A gong or tam-tam built on the Plate body cannot produce the velocity-dependent glide that identifies an opera gong, and neither glide direction is available. The pitch envelope can fake a glide, but at the same depth for soft and hard hits. Gong patches sound static, more like a modal chime.

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: 2026-06 research[1] (Plate) noted the body was "missing the cymbal/gong dynamic nonlinearity (pitch glide, HF energy cascade)". The N-1 fix reworked tension modulation for Membrane only, so the plate and gong glide gap remains.

**Suggested fix.** Allow the existing energy-driven fundamental scaling (updateModalFundamentalOnBank) for Plate and NoiseBody as well, with a signed per-pad direction: hardening, pitch = 1 + amt*E, falls as the hit decays; softening, pitch = 1 - amt*E, rises. Keep the 3-semitone cap. Test: Plate, tension 1, vel 1. The measured fundamental at 20 ms vs 500 ms differs by >= 1 semitone in the chosen direction, and by < 0.2 semitone at vel 0.3.

**Verifier notes.**
- Code lens: confirmed. drum_voice.h:722-724 and 945-947 gate `tensionActive` on `BodyModelType::Membrane` (comment at 718-721: "a Membrane-only physics path"); every other body gets tensionPitchMod 1.0 (725-728, 948-951), and retuneFundamental (1587-1593) has no energy term. AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:92, 122 and 323 confirm only Membrane got the fix. A repeat of an open 2026-06 literature gap; a documented design simplification, low is right.
- Research lens: confirmed. Plate explicitly models cymbals and gongs (bodies/plate_modes.h:8-27), and the preset generator builds gongs on Plate/Bell with tension zeroed because it is a no-op (tools/membrum_preset_generator.cpp:2746-2777, 5252-5254, 6171). Chaigne/Touzé/Thomas Sec. 4.1 quoted verbatim, peer-reviewed, same system. Nuances: the source says thin cymbals do NOT glide, so extending to NoiseBody is unsupported and the glide must stay opt-in; the flat Plate corresponds to the hardening (downward) case.
- Context/impact lens: refutes as a defect. The gating is deliberate (drum_voice.h:718-721; AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:92, 47) and stated as a preset constraint (PRESET-RETUNE-PLAN.md:119; preset-retune/00-param-dictionary.md:67); the gong archetype (preset-retune/archetypes/gong-tam-tam-large-struck-bronze-metal.md:6, 21) voices a static fifth on Mallet + Bell. Cymbals, hats, bells and tam-tams are most of the metal pads and should not glide; only a hypothetical opera-gong patch misses it, so this is a feature request.

#### MB-239 — Physics (contradicted): The factory '808' and default kick pitch sweeps match TR-808 / TR-909 kick pitch behaviour

**Severity:** medium (final: low) · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-contradicted · **Dimension:** research:pitch-envelope-808

**Location:** [tools/membrum_preset_generator.cpp:1126-1143](tools/membrum_preset_generator.cpp#L1126) (808 Electronic Kit pad 0), [2926-2934](tools/membrum_preset_generator.cpp#L2926) (909 Drum Machine pad 0), [3747-3754](tools/membrum_preset_generator.cpp#L3747) (Trap Modern "Sub 808"); [plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h:54-61](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/default_kit.h#L54)

**Problem.** The "808 Electronic Kit" kick ("TR-808: sub-sine kick") sweeps 200 -> 40 Hz over 30 ms (tsPitchEnvTime 0.06 x 500 ms), curve p = 0.233, on a Membrane body (size 0.90, inharmonic Bessel partials 1 : 1.59 : 2.14 ...), with tensionModAmt 0.30. The "909 Drum Machine" kick sweeps 180 -> 55 Hz over 20 ms. The default-kit kick sweeps 160 -> 50 Hz over 20 ms with p = 0.125. All are single large sweeps (3.3:1 to 5:1) that land at a fixed time and then hold the pitch constant.

**Why wrong.** TR-808 BD (Werner, Abel & Smith 2014): bridged-T centre frequency at rest about 49.5 Hz (Roland chart "typical" 56 Hz). Two distinct pitch events, "often conflated": (1) an attack jump of the centre frequency "by more than an octave" for about 6 ms, "less than a single period at the higher frequency", which is not perceived as a pitch shift but makes the attack "punchier" and "crisper"; (2) the "pitch sigh", "a subtle modulation caused by leakage through R161". In Fig. 11 the instantaneous frequency runs from about 56 Hz down to about 49-50 Hz over the first 300 ms. There is no 200 -> 40 Hz, 30 ms sweep, and the resting pitch is near 50 Hz, not 40. The sustained part is a single damped pseudo-sinusoid, not an inharmonic membrane. TR-909: a sawtooth core waveshaped toward a sine, pitch from an instant-attack, slow-decay RC envelope (Reid). A large downward sweep is the right idiom there, and 180 -> 55 Hz is plausible. No peer-reviewed measurement of the 909 sweep's Hz and ms was found, so that preset's numbers are unsupported rather than wrong.

Sources (evidence quality strong):
- Werner, Abel & Smith, "A Physically-Informed, Circuit-Bendable, Digital Model of the Roland TR-808 Bass Drum Circuit", DAFx-14, pp. 159-166 [paper] <https://dafx14.fau.de/papers/dafx14_kurt_james_werner_a_physically_informed,_ci.pdf>: bridged-T centre frequency about 49.5 Hz (Roland chart 56 Hz). Sec. 8.1: a 6 ms attack rise of more than an octave, under one period, not perceived as pitch. Sec. 8.2: the "pitch sigh" is a subtle leakage-driven modulation. Fig. 11: instantaneous frequency about 56 -> 49.5 Hz over 0.3 s.
- Gordon Reid, "Synth Secrets: Practical Bass Drum Synthesis", Sound On Sound (mirror) [blog] <https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/bassdrumsynth.html>: the TR-909 kick pitch comes from EG3 (instant attack, slow decay) driving an oscillator waveshaped to near-sine. The TR-808 bridged-T rings on its own and "goes slightly flat at long decays".

**Consequence.** The kick labelled "808" is designed as a 909-style or trap-style zap, a 2.3-octave sweep ending sub-50 Hz. The real 808 sound is a near-50 Hz boom with a sub-period click-like attack jump and a slow sigh of about 12 %. A user who picks the 808 kit gets a sound that is not 808-like, and it lands close to the 909 and Trap kicks (all three are big Start -> End sweeps on Membrane+Impulse), which adds to the kits sounding alike. In current builds the first claim hides all of this, since every one of them plays at about 80 Hz at host block sizes.

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: none (no prior literature verdict on drum-machine pitch envelopes; the 2026-06 research array covers membrane, plate and shell ratios, damping and tension modulation only).

**Suggested fix.** For the 808 kit pad 0, use the three-point envelope (knee enabled): Start about 110 Hz -> Mid 56 Hz with midFraction about 0.02 of a 300 ms total (about 6 ms, curve1 fast), then Mid 56 -> End 49.5 Hz over the remaining about 294 ms with an exponential curve2. Keep tensionMod low, and prefer a body or material setting that leaves the fundamental dominant (Werner: a single pseudo-sinusoid). Leave the 909 and Trap kicks as large sweeps, but make the three kicks distinct. Test (after the first claim is fixed): render the factory 808 kick at 512-sample blocks and require the zero-crossing frequency at 50 ms to be in [52, 59] Hz and the mean over 250-300 ms in [48.5, 51.5] Hz.

**Verifier notes.**
- Code lens: confirmed; downgrade. Generator 1132-1143 sets pad 0 to Impulse/Membrane, 200 → 40 Hz, time 0.06, curve 0.15, tension 0.30, knee off; 909 at 2926-2939 and Trap at 3747-3757 as stated; default kick at default_kit.h:54-61. pad_config_apply.h:101-111 maps Hz = 20*100^norm, time = norm*500 ms, curve 2*norm-1; the pitch then holds at endValue_ (pitch_segment_envelope.h:101-106; tone_shaper.h:380-390). The three-point knee (tone_shaper.h:267-283) makes the fix feasible. This is preset voicing against one reference circuit, not code correctness; the "~80 Hz at host block sizes" consequence rests on a separate unverified claim.
- Research lens: not refuted for the one preset that claims TR-808; drop to low or nit. The Werner/Abel/Smith quotes (Sec. 4 49.5 Hz vs 56 Hz chart, Sec. 8 conflation, Sec. 8.1 6 ms jump, Fig. 11 48-56 Hz axis) are accurate. The pad plays a heard 2.3-octave sweep, not the paper's sub-period shift and sigh. Overreach: the default kick is a generic template; Trap's "Sub 808" names the modern gliding idiom; the 909 numbers are conceded as plausible.
- Context/impact lens: refutes as a defect. preset-retune/archetypes/808-kick-roland-tr-808-bass-drum.md records the real 49.4/56 Hz fundamental and ~6 ms attack (lines 8, 10, 57), then deliberately chooses the producer-style "200 -> 40 Hz, 30 ms" boom (line 10, 21) and zeroes every physics axis so the bank collapses toward a sub-sine (lines 4, 9, 20). It is subjective voicing of one factory preset, editable with the existing three-point envelope.

#### MB-240 — Physics (unsupported): SC-009 '808 kick' test pins the pitch envelope to 808 behaviour and covers the real render path

**Severity:** medium (final: low) · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-unsupported · **Dimension:** research:pitch-envelope-808

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/tests/unit/tone_shaper/test_pitch_envelope_808.cpp:1-13, 74-88, 92-142, 173-203](plugins/membrum/tests/unit/tone_shaper/test_pitch_envelope_808.cpp#L1)

**Problem.** The test is named "808Kick" (SC-009). It sets Start 160, End 50, Time 20 ms, Curve Exp (legacy setter -> amount -0.7), renders 200 ms with voice.process() ONE SAMPLE AT A TIME (118-119), and checks only that the 30-80 Hz Goertzel peak over 20-100 ms lies in [45, 55] Hz. It never checks the start pitch, the trajectory, or DrumVoice::processBlock, which is the path VoicePool uses. Its comment says a 0.001 ms time "should clamp to 1 ms internally" (179); in code msToSamples rounds it to 0 samples and the envelope is simply inactive (pitch_segment_envelope.h:142-146). Its hasNaNOrInf helpers (74-88, 193-195) are the (bits & 0x7F800000) clone that CLAUDE.md forbids because Apple clang folds it to "finite".

**Why wrong.** The 160 / 50 Hz, 20 ms values have no 808 source behind them (the measured 808 rests near 49.5-56 Hz, with a 6 ms jump of more than an octave and a slow sigh; Werner et al. 2014). The test should be labelled as a generic sweep test or fixed to cited 808 numbers. It must exercise processBlock at realistic host block sizes and assert the start of the trajectory as well as the end.

Sources (evidence quality strong):
- Werner, Abel & Smith, DAFx-14 TR-808 bass drum [paper] <https://dafx14.fau.de/papers/dafx14_kurt_james_werner_a_physically_informed,_ci.pdf>: 808 rest frequency about 49.5 Hz, attack jump of more than an octave for about 6 ms, pitch sigh about 56 -> 50 Hz over 300 ms. There is no 160 -> 50 Hz, 20 ms sweep.

**Consequence.** The test passes (per-sample path: 51.5 Hz at 20 ms, 50.1 Hz settled) while every host-facing render of the same patch settles at 55-78 Hz depending on block size (see the first claim). It gives false confidence that the 808 pitch envelope works. Its NaN check is vacuous on the macOS fast-math leg.

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: findings.json confirmed[17] already noted "The 808 test ... exercises only the per-sample process() path, so the block-path coarseness/divergence is entirely untested". Still true: the test is unchanged and still passes over the block-path failure measured above.

**Suggested fix.** Rename the test to a generic "pitch sweep reaches End" test, or set cited 808 values. Render through DrumVoice::processBlock at block sizes {1, 64, 512, 2048} (every size must pass). Add a start-of-sweep assertion: the frequency from the first zero-crossing periods must be at least 0.85 x Start. Replace the bit-mask helpers with Krate::DSP::detail::isFinite (core/db_utils.h). Fix the stale "clamp to 1 ms" comment, or make msToSamples clamp to at least 1 sample when ms > 0.

**Verifier notes.**
- Code lens: confirmed at lower severity. Per-sample process() only (118-119), end-window-only Goertzel check (127-141), bit-mask finiteness clones (74-88, 193-195), stale comment at 179 (msToSamples gives 0, no clamp), legacy Exp → -0.7 (tone_shaper.h:289-294), and 160/50 Hz from the SC-009 contract (lines 4-8). Overreach: at 0.001 ms the envelope is not inactive but jumps straight to End (tone_shaper.h:310-313, 380-390); the block path is no longer entirely untested (tests/unit/dsp/test_pitch_env_all_bodies.cpp:38-54, 91-141, 256-sample blocks, but only endFreq < 0.5*startFreq); the settled pitch is 50 Hz, so "55-78 Hz" is at most a stale-chunk effect inside the analysis window (drum_voice.h:607, 701-746).
- Research lens: code/test defects not refuted; literature only partly confirmed. The spec's acceptance scenario asks for the glide shape and the first-50 ms trajectory (specs/137-membrum-phase2-exciters-bodies/spec.md:109, 113), so the missing start check is a real gap and repeats confirmed[17]. The bit-mask hit is already in tools/lint-finite-bitmask-baseline.json:53. Werner quotes accurate, but End 50 Hz matches 49.5 Hz and "808" is a stylistic label from spec.md:332 / tone_shaper_contract.md:89-91, with a real 808 model deferred (spec.md:499); the physics framing is a naming issue.
- Context/impact lens: refutes as physics. Values are a documented acceptance criterion (spec.md:332; contracts/tone_shaper_contract.md:89-94; specs/135-membrum-drum-synth.md:194 gives a generic kick range). Renaming changes only test code. The audible issue is the chunk-rate retune (drum_voice.h:589, 613-619, 734-746), already confirmed[17]. The 0-sample behaviour satisfies the contract's "snaps to End within 1 sample" option (tone_shaper_contract.md:85-87). What survives is a test-coverage and comment nit on an item already confirmed.

#### MB-241 — Physics (oversimplified): A zero-look-ahead, instantaneous-attack limiter is an acceptable brickwall stage for percussive material

**Severity:** low · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-oversimplified · **Dimension:** research:bus-limiter · **Also flagged by:** research:bus-limiter

**Location:** [dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/true_peak_limiter.h:4-18, 246-257](dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/true_peak_limiter.h#L4) (used at [plugins/membrum/src/processor/processor.cpp:710-717, 1086-1088](plugins/membrum/src/processor/processor.cpp#L710))

**Problem.** Header comment, lines 17-18: "The trade-off vs a look-ahead limiter is a harder (instantaneous) attack, which for percussive material is acceptable." Code, lines 248-251: when required = ceiling/tp is below currentGain_, currentGain_ = required on that same sample (attack = 0). Otherwise a one-pole release runs toward 1 with tau = 80 ms (kDefaultReleaseMs, line 50; coefficient at line 143). Output, lines 256-257: clamp(in*gain, +-ceiling). Membrum calls prepare(sr, maxBlock) and setCeilingDb(-1) only (processor.cpp:1087-1088). It never calls setLookaheadSamples or setHalfbandDetector, so it runs the zero-look-ahead IIR-detector path. Probe (default kit, real DrumVoice renders at 44.1 kHz, scratchpad tpl_probe.cpp):
- Kick+snare+hat+crash at velocity 1 (bus 1.08 dBFS sample peak, 1.58 dBTP): the limiter keeps gain at 1.000 through the first 1 ms, then reaches gain 0.757 by 1.59 ms. It drops up to 1.85 dB in one sample, and 2 output samples sit exactly at the ceiling.
- Kick+snare at velocity 1, +6 dB: gain 1.000 at 1 ms, 0.510 at 2 ms, one-sample drops up to 2.13 dB, 7 samples flat at the ceiling.
- Kick at velocity 1, +9 dB: 21 samples flat at the ceiling.
- The class already has an opt-in look-ahead (lines 114-131, 217-243). With 64 samples of look-ahead on the same inputs, the gain ramps over the ~1.45 ms look-ahead window (0.880 at 0.1 ms, 0.742 at 0.5 ms, 0.573 at 1 ms), the largest one-sample drop is 0.12-0.18 dB, and 0 samples sit at the ceiling.

**Why wrong.** The literature treats instantaneous attack as the distortion case, not as acceptable. Giannoulis, Massberg and Reiss (JAES 2012, sec. 1) say instantaneous response "is not sought because it introduces distortion". Hämäläinen (DAFx-02) shows two things. First, the output is x*g, so the spectra convolve, and the faster the gain reacts the stronger the artifacts. Second, zero attack is the only way to guarantee no clipping without a delay, and it "produces sharp gain transitions that can be heard as clicks". His fix is a look-ahead delay with a running-max filter plus averaging over the delay length (N = 64 "already gives good results"). The DAFX textbook limiter (Holters, limiter.m, sec. 4.2.1) uses a smoothed attack (coefficient 0.3) and a 5-sample delay line in the signal path. So a brickwall that is clean on drum transients needs look-ahead of at least about 1 ms with a ramped gain. Without it, the leading edge of each over-ceiling hit is hard-clipped sample by sample: each new maximum sample is set to exactly +-ceiling.

Sources (evidence quality strong):
- D. Giannoulis, M. Massberg, J. D. Reiss, "Digital Dynamic Range Compressor Design - A Tutorial and Analysis", JAES 60(6):399-408, 2012 [paper] <https://web.archive.org/web/2016/http://www.eecs.qmul.ac.uk/~josh/documents/2012/GiannoulisMassbergReiss-dynamicrangecompression-JAES2012.pdf>: Sec. 1: instantaneous response is not sought because it introduces distortion. Sec. 4.1 / Fig. 9: smoothing the detector visibly reduces THD; the decoupled smooth detector minimises distortion at the attack/release transition. Sec. 3: a feedforward design can act as a perfect limiter and allows look-ahead.
- P. Hämäläinen, "Smoothing of the Control Signal without Clipped Output in Digital Peak Limiters", Proc. DAFx-02, pp. 195-198, 2002 [paper] <https://dafx.de/paper-archive/2002/DAFX02_Hamalainen_smoothing_peak_limiters.pdf>: x*g convolves the spectra; faster reaction gives stronger artifacts. Preventing clipping without look-ahead requires zero attack, which gives sharp gain transitions heard as clicks. A delay with a max filter, clipping control and averaging gives a smooth gain with no clipped output; N = 64 already gives good results.
- M. Holters, limiter.m, companion code to U. Zölzer (ed.), DAFX, 2nd ed., Wiley 2011, sec. 4.2.1 [textbook] <https://dafx.de/DAFX_Book_Page_2nd_edition/M_files_chap04.zip>: attack coefficient 0.3, release 0.01, a gain smoother with the same coefficients, and a 5-sample delay buffer in the audio path: y(n) = g * buffer(end).
- Faust compressors.lib, limiter_lad_N (D. Sanfilippo), after J. Zmölnig / P. Falkner [docs] <https://sources.debian.org/src/faust/2.30.5~ds0-2/libraries/compressors.lib>: the input path is delayed by the attack time (look-ahead); gain fluctuations above about 15 Hz are perceived as timbral effects.
- J. Zmölnig, digital limiter notes, IEM Graz, 1999 [docs] <https://users.iem.at/zmoelnig/publications/limiter/>: delaying the signal lets the limiter regulate the gain before the triggering moment; very fast, hard regulation removes dynamics and adds inharmonic components.

**Consequence.** The stage hard-clips only when it is engaged. With the default kit at default levels it never engages on a single hit (the hottest voice is the snare at velocity 1, -4.49 dBFS) or on kick+snare (-1.40 dBFS). It does engage on dense full-velocity downbeats (4 coincident hits: 2.4 dB of reduction) and on hot or layered kits. When it engages, the first 1-1.5 ms of the kick or snare (the stick attack) pass at full gain, then the rising edge is flattened to the ceiling. The audible result is a click or crunch on the attack instead of a clean level drop, plus an 80 ms duck of the whole kit afterwards. It does not make kits sound alike in normal playing, because it is inactive there. Whether the instantaneous attack is acceptable for drums is a deliberate, documented choice (header lines 17-18), made to keep the aux buses sample-aligned with zero latency, but the cited sources do not support it.

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: the 2026-06-07 audit never reviewed this limiter as a literature item. Its research[9] (softClip, "nuanced") and H-1 recommended "keep the per-voice output linear and bound the summed bus with a true-peak/brickwall limiter". This limiter was the H-1 fix (#244, commit 08975a47, 2026-06-07). Since then the header gained only an opt-in halfband detector and an opt-in look-ahead, both off by default (Profundum #274, 021fe07d), plus a clang-tidy sweep (#293). Membrum enables neither, so the Membrum path is unchanged since that audit, and this is a new finding (MB series).

**Suggested fix.** In Processor::setupProcessing, call busLimiter_.setLookaheadSamples(round(1.0e-3 * sampleRate)) (about 44 samples at 44.1 kHz, 96 at 96 kHz) before prepare(). Return that value from getLatencySamples(), and delay the aux buses by the same N samples so they stay aligned with the main bus (the reason the code chose zero latency). The look-ahead path already exists and is tested (true_peak_limiter_test.cpp:316-383). Test to add: in membrum_tests, render kick+snare+hat+crash at velocity 1 and kick+snare at +6 dB through Processor::process. Assert (a) no more than 0 output samples within 1e-5 of the ceiling, and (b) the largest one-sample gain drop (out/in on samples with |in| > 1e-2) is below 0.5 dB. Today the measurements are 2 and 7 samples at the ceiling and drops of 1.85 and 2.13 dB, so the test would fail.

**Verifier notes.**
- Code lens: confirmed (probe numbers not re-run). true_peak_limiter.h:246-251 sets the gain on the same sample, 256-257 clamps, release is a one-pole at 80 ms (50, 139-144); look-ahead (`lookaheadRequested_ = 0`, 278) and the halfband detector (`halfbandDetector_ = false`, 275) are off by default. Membrum only calls prepare/setCeilingDb(-1) (processor.cpp:1087-1088), reset (1104) and processBlock (717), with no getLatencySamples. The library's own look-ahead doc (true_peak_limiter.h:118-122) calls the zero-look-ahead step "a clipper". Low stands: engages only on dense hot hits, and the fix adds latency to report and match on the aux buses.
- Research lens: confirmed. Because tp >= |sample| (line 193), any sample that is the detected peak comes out exactly at the ceiling: clipper behaviour on each rising-edge maximum. Hämäläinen DAFx-02 (lines 12, 230, 232, 569 of the extracted text) and Giannoulis/Massberg/Reiss (lines 65, 309) are quoted correctly and cover peak limiters. Hämäläinen also shows zero latency forces zero attack, so the choice is coherent but click-prone, not "acceptable".
- Context/impact lens: refutes as a defect. The zero-latency design is documented (header 4-10, 17-18) and was reviewed: AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:417-423 records look-ahead rejected (item W1) to keep the aux/multi-out buses aligned, and 190-192 rejects a look-ahead follower per voice. It is a mix-safety stage, not drum acoustics, so "physics-oversimplified" is the wrong category; the voice budget (kBodyHeadroom -6 dBFS, audit 400-403) keeps it rarely engaged; reversing W1 is a product decision for the user. Side note: audit line 421 ("non-finite input sanitized") is stale against header 189-192.

#### MB-242 — Physics (oversimplified): The 80 ms one-pole release is a 'program-dependent recovery'

**Severity:** low · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-oversimplified · **Dimension:** research:bus-limiter

**Location:** [dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/true_peak_limiter.h:50, 139-144, 248-251](dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/true_peak_limiter.h#L50)

**Problem.** kDefaultReleaseMs = 80 ms with the comment "program-dependent recovery" (line 50). The release is a fixed one-pole on the linear gain: currentGain_ += (required - currentGain_)·(1 - exp(-1/(0.08·fs))) (lines 143, 251). No branch depends on the programme, and the detector has no smoothing. Probe: a default-kit kick (velocity 1) pushed +9 dB to about 0.77 dBTP. The gain bottoms at 0.816 at 21 ms (the second cycle of the kick, not the attack), and the gain recovers between cycles. Residual y - x·g_15Hz (gain fluctuation faster than 15 Hz) is -27.6 dB relative to the output with no look-ahead and -27.5 dB with 64 samples of look-ahead. So this in-cycle gain ripple comes from the release law, not the attack.

**Why wrong.** Giannoulis et al. (2012, sec. 2.3 / 4.1, Fig. 9) show the trade-off. Unsmoothed branching detectors give abrupt attack/release switching and higher THD. Smoothed decoupled detectors, and release in the log (dB) domain, give "smooth and subtle (artifact-free)" behaviour and lower THD. A release whose time constant is comparable to a kick's 15-25 ms period modulates the gain within each cycle, which adds harmonic distortion. Faust's limiter_lad notes that gain fluctuations above about 15 Hz are heard as timbre and uses a hold to minimise low-frequency distortion. A fixed 80 ms linear-gain one-pole is not program-dependent: it is a plain single time constant with no hold.

Sources (evidence quality moderate):
- D. Giannoulis, M. Massberg, J. D. Reiss, JAES 60(6), 2012 [paper] <https://web.archive.org/web/2016/http://www.eecs.qmul.ac.uk/~josh/documents/2012/GiannoulisMassbergReiss-dynamicrangecompression-JAES2012.pdf>: Fig. 9 (THD vs frequency, attack 1 ms, release 15 ms): smoothing visibly reduces harmonic distortion; the decoupled detector minimises distortion at the attack/release transition; a log-domain smooth release is used for artifact-free compression.
- Faust compressors.lib, limiter_lad_N (D. Sanfilippo) [docs] <https://sources.debian.org/src/faust/2.30.5~ds0-2/libraries/compressors.lib>: fluctuations above about 15 Hz are perceived as timbral effects; a hold time allows minimal distortion of the low frequencies.
- J. Zmölnig, IEM 1999 limiter notes [docs] <https://users.iem.at/zmoelnig/publications/limiter/>: the gain is held for a hold time, then recovers exponentially.

**Consequence.** Only when the limiter is engaged on low-frequency content (hot kicks or 808-style long kicks): about 4 % (-27.6 dB) gain-ripple distortion on the kick body, with the whole kit ducked for 60-80 ms afterwards. On the default-kit downbeat, >1 dB of reduction lasts 64.5 ms, and gain is 0.767 at 5 ms and 0.867 at 50 ms. In ordinary default-kit playing the limiter is inactive, so this is inaudible there.

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: not covered by the 2026-06 audit. Unchanged since #244.

**Suggested fix.** Change the comment to "fixed one-pole release". Optionally add a hold of about one kick period (20-30 ms) before the release, or run the release in the dB domain, as in Giannoulis' smooth decoupled log-domain detector. Test: the kick +9 dB render above, asserting that the residual y - x·g_15Hz falls below -40 dB re output with hold and release fixed (today -27.6 dB).

**Verifier notes.**
- Code lens: confirmed. setReleaseMs (139-144) computes one fixed coefficient; the zero-look-ahead path (246-251) is instant attack plus a linear-gain one-pole release; the detector (193-215) is the raw 4x-oversampled max with no smoothing; no hold, no second time constant. Membrum keeps the defaults (processor.cpp:1087-1088, processBlock at 717). The "program-dependent" comment is wrong; the ripple mechanism fits the code (an 80 ms one-pole recovers ~20 % of the deficit per 20 ms kick period). Probe not re-run; low is right.
- Research lens: confirmed. Faust limiter_lad (sources.debian.org) is quoted correctly: fluctuations above ~15 Hz are timbral, and a hold equal to the lowest expected period minimises LF distortion. Giannoulis could not be fetched (archive blocked, QMUL SSL error) and is not relied on. "Physics" is a misnomer (limiter design), but the false comment and undocumented in-cycle ripple stand; the header (17-18) acknowledges only the attack trade-off.
- Context/impact lens: refutes as a behaviour defect. The header (4-18) defines a zero-latency brickwall with "a smoothed release"; AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:417-423, 392, 403 record it as the bus safety ceiling with look-ahead rejected (W1), so compressor-smoothing literature does not describe a defect here. The finding concedes inaudibility in ordinary playing, and the -27.6 dB residual needs +9 dB of overdrive. Remaining: the "program-dependent recovery" comment at line 50 is a nit.

#### MB-247 — Physics (contradicted): (m,n) group assignments of the bell partials (nodal meridians per partial)

**Severity:** low · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-contradicted · **Dimension:** research:extra:bell-partials-hibberts

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/bell_modes.h:35-40, 68-76](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/bodies/bell_modes.h#L35)

**Problem.** kBellIndices = {(2,0) hum, (2,1) prime, (3,1) tierce, (3,1) quint, (4,1) nominal, (4,1) for ratio 1.5, (5,1) for 2.0, (5,1) for 2.6, (6,1) for 3.2, (6,2) for 4.0, (7,2), (7,2), (8,2), (8,2), (9,2), (9,3)}. m is used only in the |cos(m*theta)| strike factor, and n only in the taper 1/(1+0.12n).

**Why wrong.** The principal five are correct in m: hum (2,0) and prime (2,1#) both have m = 2, i.e. 4 nodal meridian lines (Hibberts lists 4 lines for each). Tierce (3,1) and quint (3,1#) have m = 3 (6 lines), nominal (4,1) has m = 4 (8 lines). The hum and prime are NOT wrong. Above the nominal the labels are off by one to three meridians. The partial at 1.5 x nominal is the twelfth/superquint (5,1), coded m = 4. The 2.0 partial is the octave nominal (6,1), coded m = 5. 2.6 is (7,1), coded (5,1). 3.2 is (8,1), coded (6,1). 4.0 is (9,1), coded (6,2). The coded n is also wrong: the rim partials all have n = 1 (Hibbert 2014 labels them by m only). The prime and quint are "#" modes (their nodal circle is in the waist, at 0.30 and 0.19 of the lip-to-shoulder distance), which the coded n = 1 cannot express.

Sources (evidence quality strong):
- Hibberts, "Identifying bell partials" (nodal-line census of the Perrin, Charnley & DePont bell) [docs] <https://www.hibberts.co.uk/identifying-bell-partials/>: nodal meridian lines: hum 4, prime 4 (group II, nodal circle at 0.30), tierce 6 (circle 0.54), quint 6 (circle 0.19), nominal 8 (0.54), superquint 10 (0.54, 1.00), octave nominal 12 (0.28, 0.98), I-7 14, I-8 16.
- Fletcher & Rossing (2008) p. 682 via Wikipedia "Strike tone" [textbook] <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_tone>: mode labels: (2,0) hum, (2,1#) prime, (3,1) tierce, (3,1#) quint, (4,1) nominal, (4,1#) deciem, (2,2) undeciem, (5,1) twelfth, (6,1) upper octave, (7,1), (8,1), (9,1).

**Consequence.** The labels only feed the azimuth comb (see the next claim). With them, the comb puts the nulls of the upper partials at the wrong knob positions. If the azimuth weighting is removed, the labels become inert documentation errors.

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: the m/n table did not exist at the 2026-06 audit. It was added by commit d9cd848b (#248, "audit §3-B") in response to research entry #13. Its header already admits the assignments above the principal five are approximate. This claim quantifies the error.

**Suggested fix.** Relabel each entry with its real (m, n, sharp) mode, e.g. a struct {m, n, bool waistCircle}, so that a strike-height model can use the nodal-circle positions. Add a test asserting that kBellIndices[k].m equals the published m for the table's partial names.

**Verifier notes.**
- Code lens: not refuted; the table is live. bell_modes.h:72-76 matches; ratios at 56-60 put indices 5-9 at 1.5, 2.0, 2.6, 3.2, 4.0 (coded {4,1}, {5,1}, {5,1}, {6,1}, {6,2}); computeBellAmplitude (89-101) uses m in |cos(m*theta)| and n in the taper; bell_mapper.h:43-47 applies it per mode with a 0.05 floor, so the labels change the sound whenever Strike Position moves on a Bell. Standard labels put the twelfth at (5,1) and the upper octave at (6,1), so the code is one meridian off above the nominal. The header note (35-40) admits but does not fix it. Low is right; the n taper is mild (1/1.12 to 1/1.36).
- Research lens: confirmed from both sources. Hibberts (fetched) gives superquint 10, octave nominal 12, I7 14, I8 16 meridian lines; the "Strike tone" table (fetched) gives (5,1) 3.011, (6,1) 4.166, (7,1) 5.433, (8,1) 6.796, (9,1) 8.215 relative to the prime (÷2 → 1.5, ~2.0, ~2.67, ~3.33, ~4.0 of nominal). Published m above the nominal: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 against coded 4, 5, 5, 6, 6. The header's justification that "Hibberts' data resolves the partial FREQUENCIES, not a full (m,n) census" is factually wrong, since Hibberts publishes the meridian counts. The n = 2 labels from the 4.0 entry onward also disagree.
- Context/impact lens: refutes as a defect. The approximation is documented (bell_modes.h:35-40, 68-71) and accepted by the prior remediation (AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:76). In a real axisymmetric bell each (m,n) mode is a degenerate cos/sin pair, so the knob-to-azimuth comb (theta = strikePos*pi/2, line 96) has no physical meaning to restore; correct m values would only move the dips elsewhere, never to full nulls (0.05 floor, bell_mapper.h:46). Setting n = 1 changes entries 9-14 by 0.9 dB and entry 15 by 1.7 dB, on fast-decaying high partials, and bell-pad presets tuned Strike Position by ear against this table (preset-retune/recipes.json, e.g. lines 4267, 8779, 11657).

#### MB-248 — Physics (oversimplified): Contact time follows Hertzian scaling T ~ m^(2/5) k^(-2/5) v^(-1/5)

**Severity:** medium (final: low) · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-oversimplified · **Dimension:** research:extra:hertz-contact-time

**Location:** [dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/impact_exciter.h:119-143](dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/impact_exciter.h#L119)

**Problem.** Comment: "Pulse duration from mass (Hertzian scaling)". Code: T = 0.0005 + 0.0145*pow(mass,0.4), then T *= pow(max(1-velocity,0.01),0.2). Hardness enters only gamma (peakiness), skew and the SVF cutoff, never T. The mass exponent 0.4 is Hertzian. The velocity factor is a function of (1 - MIDI velocity), not of impact speed. The 0.5 ms additive floor breaks the power law. Code ratios: T(v=1)/T(v=0.5) = 0.457 and T(v=1)/T(v=0.1) = 0.407, against 0.871 and 0.631 for a Hertz v^-0.2 law with speed proportional to velocity. Most of the change happens in the top 10 % of the range: 5.97 ms at v=0.9 and 3.77 ms at v=1.0, because d/dv (1-v)^0.2 diverges at v=1.

**Why wrong.** Hertz elastic impact: Te = 2.8683 (M^2/(R V E*^2))^(1/5), so T ~ M^(2/5) V^(-1/5) E*^(-2/5) (He & Wettlaufer 2014, eq. 1a). For a general power-law contact F = k x^alpha (Avanzini & Rocchesso), t0 ~ (m/k)^(1/(alpha+1)) * v^((1-alpha)/(1+alpha)), which gives m^0.4 k^-0.4 v^-0.2 for alpha = 1.5. The dependence on velocity is very weak. On a drumhead the measured shortening with dynamic level is larger than Hertz alone predicts, because of membrane reflections and tension (Wagner: about 7 to 4.5-5 ms at the centre, ratio about 0.65, spread smoothly over the crescendo). Stiffer mallets (larger k) shorten T. The code gets the mass exponent right, has no stiffness dependence, and its velocity law has a much steeper and singular shape at the top of the range.

Sources (evidence quality strong):
- A. He & J. S. Wettlaufer, "Hertz beyond belief", Soft Matter 10, 2014 (arXiv:1306.4952) [paper] <https://arxiv.org/pdf/1306.4952>: Eq. (1a): Te = 2.8683 (M^2 / (R V E^2))^(1/5); "both the collision time and maximum contact area have a very weak dependence on the impact velocity".
- F. Avanzini & D. Rocchesso, SMC 2004 [paper] <https://avanzini.di.unimi.it/downloads/publications/avanzini_smc04_finalsub.pdf>: Eq. (12): t0 depends only on the dissipation, alpha and m/k, plus vin; "the power-law dependence t0 ~ (m/k)^(1/(alpha+1)) holds"; the centroid is strongly correlated with the contact time.
- A. Wagner, KTH MSc thesis, 2006 [thesis] <https://www.speech.kth.se/publications/masterprojects/2006/AndreasWagner.pdf>: Fig. 4.7: contact time falls gradually over an 8-stroke piano-to-forte crescendo, about 7 to about 4.5-6 ms at the centre.

**Consequence.** Velocity to brightness is flat for most of the range, then jumps at the top. Between v = 0.9 and 1.0 (MIDI 115 to 127) the Mallet pulse goes from FWHM 2.63 to 1.60 ms, the -3 dB corner from 135 to 217 Hz and the first null from 745 to 1753 Hz. Below v = 0.8 the contact hardly changes (8.8 to 6.9 ms). Drummers playing ghost notes to accents hear little contact change until the top velocity layer, which flattens velocity-to-timbre dynamics. Because T has no stiffness term, Mallet and Impulse cannot differ in contact length at the same velocity.

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: the June audit (findings.json impact-exciter research entry) noted that T is "a direct lerp, not derived from any force-compression law" with the sign of the velocity effect correct, and ruled "nuanced". This entry adds the measured magnitude and shape mismatch and the missing stiffness term. impact_exciter.h lines 131-139 are unchanged since 2026-03 (git log: b9b7445b; later commits only #293 tidy), so the finding is still present.

**Suggested fix.** Replace the velocity factor with a power law of impact speed, and add stiffness: T = T0 * (mass/0.3)^0.4 * (kRel)^-0.4 * (u/u_ref)^-0.2 * g_mem(v). Here u = 0.1 + 0.9v maps MIDI velocity to speed, kRel = 2^(4*(effH-0.5)) maps hardness to relative stiffness, and g_mem is a smooth membrane term calibrated so the centre-strike pp-to-ff ratio is about 0.6 (Wagner). Pin it with a DSP unit test on ImpactExciter (a T accessor or a rendered-FWHM measurement): T monotonic in v; T(1)/T(0.5) in [0.6, 0.9]; max over v of |dT/dv| / T below 1.5 (no top-end cliff); T decreasing in hardness at fixed v and mass; T ~ mass^0.4 within 5 % over mass 0.05..1 with the floor removed. ImpactExciter is shared with Innexus, so gate its consumers. The existing Mallet centroid-window and velocity-ratio tests (mallet_exciter.h:61-63, 71-76) must be re-baselined deliberately.

**Verifier notes.**
- Code lens: confirmed; downgrade. impact_exciter.h:131-139 is exactly as described; hardness (effectiveHardness, line 120) only sets gamma (123), skew (126), noise (157), SVF cutoff (165) and micro-bounce (194-217). Callers pass mass 0.3 (impulse_exciter.h:39; mallet_exciter.h:88-90 for size >= 0.5). Hand-recomputed: base 9.46 ms, 3.77 ms at v=1, 5.97 at 0.9, 6.86 at 0.8, ratios 0.457 / 0.407; the top-end cliff is real. But brightness is driven mostly by the SVF cutoff (500·24^effH × exp2(1.5·v), lines 165, 171; ~490 Hz to ~11 kHz for Mallet), so "flat velocity-to-brightness" is overstated; "Mallet and Impulse cannot differ" holds only for size >= 0.5.
- Research lens: core physics confirmed, severity down. He & Wettlaufer: collision time has "a very weak dependence on the impact velocity". Wagner (extracted): "3-6 ms of contact"; contact decreases with dynamic level (Fig. 4.7), and also with tension and distance from centre. Avanzini & Rocchesso PDF not decodable; the power-law form is standard. Felt-mallet models (Stulov/Hall) give stronger velocity dependence, but every published form is smooth in impact speed with a stiffness term, and none is singular at maximum velocity.
- Context/impact lens: refutes as a defect. The line is specified as a perceptual choice (specs/Innexus-physical-modelling-roadmap.md:644-648: "Subtle shortening at high velocity ... perceptually motivated"), and the June audit ruled it "a defensible perceptual emulation" (AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.findings.json:1209-1213). Velocity drives timbre through several continuous paths (Mallet hardness lerp, mallet_exciter.h:81; effectiveHardness +0.1v, impact_exciter.h:120; gamma and skew 123, 126; SVF ~680 Hz → ~13 kHz, 165, 171; amplitude v^0.6, 129); hardness narrows the sin^gamma pulse (FWHM ~0.67T → ~0.36T), so Impulse and Mallet do differ. Remaining point: the steepest change sits at the top of the velocity range.

#### MB-249 — Physics (oversimplified): The struck body's size sets the mallet contact time (D4 piecewise cubic mass scaling)

**Severity:** low · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-oversimplified · **Dimension:** research:extra:hertz-contact-time

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/src/dsp/exciters/mallet_exciter.h:51-67, 88-90](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/exciters/mallet_exciter.h#L51) (caller [plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h:336-340](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/drum_voice.h#L336))

**Problem.** DrumVoice passes the pad's normalized Size as a hint. mass = 0.3 * min(size/0.5, 1)^3, so sizes >= 0.5 keep the legacy 0.3 exactly. Measured T at v=0.5 / v=1.0: size 0.12 1.84 / 0.84 ms (FWHM 0.90 / 0.35 ms); size 0.25 3.83 / 1.75 ms; size 0.4 6.40 / 2.93 ms; size 0.5 8.23 / 3.77 ms. This is a documented, deliberate perceptual rule (D4, 06-orchestralKit-fix-plan.md; "Cubic, not quadratic" because the measured envelope carries an SVF and noise tail). It applies only to Mallet: Impulse keeps a fixed mass 0.3 (impulse_exciter.h:39) on any body. It ignores body type, Tension and Strike Position.

**Why wrong.** Physically, contact time is set by the mallet mass and the combined stiffness of mallet and struck object (Hertz: T ~ (m/k)^(2/5)). On a membrane the local compliance dominates: contact time drops from centre to rim and with higher head tension (Wagner Fig. 4.7: centre about 7 ms, rim 3-4.5 ms; Fig. 4.10: forte about 4.6 ms at low tension to 3.5 ms at high tension). Avanzini & Rocchesso found t0 rises with the compliance of the struck object. Using Size alone as a stiffness proxy is directionally right for membranes, since a larger head at equal tension is more compliant. It is ad hoc, though: the piecewise knee at 0.5 and the cubic law are tuned to a test window, not derived. It leaves out tension and strike position, the two variables measured to matter most, and it does not cover hard bodies (Plate, Bell) or the Impulse exciter.

Sources (evidence quality moderate):
- A. Wagner, KTH MSc thesis, 2006 [thesis] <https://www.speech.kth.se/publications/masterprojects/2006/AndreasWagner.pdf>: Fig. 4.7: contact time falls moving the strike from centre to rim; Fig. 4.10: "With increasing tension, shorter force pulses and an earlier arrival of the reflected wave cause decreasing contact times."
- F. Avanzini & D. Rocchesso, SMC 2004 [paper] <https://avanzini.di.unimi.it/downloads/publications/avanzini_smc04_finalsub.pdf>: t0 ~ (m/k)^(1/(alpha+1)); against a resonator, t0 exceeds the rigid prediction "due to the compliance of the struck object".

**Consequence.** Contact length does not follow Tension or Strike Position, so turning up head tension or striking near the rim does not sharpen the attack as a real drum does, and those parameters feel weaker than they should. Small metal pads on the Impulse exciter keep an 8 ms contact and sound duller than a stick on metal. A Mallet on a size-0.45 tom gets a contact 27 % shorter than on a size-0.5 tom (mass 0.219 vs 0.3), from a knee that is not physical.

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: not covered by the June audit: the D4 size hint was added after it (2026-07-17/18).

**Suggested fix.** Compute a struck-body stiffness proxy in DrumVoice: kRel = f(bodyType) * (1 + a*tensionNorm) * (1 + b*strikePos) / sizeScale. Pass it to both Impulse and Mallet (one setContactStiffness API on ExciterBank), and apply T ~ kRel^(-0.4) inside ImpactExciter. Keep size >= 0.5 Membrane at kRel = 1 so the tension-glide calibration noted at mallet_exciter.h:56-57 is preserved. Tests: at fixed velocity, FWHM decreases monotonically with tension and with strike position on Membrane; FWHM on Plate/Bell is below 2 ms for Impulse and Mallet at size <= 0.3; T at size 0.5 is byte-equal to today (extend test_mallet_contact_hint.cpp).

**Verifier notes.**
- Code lens: confirmed at low. mallet_exciter.h:64-67 clamps the hint, 88-89 compute the cubic mass, 90 triggers with strike position hard-coded to 0; drum_voice.h:340 is the only caller (size only); exciter_bank.h:174-179, 250-251 pass it to Mallet only; impulse_exciter.h:39 is fixed at 0.3. Numbers recomputed (8.23 / 3.77 ms; mass 0.219 at size 0.45). One overstatement: 27 % less mass gives only ~11 % less contact time (8.39 vs 9.46 ms), not 27 %.
- Research lens: confirmed at low with corrections. Wagner (extracted) says contact decreases toward the rim (Fig. 4.7, ~7 → ~4 ms) and with tension (Fig. 4.10, ~4.6 → ~3.5 ms), for the same system. But Membrum has no static head-tension parameter (kTensionModAmtId = 308 is the pitch-glide amount, plugin_ids.h:159), so the "turning up tension" consequence names the wrong control; Wagner notes the strike-position result contradicts Sánchez and Irwin; and part of his effect is the reflected wave, outside Membrum's feedforward exciter (MalletExciter::process calls core_.process(0.0f)). The knee is pinned by test_mallet_contact_hint.cpp:87-107.
- Context/impact lens: refutes. The rule is documented in mallet_exciter.h:51-63, 83-89, preset-retune/kits/06-orchestralKit-fix-plan.md:183, 299 (velocity-mapped mass rejected) and CHANGELOG.md:100-105. Static pitch comes from Size (f0 = 500*0.1^size, AUDIT-signal-path-2026-06-07.md:180), so Size already stands in for diameter and tension. Strike Position already does its main job (Bessel weighting, audit:314; Bell and shell, audit:76-77); extra contact shortening would only move the exciter low-pass, masked by the hardness SVF (impact_exciter.h:131-168) and the ClickLayer. Small metals are routed through Mallet with D4 on purpose; the curve is continuous at the knee (~12 % T change at 0.45).

#### MB-250 — Physics (contradicted): Mallet velocity mapping gives an 8 ms (soft) to 1 ms (hard) contact (header comment, spec FR-011 / spec 135)

**Severity:** low · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-contradicted · **Dimension:** research:extra:hertz-contact-time

**Location:** [plugins/membrum/src/dsp/exciters/mallet_exciter.h:10-18](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/exciters/mallet_exciter.h#L10) (comment) vs [81-90](plugins/membrum/src/dsp/exciters/mallet_exciter.h#L81) (code); [specs/135-membrum-drum-synth.md:127, 644-648](specs/135-membrum-drum-synth.md#L127)

**Problem.** The header comment says: hardness = lerp(0.05,0.45,v), mass = lerp(0.6,0.3,v) ("spec FR-011: 8 ms -> 1 ms"), brightness = lerp(-0.8,-0.1,v). The code does: hardness = lerp(0.1,0.6,v), brightness = lerp(-0.5,-0.2,v), mass = 0.3*t^3 with no velocity term. Actual range: T 9.26 ms (v=0.1) to 3.77 ms (v=1). Spec 135's table gives soft felt 5-8 ms and wood stick tip 1-3 ms, and the spec 137 data-model FR-011 asks for 8 -> 1 ms with alpha 1.5 -> 4.0. The code reaches neither 1 ms nor any alpha.

**Why wrong.** On a drumhead a 1-3 ms stick contact contradicts the measurements: about 3-7.5 ms (Wagner), 5-8 ms at mf (Dahl). Contact as short as about 1 ms belongs to hard targets such as bars and metal. The code's 3.8 ms ff floor is closer to the literature than its own comment and spec, so the stale comment and the spec table are the defects. The spec's turnover rule f ~ 1/(pi*tau) is a rough rule; for the coded pulses the measured -3 dB corner is 0.66/T to 0.82/T.

Sources (evidence quality strong):
- A. Wagner, KTH MSc thesis, 2006 [thesis] <https://www.speech.kth.se/publications/masterprojects/2006/AndreasWagner.pdf>: contact between drumstick and membrane lasts 3-6 ms (abstract); the forte minimum is about 3 ms at the rim (Fig. 4.7).
- S. Dahl, Acoust. Sci. & Tech. 32(5), 2011 [paper] <https://vbn.aau.dk/ws/files/65339564/Dahl_J_AST_review_submi.pdf>: typical drumstick-drumhead contact durations are 5-8 ms for a mezzoforte stroke.

**Consequence.** No audible defect: the code is more realistic than the comment. The stale comment and spec mislead a later retune. Someone "fixing" the code to the spec's 1 ms on drums would make mallet toms clicky and unnatural, and the comment misstates which knobs exist (there is no velocity-mapped mass).

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: none.

**Suggested fix.** Rewrite mallet_exciter.h:10-18 to the real mapping (hardness 0.1..0.6, brightness -0.5..-0.2, mass 0.3*min(size/0.5,1)^3, T about 9.3 to 3.8 ms over velocity at size >= 0.5). Correct the spec 135 table at lines 644-648 to cite drumhead contact times of 3-8 ms (Wagner 2006, Dahl 2011), keeping 0.5-2 ms for metal and bars. No test needed beyond the T-range pin proposed in the Hertzian-scaling entry (MB-248).

**Verifier notes.**
- Code lens: confirmed. Header 10-15 vs code 81 (hardness 0.1+0.5v), 82 (brightness -0.5+0.3v), 88-89 (mass 0.3*t^3, no velocity term; 61-63, 73-76 say velocity-mapped mass was tried and reverted); 25 says the core exposes no alpha. impact_exciter.h:132-139 gives 9.26 ms at v=0.1 and 3.77 ms at v=1 (±5 % jitter, 143). Spec 135:127, 646-648, specs/137 data-model.md:93 and contracts/exciter_contract.md:74 ask for 8 → 1 ms with alpha; tasks.md:138 T038 is done and spec.md:536 marks FR-011 MET though the code does neither. Small bodies reach ~1.3 ms via the cubic shrink (:58), so "never 1 ms" holds only at size >= 0.5. Low: documentation drift.
- Research lens: confirmed. The spec table under "Mallet-Membrane Interaction" cites Chaigne & Doutaut (bar percussion) and piano hammers (:656), so it applies bar/hammer contact times to a membrane. Dahl ("5–8 ms for a mezzoforte stroke") and Wagner ("3–6 ms") put drumhead contact at ~3-8 ms; quotes taken from search-tool excerpts of those documents (no PDF tool available).
- Context/impact lens: refutes as physics. The departure from FR-011 is deliberate and documented in the same file (mallet_exciter.h:61-63 velocity-mapped mass reverted because it broke the US1-2 tests; 71-80; D4 at 51-60). The code agrees with the cited literature, and correcting the comment or spec changes no sample: a documentation / stale-comment nit.

#### MB-251 — Physics (contradicted): The noise component of the impact pulse is 'pinked' by a one-pole filter

**Severity:** low · **Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE · **Category:** physics-contradicted · **Dimension:** research:extra:hertz-contact-time

**Location:** [dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/impact_exciter.h:244-250](dsp/include/krate/dsp/processors/impact_exciter.h#L244)

**Problem.** Comment: "One-pole pinking: pink = white - 0.9 * prev". Code: pink = white - 0.9f*pinkState_; pinkState_ = pink, that is y[n] = x[n] - 0.9 y[n-1]. Its pole is at z = -0.9. |H| = 0.526 at DC (-5.6 dB), about 0.53 at 1 kHz, 0.56 at 5 kHz, 0.66 at 10 kHz, 0.94 at 15 kHz, 2.0 at 20 kHz and 10 (+20 dB) at Nyquist (48 kHz): a high-frequency boost of up to +25.6 dB relative to DC. The noise rides the pulse envelope at noiseLevel = lerp(0.25,0.08,effH), not scaled by amplitude_.

**Why wrong.** With a1 = +0.9 the one-pole y(n) = x(n) - a1 y(n-1) has its pole at z = -a1 = -0.9, which is a highpass, not a pinking (lowpass, -3 dB/oct) filter. A one-pole lowpass approximation would be y[n] = x[n] + 0.9 y[n-1] (pole at +0.9). A true pink filter uses a multi-pole Kellet or Voss design. The physical model calls for contact noise that is broadband or low-tilted, following the force pulse.

Sources (evidence quality moderate):
- J. O. Smith III, "Introduction to Digital Filters", CCRMA online book, One-Pole section [textbook] <https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/fp/One_Pole.html>: "The filter has a pole at z = -a_1"; "the lowpass character occurs when the pole is near the point z = 1 (dc), which happens when a_1 approaches -1"; "the highpass nature occurs when a_1 is positive."

**Consequence.** Below about 10 kHz the noise is close to white, so the attack noise sounds about as intended. Above 15 kHz it is boosted 5-25 dB before the SVF. For Mallet at v=1 the cutoff is about 11.4 kHz, so the 15-22 kHz noise comes out near or above its DC level. For Impulse at high velocity the cutoff is clamped near Nyquist (about 23.8 kHz at 48 kHz), so a near-Nyquist hiss spike reaches the body bank and the energy cap. That spike is mostly inaudible but counts toward the energy cap and any peak-based strike normalisation, slightly lowering the useful pulse. The effect depends on sample rate: at 96 kHz the boost moves out of band. ImpactExciter is shared with Innexus.

**Evidence.** Prior audit ruling: not reported by the June audit or by docs/correctness-audit.md (no mention of the pinking filter). Code unchanged since commit b9b7445b (2026-03).

**Suggested fix.** Change the recursion to pink = white + 0.9f*pinkState_ (with a (1-0.9) gain trim to keep the low-frequency level), or a proper 3-pole pink filter, and correct the comment. Pin it with a DSP test: drive ImpactExciter with hardness 1 and noise only (or expose the noise shaper), average the spectrum over many triggers, and assert the 16-20 kHz band level <= the 1-2 kHz band level. Gate Innexus consumers (node tools/header-consumers.js).

**Verifier notes.**
- Code lens: confirmed. impact_exciter.h:246-248 is H(z) = 1/(1 + 0.9 z^-1), a highpass; magnitudes at fs = 48 kHz verified (0.526 DC … 10 at Nyquist, +25.6 dB). "Nyquist (48 kHz)" is a labelling slip (Nyquist is 24 kHz). State reset per trigger (160), noise level lerp(0.25, 0.08, h) at 157 times pulseEnvelope only (250), added before the SVF (285), comb and energy cap (297-301); the SVF cutoff clamps at 0.495*fs (174-175). Live in Membrum (impulse_exciter.h:14, 39, 54; mallet_exciter.h:32) and Innexus (innexus_voice.h:25, 52). No test covers the noise tilt (impact_exciter_test.cpp). Low fits.
- Research lens: confirmed. J. O. Smith's One_Pole page quoted correctly; a_1 = +0.9 is a highpass by plain filter theory. Not intentional per the archived spec: specs/_archive_/128-impact-exciter/spec.md:113 says b = 0.9f "gives noticeable HF rolloff", and FR-010 (:136) plus specs/Innexus-physical-modelling-roadmap.md:600-603 say it "models felt's inherent high-frequency absorption", so the formula does the opposite of its stated purpose.
